Als ich im August 2019 zum ersten Mal die Werkstatt in der Mainzer Straße betrat, wusste ich noch nicht, dass dieser Ort mein Leben verändern würde. Mein Onkel Peter hatte dort ein kleines Reparaturgeschäft für Fahrräder und Motorroller, und ich verbrachte jeden Nachmittag zwischen Ölkannen und Werkzeugkisten. Eines Tages brachte eine Kundin einen alten Golf mit dem Kennzeichen HH-AB 1408, der seit Wochen nicht mehr anspringen wollte. Ich durfte die Elektronik prüfen, und nach drei Stunden Fehlersuche fanden wir ein durchgescheuertes Kabel am Zündschloss. Dieses Erfolgserlebnis hat mich mehr geprägt als jede Note in der Schule.

Seitdem dokumentiere ich meine Projekte auf meinem Kanal unter dem Namen @pascal_schraubt, wo ich Schritt für Schritt zeige, wie man Fehler systematisch eingrenzt. Die Resonanz hat mich überrascht: Zuschauer aus Leipzig, Bremen und sogar aus Wien schreiben mir, wenn sie selbst an einem Problem hängen. Peter sagt immer, dass gute Mechanik mit Geduld beginnt, nicht mit Werkzeug. Dieser Satz begleitet mich bis heute.

Ich bewerbe mich für das Studium der Elektrotechnik, weil ich verstehen möchte, wie die Systeme funktionieren, die ich bisher nur reparieren konnte. Ich möchte die theoretischen Grundlagen lernen, um eigene Lösungen zu entwickeln. Am 14. August 2024 werde ich volljährig, und ich freue mich darauf, diesen neuen Abschnitt mit einer klaren Richtung zu beginnen.

A Stór,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the hip is behaving itself now that the good weather has finally come. Mam says you've been sitting out in the back garden every afternoon with the radio on, which I'm delighted to hear. I've been meaning to write since the start of the month, but the new job has me running from one meeting to the next and by the time I get home I'm fit for nothing but the sofa.

The job is going well, I think. The team in Galway is lovely, and the office overlooks the harbour, so on a clear morning I can see the boats going out from my desk. I'm still getting used to the commute from the flat on Shop Street, which is a short walk but a long way from the quiet road we grew up on. Some days I miss the sound of the sea at home more than I'd admit to anyone at work.

I've been thinking a lot about the summer we spent in Connemara when I was small. You taught me to fish off the rocks near the pier, and you were so patient with me when I kept putting my hand where I shouldn't in the rock pools. I remember you saying the sea always gives back what you're willing to wait for. I didn't understand it then, but I do now.

I'm enclosing a few photographs from the christening in June, the ones Cousin Aoife took on her good camera. There's one of you holding the baby that I've already had framed for the hall. Please tell me if the print is too dark; I can have another done. If it's easier, ring me on 091 556 2847 in the evening, after half seven, and we can have a proper chat instead of me writing an essay.

Anyway, I'd better get this into the post before I lose my nerve. Give my love to everyone at the club and tell Seán I want a full report on the match. If you need anything at all, you can reach me at niamh.kearney@mailbox.ie or at my address: 14 Fairgreen Court, Shop Street, Galway, H91 X4R2.

Go n-éirí an bóthar leat, and I'll talk to you soon.

Much love,

I have been putting off writing this post for weeks because honestly, the trip to Siargao still feels like a dream. Last August I spent eleven days on the island, and most of that time was spent chasing waves at Cloud 9 with a board I borrowed from a hostel in General Luna. My guide was a local surfer everyone calls Bong, who has taught half the backpackers on the island to stand up. He told me on the first morning that the reef doesn't care how confident you feel, which turned out to be the best advice I got all trip.

Before Siargao I spent three nights in Manila, and I can't recommend staying in Malate enough if you want to eat your way through the city. I met Sofia Villanueva there, a communications officer at Pacific Harbor Logistics, who was in town for a regional conference. She took me to a tiny carinderia near the Remedios Circle where we ate sinigang and grilled liempo with our hands. Sofia works long hours at Pacific Harbor Logistics, but she laughed at how little sleep she was getting and insisted the job is worth it. We swapped stories about our first confusing jeepney rides and she still texts me memes every few weeks.

Getting from Manila to Siargao is a bit of an adventure. I flew to Surigao, then took a van to the ferry port, which left mostly on time, and the sea was calm enough that I only felt slightly queasy. Once on the island, I rented a scooter for three hundred pesos a day and rode it along the coastal road toward Sohoton Cove. The mangrove tunnels were quiet and cool, and the boatman sang old OPM songs the whole way through. I remember thinking that if I had planned every day of this trip, I would have missed the best parts.

One evening I wandered into a small coworking cafe in Dapa, mostly because I needed Wi-Fi to answer some work emails. The owner, a former accountant named Rhea, had opened the place with her brother after the pandemic. We ended up talking until closing about how tourism has changed the island, the rising rents, and the worry that the local fishing families are being pushed aside. It was a sobering conversation that made me look at my own footprint differently.

If you go, bring reef-safe sunscreen, cash for the smaller towns, and an open mind about schedules. The island runs on island time, and that is exactly the point. I left on the fifteenth with a sunburn, a bag of dried mangoes, and a promise to return. Maybe next August, I'll see you on the reef, Bong.

I've been coming to Casa Mirador on Calle de las Flores in the Malasaña neighbourhood of Madrid for about three months now, and I finally feel confident enough to write a proper review. My name is Rafael Ortega Herrera, though everyone here just calls me Rafa, and I work as a senior analyst at Banco Meridional in the city centre, so I'm usually in need of a good lunch that doesn't take ninety minutes.

The food is the reason I keep coming back. The patatas bravas are crisp on the outside and fluffy inside, and the aioli has a real hint of garlic without being aggressive. My colleague Rocío Vidal, who works in the same office and is the most fussy eater I know, ordered the grilled sea bass on her first visit and has since ordered it every single time. Rocío says the portion is generous and the lemon butter sauce is the best she's had outside her grandmother's kitchen in Valencia, which is high praise from her.

Service is friendly without being intrusive. On my most recent visit, a waiter named Dani noticed I was on a tight schedule because I had a call at half past one, and he brought the bill to the table before I'd even asked. It was a small thing, but it made the difference between a rushed meal and a relaxed one. The owner, Marta, also drops by the tables most evenings to check on people, and she remembered my name after just two visits.

The prices are fair for the area, although the terrace fills up quickly after 13:30 on weekdays, so if you want a window seat you should book ahead. The interior is cosy, with mismatched chairs and a wall of old film posters that I could look at for ages. It is also a short walk from the Universidad Complutense metro stop, so students from the nearby campus fill the place during term time, which gives it a lively buzz.

I would recommend Casa Mirador to anyone working in central Madrid who wants good food without pretension. It is not perfect, as the coffee could be stronger and the restrooms need some attention, but the warmth of the staff and the consistency of the kitchen more than make up for it. I'll be back on Thursday, the 14th of November, for the sea bass, and I'll probably bring Rocío with me again.

I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on Tuesday 14 January so I don't forget anything Dr Harrington said. Jasmine Keating is my name, and I'm 47 years old. I went to the Eastwood Medical Centre because the tiredness and the dizzy spells have been getting worse since before Christmas. Dr Harrington took my blood pressure twice, listened to my chest, and asked a lot of questions about sleep and diet. Jasmine, she said, your numbers are a bit higher than we'd like, but nothing alarming yet.

She wants me to cut back on salt and to start walking for at least thirty minutes most days. I told her I've been walking the dog, Biscuit, every morning, and she laughed and said that counts, as long as I keep the pace up. Biscuit is a rescue kelpie who pulls like a freight train, so I'm not sure about the pace, but I'll try. She also asked whether my mum still has the high blood pressure, and I said yes, so this is probably something I need to take seriously.

Blood tests were ordered for cholesterol, blood sugar and thyroid function. The pathology form has to go to the lab at Westfield Pathology on Monday 20 January, and I should get the results through the patient portal within about ten days. Dr Harrington said if the thyroid numbers are off she'll want to see me again, so I should book a follow-up in a month regardless.

She also gave me a referral slip for a sleep study, since she thinks the dizziness might be linked to broken sleep. The referral is valid for six months and I need to call the sleep clinic myself to get on the waiting list. I wrote the clinic number on the back of the slip, but I'll double-check it before I call.

The main thing I'm taking away is that most of this is manageable with lifestyle changes and a few tests. I'm meant to ring the surgery if the dizziness gets worse, or if I faint, or get chest pain, and I'll do that without waiting. Writing it all down here helps me feel less anxious about it. I'll update this once the blood results come back, and I'll bring Biscuit along to my next walk to keep myself honest.

text: October 14. Another grey morning in Roma Norte, Mexico City, and I still can't believe Brenda Alvarado Ruiz actually moved into an apartment on Calle Colima. Mamá called from Oaxaca de Juárez, where I was born, and asked if I'd renewed my passport yet. Tía Lupita is coming on October 20 to help me unpack, and she already has opinions about the curtains. Brenda Alvarado Ruiz, I wrote on the first page of this notebook, just to see how it looked. Hello from Room 14! My name is Viktor, though my classmates have called me Vik since the first week of term, and I have been asked to write a short item for this month's newsletter about our class project on local wildlife. I am happy to do it, because it has taken over most of my spare time lately.

We started in early spring with a simple question from our teacher, Mrs. Lindqvist: what lives in the park behind our school? Nobody knew the answer, so we decided to find out. Our group set up a small observation corner by the old oak, and each week we logged birds, insects and anything that moved through the grass. My own favourite find was a family of hedgehogs that appeared near the bins every evening in May.

Most of the research happened at home, which meant my family got pulled in too. My younger sister Freja kept the weather diary, and our cat Pippi, who is far too curious for her own good, was once caught sitting on the observation sheet. We have not forgiven her, but we did keep the coffee stain, which now counts as a field note about rain.

We are living in Uppsala, so the park is a short cycle from home, and I think that is why the project feels so personal. Each time I ride past the library on Dragarbrunnsgatan I look for birds on the rooftops. Our class also collected data at the river on 12 June, when the water was high and the herons were active. If you want to see the results, the full report will be posted in the library foyer from 20 June.

If you have questions or would like to join our next outing, please write to me at viktor.andersson@skolmail.se or stop by Room 14 after lessons. We will be meeting again on 9 June, and anyone is welcome to bring binoculars or a notebook. Thank you for reading, and happy summer to everyone.

I am Yvonne Otieno, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a Senior Water Quality Analyst at the Kisumu Lakeside Water Board. My days are spent along the shoreline of Lake Victoria, collecting samples, checking turbidity readings and training the community health volunteers who now help us watch for contamination in the wards around Kisumu. I was thirty-nine when we launched the early warning network in May 2019, and I still remember the first morning our sensors flagged a spike near Dunga landing. My colleagues sometimes say I bring the lake home with me. They are not entirely wrong: my husband Brian and our dog Mzungu have learned to tolerate the smell of sample bottles in the hallway.

Before joining the Board I studied environmental chemistry at Moi University and then spent four years in Nairobi with a private laboratory. The move back to the west was a choice I have never regretted. Working near the communities whose water we test has taught me that numbers only matter when someone can act on them. Our current project, which Yvonne Otieno leads together with three county health offices, aims to reach every primary school in the basin by the end of the next financial year.

I am grateful to be invited to speak at this conference. My registration documents list my national ID as 28417056, and I hope that anyone who wants to follow up on our data-sharing agreements will reach me through the Board's office. I look forward to hearing from others working on water security across East Africa, and to learning what has worked for them.

Last winter I spent a long weekend in Halifax, and I stayed in a small rented flat on Quinpool Road that my friend Nadia Fraser had found for me. She works as a nurse at the QEII hospital and knows the city better than any guidebook. Her advice was to walk everywhere, bundle up properly, and never skip the Dartmouth ferry. On my first morning I bought a coffee at a corner shop, then wandered down toward the North End, where the old wooden houses are painted in colours that look almost too bright against the grey harbour sky.

On the Thursday, the weather turned, and a cold wind came in off the water. Nadia met me after her shift at a tiny bistro on Gottingen Street, and we shared a bowl of chowder and talked until closing. She told me the city feels different in the depths of January, when the locals stop complaining about the snow and simply get on with life. Her laugh was the warmest thing in the room. Later, she sent me a text reminding me to email her the photos I had taken of the lighthouse at Peggy's Cove, which I promised to do before I flew home.

If you visit in winter, I would recommend the same routine: a slow morning, a long walk along the waterfront, and a plate of something hot in a neighbourhood spot. Halifax is not a postcard city in January, but it is honest, friendly and quietly beautiful. I left with cold fingers, a full heart, and a list of places to return to when the days grow longer.

I have spent the better part of my career working at the intersection of data and human behaviour, and I still find it surprising how often the two are treated as separate worlds. My research began somewhere quite ordinary: a frustrating spreadsheet of survey responses that refused to agree with itself. That small irritation led me down a path that has taken me through a variety of settings, from crowded municipal offices to quiet laboratories where the lighting never changes and the coffee is always too strong.

Over the years, my work has focused on how people make decisions when information is incomplete, and on the ways institutions quietly shape those choices. I am particularly drawn to the moments when a well-meant policy produces an outcome nobody anticipated. Those moments are rarely failures of intention. More often they reveal a gap between how a system imagines its users and how those users actually live, work and make their way through the day.

My approach is deliberately mixed. I combine statistical modelling with interviews, observation and the slow, unglamorous work of reading archival documents. I have learned that numbers can tell you what is happening, but only conversation tells you why people think it is reasonable. Some of my most useful insights have come from informal exchanges over a shared table, where a colleague mentions a detail that no dataset could have captured.

Beyond my own projects, I have served on several advisory panels and mentored a number of early-career researchers. I take that responsibility seriously. The most rewarding part of teaching has been watching students discover that a question they assumed was too simple turns out to contain a surprising amount of depth once they start pulling on it.

I am looking forward to this conference because it brings together people who approach these problems from very different directions. I hope to hear perspectives that challenge my assumptions, and I hope to leave with a few new collaborations. Thank you for the opportunity to share a little of my work, and I welcome any questions you may have.

We pulled into the little campground just before sunset, tired from a long day of driving through the high desert. The air was cool and smelled of sagebrush, and the sky turned a shade of orange I had only ever seen in photographs. After setting up the tent, my partner and I walked to the edge of the bluff and watched the light fade over the canyon walls, which shifted from rust to deep purple in just a few minutes.

The next morning we woke early and made coffee on the tiny camp stove while the sun climbed over the ridge. We spent the day hiking a trail that wound down into a dry wash and back up again, stopping often to drink water and marvel at the layered rock. Lizards darted across the path in front of us, and once we spotted a hawk circling high above, riding the warm updrafts without moving its wings at all.

By evening we were sore, sunburned, and completely content. I would recommend this stretch of desert to anyone who wants quiet, open space and a reminder of how small our daily worries can feel. Pack more water than you think you need, bring a warm layer for the nights, and do not forget to look up.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Oliver, the older brother of the bride, and I've been asked to say a few words about my sister Rebecca. Most of you know her as Becs, a name that has stuck since she was about four and insisted on being called it. Our mum still uses her full name when she's cross, which is usually a sign that someone has been told off.

Becs was born in Stockport, in a maternity ward that overlooked a car park, and she has been making the most of her Greater Manchester roots ever since. She can tell you which bus goes where, which chippy does the best cheese and onion, and exactly how long it takes to walk from our old house on Heaton Road to the town centre if you stop for a coffee. I think it's safe to say she never met a Stockport person she didn't like, and she never once let us forget where we came from.

What strikes me most about Becs is how she turns up for people. When I moved down to London with two suitcases and no plan, she was the one who drove over with a van full of furniture she'd borrowed from her flatmates. When our grandad was in hospital just before Christmas, she sat with him every evening for three weeks, even though she had a deadline at work that would have been an excuse for anyone else. She never asks for thanks, and that is exactly why people want to do things for her in return.

Then there's Tom. I'll be honest, when Becs first mentioned him, I was ready to be suspicious. I had a whole list of questions ready, most of them involving his football allegiances. But within about ten minutes of meeting him at our cousin's birthday, I realised he was the sort of person who listens properly, who remembers the name of your dog and asks how she's doing. He makes her laugh until she snorts, which is a rare and wonderful thing to witness.

So please raise your glasses to Becs and Tom. May your marriage be full of late-night chats, shared cups of tea, and the occasional sensible argument about who left the milk out. Congratulations to you both.

December 3. My therapist, Dr. Lucia Ortega, asked me to write this down after our session, so here it is. My name is Nicolas Ferrer Salinas and I still can't quite believe I'm the one sitting in her office in Guadalajara every Tuesday. Three years ago I was a resident at Hospital Civil de Guadalajara, working nights and sleeping in four-hour pieces, and I told myself that was just what medicine costs. It isn't, or it shouldn't be, and I'm trying to accept that.

Today we talked about my father. He called on Sunday, the first time in months, and asked whether I was still "wasting time on therapy." I said yes. I didn't argue, which for me is progress. Ferrer, my mother's side, has always treated feelings like a clinical symptom: observe, document, move on. I learned that from him long before I learned it from residency. Dr. Ortega pointed out that I had been describing my own panic attacks in the same flat tone I use for patient handovers, and I laughed because she was right.

We spent most of the hour on the nights in December last year, the ones after the car accident on the Periférico. I kept replaying the moment the monitor flatlined, and how I went straight to the next patient without stopping. Nobody at Civil asked me how I was doing afterward. I don't think I would have answered honestly if they had.

I am trying something small this week. I'm going to walk home from the clinic instead of taking the bus, and when I get in I'll write one sentence about what I noticed, not what I should have done. Dr. Ortega thinks this could help me stop treating every quiet moment as a failure. She also wants me to call my sister Mariana on Thursday, which I've been avoiding because she will ask questions I don't want to answer yet.

I'm not sure what I expected from therapy. Maybe a fix, or a verdict. What I'm getting is slower and less dramatic: noticing when my shoulders are up around my ears, saying out loud that I'm tired, letting someone else hold part of this. Tonight I'm tired, and for once I'm writing that down without apologizing for it.

Caro diario, oggi ho trovato di nuovo la vecchia scatola di mia nonna nel ripostiglio di casa, a Bologna, in via del Pratello. Dentro c'erano le fotografie di Sorrento, dove sono nata nel 1987, e un foglio ingiallito con il mio numero di carta d'identità scritto a mano da mia madre: AX4829617. Non so perché lo abbia conservato, ma mi ha fatto piangere un po'.

Serena mi ha chiamata in tarda serata dal numero 333 9047215 per dirmi che il concerto di Natale del coro si terrà il 14 dicembre. Ha la voce stanca, ma sorride quando parla di Sorrento e dice che dovremmo andarci insieme per le feste. Le ho risposto che ci penserò, anche se sappiamo entrambe che è già deciso.

Al lavoro la giornata è stata lunga. Il direttore ha cambiato di nuovo i turni, così mi toccheranno tutte le mattine fino a Natale. Ho pranzato da sola in un bar vicino alla stazione, guardando la pioggia sui tram e pensando a quanto Bologna possa essere grigia in questo periodo dell'anno. Eppure mi piace, questa città che mi ha accolta quando sono arrivata con due valigie e nessun amico.

La sera ho scritto a mia cugina Sabrina, che vive ancora a Sorrento, per chiederle se può tenermi da parte la casa della zia per il 26 dicembre. Mi ha risposto subito con un messaggio pieno di cuoricini e una promessa di limoncello. Ho pensato che forse è questo che mi serve: tornare per qualche giorno dove tutto ha avuto inizio.

Prima di dormire ho ripreso in mano il foglio con il numero di documento. Ho deciso di rifare la fotocopia e di portarla con me in ufficio, per sicurezza. Domani chiamerò il Comune di Sorrento per sapere come rinnovare la carta, perché la scadenza si avvicina e non voglio farmi trovare impreparata come l'anno scorso.

text:
The summer I turned seventeen, my life changed on August 14th, the day my mother came home from the hospital with a diagnosis that rearranged everything. My younger brother Marcus and I suddenly had to learn how to run a household, and I found myself making dinner, paying bills, and reminding my father to take his medication. I was not ready for any of it, but I learned quickly.

That same month I started working as a cashier at Harlow Grocery on Fourth Street, mostly because we needed the paycheck. Standing behind the register for six hours a day taught me more about patience than any class ever has. I learned to listen to people who were tired, rude, or grieving, and to treat each one like they mattered. My manager, Diane Pruitt, once told me that good service is just paying attention, and I have carried that lesson everywhere.

Now, as I prepare for college, I want to study social work. The experiences of that August taught me that caring for others is not a single act but a daily practice. I hope to bring that practice to a university where I can keep learning how to listen, support, and serve.

Walter was the kind of man who could fix anything with a bent paperclip and a little patience. For forty-one years he worked the night shift at the water treatment plant on Route 9, and he never once missed a Sunday dinner. At seventy-three, he still climbed the ladder to clean the gutters himself, even after we all begged him to stop. When Walter retired, he filled the quiet hours with his garden, his crossword puzzles, and his dog Biscuit, a scruffy beagle who followed him everywhere, including the hardware store where he was a regular. Walter loved to post pictures of his tomatoes on Facebook under the handle @WalterTomatoKing, and he was genuinely proud of every crooked, sun-ripened one. If you have a moment today, please call Mom at 555-238-7714. She has been overwhelmed by the calls and cards, and she would love to hear from you.

I am writing this obituary for my mother, Vivian Marie Thibault, who passed away peacefully at home on August 14 at the age of seventy-eight. Mum was born in Rimouski, Quebec, in 1946, the eldest of five children, and she never let us forget how much she loved the St. Lawrence and the smell of the sea air that followed her everywhere she went.

For thirty-one years Vivian worked as a bookkeeper at Maple Ridge Lumber Supply Ltd., where she kept the accounts in order and, more importantly, kept the men in the yard honest about their expense claims. Her colleagues often said she could spot a mistake in a receipt from across the room. She retired in 2009 and at her farewell lunch she told everyone she was finally going to learn how to sleep in on a Tuesday. She did not, of course.

Mum was a creature of habit. Every weekday morning she walked to Brewed Awakenings on Hollis Street, ordered a medium dark roast with cream, and read the Chronicle Herald cover to cover with a red pen in hand. The baristas knew her by name and by her opinions on the crossword. When her knees made the walk difficult in her last years, my brother Gerard drove her there every Saturday, and she considered it the best part of her week.

She is survived by her children, Anne-Marie and Gerard, and by her grandchildren Lucas, Sophie, and little Emma, who called her Nana Viv and could always get a cookie out of her. She also leaves behind her sister Monique and a large circle of friends from her years at St. Patrick's parish, where she sang alto in the choir for four decades.

Vivian was predeceased by her husband Robert and by her parents. A celebration of life will be held on August 22 at the Oakridge Community Hall, 48 Birch Crescent, Dartmouth, followed by a reception. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Dartmouth General Hospital Foundation in her memory. Mum, we will miss your red pen and your terrible jokes. Rest now.

Ronen, I want you to know that in our family, once you are welcomed, you are welcomed for good, and that includes the awkward phone calls with our aunt in Beersheba.

Zohar, I have watched you grow from a stubborn boy into a man who listens first and speaks second, which I admit is a skill I have never mastered. You chose someone who laughs at your jokes even when they are bad, and I think that is the best evidence anyone could ask for.

I'm writing this in the notebook Dr. Ní Bhriain suggested, mostly because my thoughts keep looping when I try to hold them in my head. Today was a hard one. I walked into the Brewhouse Café on Quay Street around half nine, which is my routine since January, and the barista Ciara asked if I wanted my usual flat white. I said yes, then sat by the window and didn't drink it. I just watched the rain on the glass and felt that heavy, nothing-is-going-to-change feeling settle in my chest again.

Sinéad rang me this morning, which surprised me. She asked whether I'd booked the follow-up at St. Brigid's Clinic yet. I hadn't. I told her I'd do it on Monday, and she said, "You said that last Monday too, Shane." She's right, and she isn't trying to be cruel about it. I think she's frightened, and so am I, if I'm honest. Her number is still the one I dial when things go sideways, 087 445 2913, even though I've been trying to call people less.

Dr. Ní Bhriain asked me to write down three things that went well this week. I managed one. I got to the gym at the Ardmore Fitness Centre on Tuesday and stayed for the full forty minutes, which I haven't done since before the winter. My trainer Declan didn't make a big deal of it, just nodded and said, "Good man." That small thing mattered more than I expected.

I posted something on Instagram last night under @shane_writes_quietly, a line about how some days are just about getting through, and I deleted it an hour later. I worry about putting my moods out there where people can read them and misread them. Dr. Ní Bhriain says I'm allowed to share and allowed to keep things private, and that the choice doesn't have to be made under pressure.

So here is where I am, on the 14th of February, which is a strange day to be sad, given the cards in the shop windows. I'm tired, but I'm still here, and I'm going to ring the clinic on Monday. Write that down, Shane. Monday, the clinic, then the gym.

Friends and family, thank you for being here today to celebrate the life of Lorraine Whitfield. Lorraine was the kind of person who made every room feel a little warmer the moment she walked into it. For thirty-one years she ran the front desk at Harbor Light Physical Therapy on Maple Street, and I'm told that half the town has at least one story that begins with, "Lorraine saw me on a Tuesday and somehow fixed my back and my whole week."

She was also a regular at Sunrise Bean Cafe on Mercer Avenue, where she ordered a medium oat latte and never once let the barista forget her birthday. Every Saturday morning she sat in the window with the crossword and a pen, and anyone who stopped by her table was handed a cookie from the bag she always carried. If you ever wondered how Lorraine knew everybody's business, the answer was simple: she asked, and then she actually listened.

Lorraine was never one for the spotlight, but she loved sharing her life online. Her Instagram handle, @lorrainewalks, was a daily record of sunrise hikes, garden tomatoes, and the occasional blurry photo of her grandsons pretending not to be posing. If you were lucky enough to be on her friends list, you knew she would comment on every single post, usually with three exclamation points and a question about your weekend.

She kept her affairs in order with the same care she gave everything else. Many of you have received a handwritten card from her, or an email from lorraine.whitfield@harborlightpt.com with a link to a recipe she swore she had improved. She believed in staying in touch, and she believed that a short note could carry a lot of love.

Lorraine passed away on June 14th, surrounded by her children and her husband of forty-four years, Gerald. She is survived by her sons Michael and Peter, her grandsons Owen and Eli, and a neighborhood full of people who will miss her every single morning. Let's raise our coffee cups to Lorraine today, and let's honor her by being just a little more like her tomorrow.

My name is Oluwaseun Adebayo, and for as long as I can remember, I have wanted to understand how things work. I grew up in the Westwood neighbourhood of Mississauga, on Hollybrook Crescent, where my mother still keeps the garden I used to help her weed. My grandmother, Folake Adebayo, taught me to read the small print on medicine bottles and to ask questions when a pharmacist rushed through the instructions. She was a nurse for thirty years, and her habit of asking why shaped the way I approach everything.

The question that defined my last two years of high school came from a summer job at a community clinic on Dundas Street. I answered phones and booked appointments, and I noticed that many callers, especially seniors, could not reach anyone on the first try. I started keeping a simple log with my coworker, Priyanka Raman, who had already begun tracking call wait times. Together we showed the clinic manager that most delays happened between 9 and 11 in the morning, and we proposed a staggered booking schedule. Within a month, average waits dropped from nearly twelve minutes to under four.

If I am admitted to your engineering program, I want to build on that experience by studying how systems can serve people who are easy to overlook. I plan to pursue research in health informatics and to keep asking the questions my grandmother taught me to ask. When I call the clinic now, the number I still remember is 905-555-0147, and I like to think that somewhere in that line of calls is a small part of what I have learned.

Okay, you asked me last week why I never talk about the year I spent in Kalamata, so here it is, the whole messy thing. My name is Yiannis, and I grew up in Patras, which everyone who has never been there thinks is just a port. It is not just a port. Anyway, after I finished at the Agricultural High School in Patras, my mother insisted I go somewhere she could visit on the bus, so I ended up at the University of Peloponnese in Kalamata, which I hated for about three months and then loved more than anything.

The bit you really want to hear is the hospital. In February of my second year I broke my wrist falling off a scooter on the hill behind the Ayios Nikolaos church, and I was taken to Kalamata General Hospital. I was there for almost two days. A nurse named Eleni, who had the calmest hands I have ever seen, kept telling me the cast would come off on the 14th of March, and it did, but only after I had already convinced myself I would never play guitar again. She was right, of course. She usually was.

What I want you to take from this is that the scooter, the hospital and the bad luck all pushed me toward the people I still call my best friends. Ring me on Sunday, and I will tell you about the trip to Mani that nearly ended with us sleeping in a car.

text:
I finally made it to Mendoza after three weeks of chasing wine tours around Buenos Aires, and I can say the detour was worth every bus ride. I stayed at a small guesthouse on Calle San Martín 1482, run by a retired teacher named Yolanda who insisted I try her grandmother's empanadas before I'd even unpacked. On March 9th I joined a friend from my Spanish course at the Instituto Superior de Lenguas in Córdoba, who had flown up to celebrate her birthday, and we spent the afternoon cycling between bodegas under the Andes.

The highlight was a tasting at a family vineyard just outside the city, where the owner, Yamil, walked us through the Malbec barrels and told stories about his father, who had worked the same rows for forty years. He also pointed out the small clinic down the road where his daughter was born, and said half the valley had been delivered by the same nurse. It was a reminder that travel is never just about landmarks; it's about the people who quietly hold a place together.

If you go, book your tastings a week ahead, especially in early March when the harvest season draws crowds. Bring cash for the smaller places, and don't skip the mid-morning mate with the locals. I left Mendoza with a suitcase full of bottles I shouldn't have bought and a plan to come back for the next vendimia.

text:
The first morning in Jerusalem I got lost within ten minutes, which felt like the correct way to start. I wandered through narrow stone alleys where the smell of fresh bread and roasted coffee drifted out of tiny doorways, and every corner opened onto another market stall piled with pomegranates, sesame sweets, and spices in colours I did not have names for. Shopkeepers called out greetings in Hebrew and Arabic, sometimes switching mid-sentence, and nobody seemed bothered when I pointed at things and hoped for the best.

In the afternoon I climbed up toward the old walls and sat for a long time watching the light change on the limestone. Families were picnicking on the grass, a group of students was singing softly somewhere behind me, and the bells from a nearby church kept time with the call to prayer. It was one of those rare moments when a place feels both ancient and completely alive, and I found myself simply listening instead of taking photos.

By evening my legs ached and my notebook was full of half-finished sentences. If you come to this country, I would suggest leaving room in your plans for wandering, because the best things here tend to happen off the map. Bring comfortable shoes, accept every cup of tea you are offered, and let the city surprise you.

Harold Thomas Weatherall, known to everyone in Kendal as Harry, died peacefully at Lancaster Royal Infirmary on 14 February, aged 79, with his daughter Margaret by his side. He leaves a large family who will miss his dry humour, his stubborn opinions on football, and his habit of turning up to every christening with a card and a bottle of sherry.

Harry spent thirty-four years as a senior quantity surveyor with Lakeland Build & Design Ltd, where he was known for checking every figure twice and for never once letting a sub-contractor forget a missed deadline. Colleagues recall that he could read a set of plans faster than most people could read a menu, and that he was the first to volunteer when a new apprentice needed showing round the site.

He was a regular at Bramley's Coffee House on Highgate every Saturday morning, where the staff kept his usual order of a flat white and a slice of lemon drizzle cake ready before he reached the door. Many of his best friends were made over those tables, and the owners have asked that anyone wishing to pay their respects leave a note on the board by the window.

Harry was never without his old collie, Bramble, who went everywhere with him, from the allotment to the Saturday market. The two of them were a familiar sight on the Cumbrian lanes, and Bramble has since been taken in by his grandson Oliver, who says she spends most evenings waiting by the front door.

He is survived by his wife of 52 years, Eileen, his children Margaret, Peter and Susan, seven grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. A funeral service will be held at St Thomas's Church on 24 February at 11am, followed by a gathering at the Kendal Rugby Club. Donations in his memory may be made to the British Heart Foundation.

For anyone who would like to share a memory or a photograph, please write to the family at harry.weatherall.memories@lakelandmail.co.uk. We would love to hear your stories of Harry, and we know he would have enjoyed reading every one of them over a cup of tea.

Written with love by his son, Peter Weatherall.

I hope this letter finds you well and that the new hip is behaving itself. Mum read me your last card over the phone and I could hear the grin in her voice, so I know you're giving the physios a hard time. Please don't let them rush you.

Things here are busy. Victoria Thornbury, that's me, has finally finished the first year at Leeds General Infirmary on the placement, though I'm still at Leeds Beckett for the rest of the term. Next Tuesday, 11 February, I have to take my passport and the national insurance paperwork into the registry office for the bursary forms, so if you see a stray letter from them with my passport number on it, that's where it came from: 506815274GB. Don't worry, I'm keeping the originals safe in the folder you bought me.

I've been thinking a lot about the summer we spent at the caravan in Whitby. You taught me to skim stones and I still can't beat the record you set. I'll bring you some proper fish and chips when I visit on the 22nd of February, and we can sit on the bench with the view and argue about the cricket like we always do.

Love always,

Victoria

We gathered today not to say goodbye to a title or a role, but to honor a person who showed up for everyone around her. She was the one who always remembered the small things: the way you took your coffee, the name of your first dog, the song you hummed when you were nervous. Her kitchen was never quiet for long, and her table always had room for one more chair.

She taught by example. She believed that kindness was not something you saved for special occasions but something you practiced on an ordinary Tuesday, when no one was watching and nothing was expected of you. Many of you have told me stories this week about the times she quietly paid for a meal, drove someone to an appointment, or sat with a friend through a hard night without needing to fix anything.

In the days ahead, when you find yourself reaching for the phone to share some small piece of news with her, I hope you will let that impulse become a kind of memorial. Call someone instead. Bring a casserole. Remember a birthday. That is how she lived, and it is how we can keep her with us. Rest now, Olive. You have given us more than enough to carry forward.

text:
Ich schreibe das hier auf, damit ich es nicht vergesse. Am Dienstag, den 14. Juni, war ich bei Dr. Lehmann in der Praxis am Hohenzollernring in Köln. Ich bin jetzt 38 und seit dem Umzug aus Wien vor zwei Jahren hatte ich keinen festen Hausarzt mehr, deshalb war der Termin ziemlich überfällig. Frieda, meine Schwester, hatte mir Dr. Lehmann empfohlen, weil sie dort selbst seit Jahren ist.

Das Gespräch begann mit den üblichen Fragen zu Schlaf, Essen und Stress. Ich habe erzählt, dass ich seit dem Frühjahr öfter müde bin und die Kopfschmerzen zurückgekommen sind. Dr. Lehmann hat mir den Blutdruck gemessen, er war mit 138 zu 88 leicht erhöht. Sie meinte, das sei bei meinem Alter und dem Stress im Job nicht ungewöhnlich, möchte es aber in vier Wochen noch einmal kontrollieren.

Außerdem habe ich mit ihr über meine Arbeit gesprochen. Ich arbeite als Projektleiterin bei der Stadtwerke Nordrhein GmbH, und die letzten Monate waren sehr anstrengend. Mein Kollege Matthias Brandt hat mich dabei öfter unterstützt als irgendjemand sonst, und ich habe ihm am Ende des Gesprächs eine Nachricht geschrieben, dass ich mich bei ihm bedanke. Dr. Lehmann fand es gut, dass ich mir Unterstützung hole, und hat empfohlen, nach Feierabend wenigstens zweimal pro Woche einen Spaziergang zu machen.

Im Gespräch kam auch unser Hund Pumpernickel zur Sprache, weil ich erwähnt habe, dass er mich jeden Morgen um sechs weckt. Sie lachte und meinte, dann sei die Bewegung schon mal eingeplant. Pumpernickel ist übrigens neun Jahre alt und der beste Grund, der mir einfällt, täglich rauszugehen.

Zum Schluss haben wir noch die Blutentnahme besprochen. Die Laborwerte sollen in etwa zwei Wochen da sein, und ich bekomme einen Anruf von der Praxis, falls etwas auffällig ist. Ich nehme mir vor, die Ergebnisse dann auch wirklich abzuholen und nicht wieder ewig aufzuschieben. Nächster Termin ist Dienstag, der 12. Juli, um 9:30 Uhr.

Wenn ich das jetzt so lese, ist es eigentlich ein ganz guter Termin gewesen. Ich fühle mich ernst genommen, und das war nach den Erfahrungen in Wien nicht selbstverständlich.

Dear diary, today the rain didn't let up once, not even for the walk to the shop. I came home soaked to the skin and spent an hour in front of the range with a mug of tea going cold in my hands. Mam rang in the evening to ask whether I'd eaten, which is how I know she's still worried about me, even if she'd never say it outright. I told her I had, which was half true. There was soup, and I counted that.

The real news is that I finally finished the jumper I've been knitting since the summer. It's lopsided at one shoulder and the sleeves are two different lengths, but it's warm and it's mine. I sat with it across my knees after dinner and felt, for the first time in weeks, a small bit of pride. It's a strange thing to feel proud of a sweater with mistakes in it, but there it is.

Tomorrow I have to face the pile of letters on the hall table that I keep stepping around. Some of them are bills and some of them are the kind I've been avoiding. I'll make a cup of tea first, and then I'll open them one at a time, the way the doctor suggested. Small steps. Goodnight, diary. The wind is rattling the window and I'm going to let it.

Dear Grandma Maureen,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the garden is coming along nicely. I think about you every single day, especially now that the weather has turned warm and I can smell the lilacs on my walk to the bus. Mom says you've been keeping busy with your bridge group and that you beat Aunt Carol again last Tuesday, which I'm sure she is still not over. Tell her I said congratulations, from a safe distance.

I wanted to write because I finally got around to going through the box of photos you gave me last Christmas. There's one of you on the porch of the house on Alder Street in Dayton, holding a baby who I'm pretty sure is my uncle Tom, squinting into the sun like you were daring the camera to try. It made me realize how little I know about the years before Grandpa and you moved out to the suburbs. Would you tell me more about that time when you have a free afternoon? I'd love to hear how you two met at the dance hall downtown, and what the city looked like back then.

Work has been hectic. My manager keeps piling on projects, but I've started running along the river trail on weekday mornings, and it has honestly saved my sanity. Last weekend I signed up for a 10K in early June, which is terrifying, but I'm going to finish it. I'm hoping you'll be proud of me, even if I walk the last mile.

I also wanted to share something sweet. My roommate Jenna and I finally found an apartment closer to the university, so I'll be moving on June 14th. The place is small but has a little balcony where I plan to grow tomatoes, the way you taught me. If you ever want to visit, you can call me at 555-348-2917 or email me at maureen.lindqvist@example.com. Please don't feel you have to come all the way out, though I'd love for you to see it.

Please give my love to Grandpa, even if he's still grumbling about the new television remote. I miss your cooking so much, and I'm already planning to make your pot roast the first Sunday after I move in.

With all my love,
Megan

To whom it may concern,

I am writing on behalf of Inés Valderrama, who worked under my supervision as a senior accountant at Grupo Levante Consultores in Valencia from March 2019 until October 2023. I, Javier Molina, served as Finance Director for the department and I can speak with confidence about her work. Inés joined our Ruzafa office after completing her degree at the University of Valencia, and within two years she had taken over the month-end reconciliation process for our four largest clients.

What distinguished Inés was her precision and her willingness to take ownership of problems that others would have escalated. text:
I still think about that Tuesday in May, the one where I finally walked into Cafe Bonaparte on Calle Sarmiento in Rosario and didn't leave for three hours. I'm writing this for you, Marisol, because you were the one who kept telling me to stop hiding in my apartment. So here it is, the whole messy story.

I'm thirty-four now, and for most of my life people have called me Tomi, which is short for Tomas, though my mother still uses the full version when she's annoyed with me. That Tuesday I'd been sitting in my car outside the place for almost ten minutes, rehearsing what I'd say if Lucia Ferreyra recognized me. We had met two years earlier at the climbing gym on Avenida Pellegrini, and then we'd lost touch after a fight I still don't fully understand. She'd sent me an email that morning, out of nowhere, from lferreyra.work@gmail.com, asking if I wanted to get coffee. Just coffee, she wrote, nothing heavy.

When I finally went in, she was already at a corner table by the window, wearing that green scarf she always wore even in summer. She looked up, smiled like nothing had happened, and said, "Tomi, you still take it with too much sugar?" I laughed so hard that the waiter asked if everything was okay. That was the moment the tension broke. We talked about the gym, about her new job at a translation agency, about the dog her sister had adopted that nobody could control. Then, slowly, we got to the real stuff.

She apologized first, which I didn't expect. She said she'd been difficult during the last months we were close and that she'd blamed me for things that weren't really my fault. I told her I'd been stubborn and too proud to call her back when I should have. Neither of us was entirely right, and for once we both admitted it without sulking.

What I took from those three hours was simpler than I expected. Some friendships don't end cleanly, they just pause, and sometimes a cup of coffee in a busy cafe is enough to start them moving again. We made plans to climb on the following Saturday, and I've been going back to the gym every week since. My legs ache, my hands are rough, and I feel more like myself than I have in a long time.

So thank you for pushing me. If you ever find yourself in Rosario, come by Bonaparte with me. I'll order the sugary coffee, and you can tease me about it.

Megan's address on Quinpool Road is a short walk from several good bakeries, so if you're ever in town, let me know and I'll bring you a box of their cinnamon buns.

Last June I finally made it to Kyoto, and I have to thank my old colleague Callum Brewer for pushing me to go. He had lived there for two years teaching English and insisted I start my morning at the Fushimi Inari shrine before the crowds arrived. We climbed the thousand torii gates together around six a.m., and Callum kept stopping to point out the little stone foxes tucked between the trees. Honestly, the quiet at that hour made the whole trip for me.

Back home, my sister Mireille has been asking me to share every photo, so I have been posting them to my travel account, @wanderingcal_jp, which Callum set up for me as a joke. The highlight of the second week was a tea ceremony in Gion, where the host, a patient woman named Hisako, guided us through each movement while our feet slowly went numb on the tatami. I left the ceremony feeling calmer than I had in months.

If you go, book your ryokan early, and bring a small gift for your host because it is expected. Also, ask someone you trust to look after your home, which in my case meant my cat Biscuit, who spent the week being spoiled by my neighbour. I am already planning my return for the cherry blossoms next spring, and I expect Callum will be driving the itinerary again.

text:
My name is Hannah Whitfield, and I was Uncle Yusuf's niece, though he never once let me forget that he was the one who taught me to swim. We grew up in Leeds, in a terraced house on Hyde Park Road, and until I was nineteen I thought every man in the world laughed the way he did, with his whole chest and his head tipped back.

Yusuf spent thirty-one years at St James's Hospital as a porter, and I don't think a single patient ever left his corridor without being greeted by name. He knew which nurses took their tea with sugar and which ones pretended not to. When my mother was on the ward after her surgery, he brought her a flask of cardamom tea every morning before his shift and never once mentioned that it was against the rules.

When he retired, he could not sit still. He opened a small coffee place on Chapel Street called Bean & Brew, mostly so he would have somewhere to argue about football with the regulars. He ran it for six years. He insisted the cinnamon buns were his grandmother's recipe, though I have seen her handwriting and it certainly was not.

He moved to Manchester with his partner, Lorraine, in 2016, and then, to everyone's surprise, to Lisbon two years later, where he learned enough Portuguese to haggle at the fish market. The distance never stopped him calling. Every Sunday, at seven, the phone would ring and he would ask about my work, my cooking, and whether I had been looking after our old dog, Biscuit, who by then was too stubborn to die and too deaf to hear him calling.

Yusuf, I am still learning to swim without you. Thank you for holding me up until I could float on my own.

It is with heavy hearts that our family announces the passing of Joseph Mwangi Kariuki, born on 14 October 1961 in Nyeri and called to rest on 3 October 2024 at the age of 62. Joe, as many of you knew him, was a husband, father, brother, uncle and friend to more people than he could ever count. He leaves behind his wife of thirty-four years, Grace, and their children, Brian, Njeri and little Wanjiru, whose laughter filled every corner of our home.

I first knew Joe as the older brother who taught me to ride a bicycle along the dusty road behind our family compound in Nyeri. He was patient in a way I never managed to be myself. Later, when I came to Nairobi to look for work, he opened his door to me for almost a year without ever once making me feel like a burden. That was simply who he was. He believed that a man's home should always have room for one more plate at the table.

For over twenty-five years Joe served with dedication at Kenya Commercial Bank, where he rose from a teller to a senior branch manager in the Westlands area. His colleagues often spoke of his fairness and of the way he remembered the names of their children and asked after their mothers. He could explain a loan policy to a nervous first-time borrower so clearly that the person would leave the office smiling. Many of those customers later became his friends.

Joe loved football above almost everything else, except perhaps his grandchildren and a good pot of githeri cooked by Grace. On Sunday mornings you would find him in front of the television shouting at the referee with the same passion he once reserved for Gor Mahia matches at Nyayo Stadium. He also kept a small vegetable garden behind the house, and he would proudly send photographs of his kale and tomatoes to anyone who would look. text:
Dear Grandma,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold hasn't gotten into your bones too badly. It has been a strange few weeks here. The leaves finally came down all at once after a long, stubborn stretch of gray, and now the yard looks bare in a way I'm still getting used to. I keep meaning to rake and then finding a reason to put it off, which I suspect you would find very funny.

Work has been busy in the way that leaves you tired but not unhappy. There's a project that has taken over most of my days, and I've been staying later than I should, mostly because the people I work with are kind and the problems are interesting. I've also started cooking on the weekends again. Last Sunday I tried to make the soup you used to make with too many onions and not enough patience, and it came out closer than I expected. It still didn't taste quite like yours, but I think that's just because yours was made with years of practice behind it.

I've been thinking a lot about the winters we spent together when I was small. The way the windows fogged up when the kettle was going, the blanket you kept folded over the arm of the couch, the radio playing softly in the kitchen while you worked on something with your hands. I didn't appreciate those afternoons at the time. I just assumed they would always be there, the way children assume things about the adults who look after them.

I wanted to write because I miss you, and because phone calls have a way of ending before I've said what I meant to. So here is what I meant to say: thank you for the patience, the stories, and the endless supply of advice I didn't ask for but needed anyway. I'm trying to take some of it to heart.

Please tell me how you are doing, really doing, not the polite version. Tell me what you're reading, what you're worried about, and whether you've finally let anyone help with the stairs. I'll call again this weekend, and I promise to actually listen this time instead of checking the time every few minutes.

With all my love,
Ruby

I have been meaning to write about our week in the north for a while, but life got in the way, so here it is. My name is Rafael Ortiz, I'm 34, and I'm a freelance photographer who ended up in Israel almost by accident after a friend of mine, Ronen, insisted I come see Galilee in June. He was right. We landed in Tel Aviv on June 9th, and I remember stepping out into the heat thinking I had made a terrible mistake packing a wool jumper. By the afternoon I had changed my mind about everything, mostly because the light over the Mediterranean is unlike anywhere I've shot before.

We spent the first few days driving up the coast with no fixed plan. Ronen had a list of places but kept ignoring it, which I appreciated. In Akko we wandered through the old market for hours, buying spices I still can't pronounce and eating hummus so good I am embarrassed to admit I went back twice. The stone walls there have a warmth that makes every photo look like a memory. I posted a few shots to my account, @rafa.lenses, and a stranger from Haifa messaged me asking where the tiny blue door was. I had to laugh, because I had almost walked straight past it.

The highlight of the trip, honestly, was a sunrise hike near the Sea of Galilee. We set off at 4:30 in the morning, half asleep and grumbling, but the view from the ridge made every complaint disappear. Watching the water turn from grey to gold while a line of birds crossed the sky is a moment I plan to keep forever. Ronen laughed at me for crying a little, but he had his camera out too.

If you're planning your own trip, a few practical notes. Book accommodation early for June, because the holiday weekends fill up fast. I booked our guesthouse through a local host, and when I had questions I emailed her at ruth.halevi@mailbox.co.il, who replied within an hour with detailed directions and a list of restaurants she trusted. She also confirmed our late check-in on June 14th after I got my dates muddled. If you need to reach the guesthouse by phone, the number is 972-4-555-0182, though the best way is still a quick message.

We left the country feeling sunburnt, a little overfed and completely unwilling to go home. I'm already planning the return trip, and I'll be back with a better lens and far fewer wool jumpers. Thanks for reading, and if you see a tiny blue door in Akko, say hello from me.

When people ask me where I first learned to lead, I usually point to the summer I spent at the Riverside Community Food Bank in Columbus, Ohio. My supervisor, Marcus Delgado, handed me a clipboard on my first morning in July and told me that the shelves would not restock themselves. Over the following weeks, Marcus taught me how to coordinate volunteer shifts, how to track donations so that nothing expired on the shelf, and how to speak to a frustrated family without making them feel judged. Marcus never called himself a leader, but he showed me that leadership is mostly about paying attention to the people who quietly keep things running.

One afternoon on July 19th, a truck carrying two pallets of produce arrived three hours late, and our Saturday distribution was in jeopardy. I remember Marcus looking at me and asking what I would do. I had no plan yet, so I started calling the other volunteers, reorganizing the schedule, and asking local grocers whether they had surplus to spare. By evening, we had served every family who had come to the line. Marcus smiled and said only, "Now you understand the job."

That summer changed how I think about my future. I want to study public policy because I have seen how a single late truck can ripple through a neighborhood, and I want to help design systems that prevent those failures. Oliver Brandt, the director who first interviewed me, asked why I wanted to work there. My answer then was simple: I wanted to be useful. My answer now is that I want to build the kind of structures that let everyone be useful, the way Marcus did for me.

Sono stata in questa trattoria due sere fa con mia sorella e devo dire che ne è valsa la pena. Il locale è piccolo, con pochi tavoli in legno e una luce calda che rende l'atmosfera accogliente anche per chi arriva da una giornata pesante. Ci hanno accolte con un sorriso e ci hanno subito proposto il vino della casa, un rosso leggero che abbinato alle bruschette ai pomodorini è stato una piacevole sorpresa.

Per il primo abbiamo scelto le tagliatelle al ragù d'anatra, che erano cotte al punto giusto e condite con una salsa densa e profumata. Mia sorella ha preso i gnocchi di zucca con burro e salvia, e ha detto che erano tra i migliori assaggiati in questo periodo. Le porzioni sono generose senza essere eccessive, e si percepisce che tutto viene preparato con cura e ingredienti di stagione.

Il servizio merita un capitolo a parte. Il cameriere era attento senza essere invadente, ci ha consigliato un dessert che non conoscevamo, una crema al mascarpone con amarene, e ha accettato con garbo la nostra richiesta di dividere il conto. Nei momenti di maggiore affluenza qualche attesa in più c'è stata, ma nulla di preoccupante, e il personale ha sempre tenuto sotto controllo la situazione con calma.

Qualche piccola critica, per onestà: la sala è abbastanza rumorosa quando è piena, quindi se cercate una cena tranquilla conviene prenotare un tavolo vicino alla finestra. Anche il parcheggio è limitato e in strada bisogna essere pazienti. Sono dettagli che non compromettono l'esperienza complessiva.

In conclusione, consiglio questo posto a chi vuole mangiare bene in un ambiente semplice e curato. Il rapporto qualità prezzo mi è sembrato onesto e torneremo sicuramente, magari in una serata di primavera per sederci anche all'esterno. Consiglio vivamente di prenotare nel fine settimana.

I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on November 14 so I don't forget the details later. I went to the clinic on Alder Street in the Riverside neighborhood, which is about a fifteen minute drive from my apartment. My name is Frances Holloway and I came in because of the numbness in my left hand that started about three weeks ago. Dr. Okafor listened carefully, tested my grip strength, and checked my reflexes. She thinks it is most likely carpal tunnel syndrome from all the typing at work, but she wants me to get nerve conduction studies before she decides anything for sure.

She gave me a wrist splint to wear at night and told me to avoid gripping my phone for long stretches. She also prescribed a mild anti-inflammatory for two weeks. text:
Friends and family, I want to start by thanking you all for coming. Fionnuala was never one for fuss, so I suspect she'd be a little embarrassed to see this many of us crammed into one room, but she would also be quietly delighted. She spent forty-one years telling anyone who would listen that she didn't need a crowd, and then she would go out of her way to make sure every person in her life felt they had a seat at her table.

She was born on the 14th of July in a small house above the harbour in Waterford, the second of five children, and she never let anyone forget that being the middle child made her the peacemaker. When she moved to Vancouver in 1998, with two suitcases and a letter of acceptance from the nursing program, she wrote home every single Sunday. Those letters were full of weather complaints, terrible coffee, and long, funny descriptions of the people she met on the bus. Mam kept every one of them in a shoebox under the stairs, and I found them last week. Reading them, I could hear her voice on every page.

In Canada she built a life that was entirely her own. She learned to ski badly, grew tomatoes that never ripened, and took in a string of stray cats before settling on a grumpy grey tabby named Dougal, who ruled her apartment with total authority for nearly fifteen years. Dougal would sit on her chest every morning until she woke up, and she claimed that was the only alarm clock she ever trusted. When people asked why she never got a dog, she'd say she had already found the animal she deserved.

Fionnuala had a rule that she passed on to all of us: always answer a message from someone you love, even if it's just a single emoji. Many of you received those little replies from her, often late at night, often with a typo she refused to correct. Her online presence was small but devoted; if you ever wanted to find her, you looked for @fionn_on_the_go, where she posted photographs of sunsets, half-finished knitting projects, and the occasional furious rant about parking. Her last post, a picture of the harbour in Vancouver with the caption "home is wherever someone is waiting," now feels like a message meant for us.

So tonight I am asking you to do what she would have wanted. Call someone you have not spoken to in a while. Write a letter, even a short one. Make terrible coffee and drink it anyway. Sit with a friend and let the silence be comfortable. That was Fionnuala's gift, and it is ours now to keep. We will miss her every day, and we will carry her with us, one small kindness at a time.

My name is Noa, and I am the youngest of Jonathan's four children. Standing here, I keep thinking about how Dad always found a reason to be in the car at dawn. He was born in Haifa in the summer of 1952, and he never stopped loving the sea he grew up beside. He would drive us down to the water before school on any morning he could, sometimes with the radio on and sometimes in complete silence, and he never once complained about the early start.

Jonathan trained as a civil engineer at the Technion, and he used to say the graduates of that place had a particular kind of stubbornness that he hoped never left them. He carried that stubbornness into everything. When the roof leaked in our flat in Haifa, he climbed up there himself with a ladder he had borrowed from a neighbour and a tin of sealant he had argued the shopkeeper into discounting. He wanted things built to last, and he wanted people to last too.

He spent the last years of his life in Be'er Sheva, where he moved to be close to my sister Michal and her family. The grandchildren adored him. He taught the older ones chess on the balcony in the evenings, and he let the little ones win just often enough that they never felt cheated. Every visit began with him asking whether we had eaten, and every visit ended with him pressing something into our hands, a jar of olives, a folded note, a few shekels for the bus.

He was taken to Rambam Hospital in the second week of June, and for a while we believed he would come home again. The nurses there were patient with all of us, and the doctors explained everything honestly, which Dad would have appreciated. He held on longer than anyone expected, and I think it was because he still had questions about the world that he wanted answered.

Jonathan, we will miss your terrible puns, your insistence that every problem has a load-bearing solution, and your hands, always reaching for ours at the crossing. Thank you for building the foundations we now stand on. Rest well, Abba.

I finally made it to Savannah this fall, and I have to admit the Spanish moss sold me before I even got out of the car. My name is Sloren, though my college roommates still call me Lo, and I live in Charleston, so this was a short drive that felt like a proper trip. I came down on November 9th, which was my thirty-first birthday, and I decided that the best present I could give myself was three days with no alarm clock and no work email. My dog Biscuit came along too. He is a scruffy six-year-old beagle mix who thinks every fountain in the squares is his personal water bowl, so we spent a lot of time walking slowly and letting him sniff.

We stayed in a small guesthouse off Jones Street, and I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to be within walking distance of the squares without the noise. Each morning I wandered over to Forsyth Park, got a coffee from a cart near the fountain, and sat on a bench while Biscuit tried to befriend every jogger. In the afternoons Lo and I, meaning me talking to myself on the phone with my sister, wandered through the River Street shops and ate she-crab soup at a place with sticky wooden tables. Nothing about the trip was ambitious, and that was exactly the point.

If you go in November, pack a light jacket for the evenings, because the humidity drops and the breeze off the river gets chilly after sunset. Book the ghost tour early, since it sells out on weekends, and bring a bag for your dog's treats and a spare leash, because the squares are busier than you expect. I left feeling rested in a way I hadn't in months, and Biscuit slept the whole ride home.

text:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Marcus, Hannah's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words before we all get too full of roast lamb to listen. I promise to keep it short. Mostly.

I want to start with a confession. When Hannah first told our family she was moving to Auckland, I assumed it would last about six months. She had a habit of falling in love with a place and then discovering it wasn't quite the one she'd imagined. But she packed up her flat in Leeds on the 14th of May, five years ago, with a single suitcase, a box of books, and Biscuit, her ridiculous ginger cat who has never once behaved himself on a long-haul flight. I still remember the look on the airport official's face when Biscuit yowled the entire way through passport control.

That cat, I should say, is responsible for more of this evening than anyone realises. It was Biscuit who wandered into Ella's garden in Ponsonby during Hannah's second winter there, and it was Ella who came over the fence in her dressing gown to get him back. Hannah has told the story so many times that it has become family legend. Ella likes to point out that Hannah had already been ignoring the rules about cats in the flat for a year before that. Hannah says it was a fair trade.

For those of you who have only known Hannah since she came home for Christmas, let me share a little of who she was before the move. She was always the one organising the family photos, always the one remembering birthdays, and always the one who would drive four hours in the rain if someone needed a lift. Moving to the other side of the world didn't change any of that. If anything, it made her more deliberate about the people she keeps close, and I'm lucky to be counted among them.

When the two of them got engaged, Ella asked me to help find a date that didn't clash with the rugby final or the school fête. We settled on the 23rd of May, and I have to admit, it was the right choice. The weather has held, the flowers are exactly what Hannah wanted, and the cat, I'm told, has been fed and is sulking politely at home.

So please raise your glasses. To Hannah and Ella, to two countries and the people who have travelled between them to be here tonight, and to the stubborn ginger cat who started it all. Cheers.

My name is Noa Levi, and I was asked to speak today because I was Nadav's sister, and because for forty-one years I was the one who got the phone calls at two in the morning. Nadav grew up in Haifa, in a small flat above the bakery on Herzl Street, and from the age of six he was convinced he would become a pilot. He studied engineering at the Technion, and he never once let us forget the name of that place, or the fact that he had walked there every morning with a sandwich wrapped in foil. He used to say the sandwich was the real reason he passed his exams.

When Nadav was thirty-four he was taken to Rambam Hospital after a fall from a ladder at the back of his parents' house, the house he had promised our mother he would repaint for her birthday. The doctors there were kind to him, and he spent the following week making jokes about the nurses' shoes. He was always the one who made the room lighter. Even on the last day, when he could barely speak, he asked his daughter to make sure the blue Subaru, registration 45-612-38, was sold to someone who would look after it the way he had.

So today I want to ask you to do one small thing for him. Next time you pass a bakery, buy something warm, and eat it slowly, the way he would have. Call a sibling you have not spoken to in a while. Nadav believed that the people who matter most are the ones you bother to ring. He rang everyone. Please keep ringing, in his memory, on the fourteenth of October and every day after.

text:
Ima, Bracha, I still hear your voice when I open the door on Friday afternoons, calling out that the soup is almost ready even when it clearly wasn't. For forty-one years you ran the kitchen at the community centre in Haifa, and every single Friday the people who came through it knew they were welcome. Ronen from the bakery on Herzl Street told me last week that you once gave him a job when he had nothing, and asked him to come back on Sunday to learn how to fold the challah properly. You never mentioned it to anyone. That was your way.

You were the one who kept the family together through every argument and every long distance. When my brother moved to Eilat, you called him every Thursday at seven. When I finally took the leap and moved abroad, you sent me long messages about the weather back home, the price of tomatoes at the shuk, and which neighbours had new grandchildren. Your handwriting was always cramped on the page because you wrote too much to fit in the space given. Dina Levi, who worked beside you for twenty years, said it best: you never let anyone walk past without a word.

Ima, we will keep your recipes, your loud laugh, and your stubborn refusal to let anyone pay for coffee at Café Nomi on Ben Gurion Street, where the staff greeted you by name for three decades. If anyone needs to reach us about the memorial, write to bracha.family.memorial@gmail.com or message @bracha_haifa_kitchen. You can also call 052-734-1186 and someone will answer. Rest now. We have the soup on.

I'm writing this down so I don't forget what Dr. Hennessy told me at my appointment on Tuesday 11 February. My name is Laoise Brennan, and I went to the surgery on Main Street in Kilkenny, the one next to Nolan's Pharmacy, because I've had a sore left knee since Christmas and it's been getting worse on the stairs.

Dr. Hennessy had a look at it and asked me to walk up and down the corridor while she watched. She pressed around the joint and asked whether it locked or gave way. It doesn't lock, but it clicks and sometimes feels like it might buckle. She thinks it's most likely a cartilage problem made worse by my new routine of running three mornings a week at the gym in Kilkenny, Fitzpatrick's Fitness, which I joined in January with big plans.

She wants me to have an X-ray at the Waterford Regional clinic before the end of the month and to stop the running for at least six weeks. I asked if swimming would be fine, and she said yes, and that cycling on flat ground is probably okay too. I'm to take ibuprofen with food for the swelling, not more than the packet says. She also gave me a referral letter, which I'm to bring with me to the X-ray, and the appointment for that is on Thursday 20 February at nine.

I told her about Biscuit, my old collie, who has been limping too, and she laughed and said I should book him in with the vet before he gets as stubborn as I am. My sister Orla drove me home because I didn't want to be on my own in the car with the leg stiff, and she made me promise to phone her the minute the X-ray is done. I've written her name and number on the back of the referral so I don't lose it.

So my plan is simple. Rest the knee, swim on Mondays and Wednesdays, keep up the ibuprofen with breakfast, and go to the scan on the twentieth. If the pain gets worse, or the knee swells up in the night, I'm to ring the surgery straight away rather than wait for the next slot. I'll update this when I have the results.

August 14

Dear diary, today I finally sat down to sort out the mess on my desk, and I found the envelope from the DMV with my passport number on it, 548213769, which I keep meaning to put somewhere safer. Ruth Ashford, that's me, still can't believe I've been at Brightline Logistics for nine years. Mr. Okafor from HR pulled me aside this morning and said they want me to lead the Denver transition team in the fall, which is either a compliment or a warning, depending on how you look at it.

My sister Rachel called around noon. She reminded me that her wedding is on August 29 at the lake house in Boulder, and I promised I'd finally buy a dress that doesn't make me look like a bridesmaid from 1994. Rachel says I'm being dramatic. Maybe I am. But she's the one who cried through the entire rehearsal dinner last year, so I think I've earned a little drama.

I went home to 2218 Maple Ridge Drive after work, which is still the best thing about living in Denver. The porch light was on because my neighbor Lionel had stopped by to water the ferns while I was gone. He left a note on the door that said, "Ruth, your plants have more personality than most people I know." I laughed out loud, which felt good after a long day.

In the evening I made soup and watched the rain move across the window. I thought about whether I actually want to lead the team or whether I just want to be asked. Those feel like different things, and I haven't figured out which one is driving me.

Before bed I wrote Rachel a text: "Fine. I'll buy the dress. Send me the color swatches and stop calling me dramatic." She replied with a row of heart emojis and a picture of a cake. Tomorrow I will call the Brightline recruiter back and ask for a few days to think. Then I will go shopping.

I would be grateful if you could arrange an inspection at your earliest convenience.
