Sunday, 14 February. Dr Mokoena asked me to write down what I notice in my body when I think about my mother, so here goes. Cwenga has been circling the same worry for three weeks now: that she will never be the daughter her mother expected. Born in Pietermaritzburg in a house with a jacaranda out front, she was always the one who got her head down and stayed there. She finished her nursing diploma at Pholela Hospital and then came to Johannesburg with two suitcases and a letter of admission she still keeps in her wallet. When I say all of this to Dr Mokoena, my chest tightens, and I notice I start tapping my foot.

We talked about Biscuit, the old Jack Russell who used to sleep on the end of Cwenga's bed when she was a child in Pietermaritzburg. He died in 2011, and she still says that was the first time she understood that love can be something you keep carrying without anyone asking you to. Dr Mokoena wondered aloud whether the guilt she feels about her mother is similar: a weight she carries because she loves her, not because she is failing her.

I want to remember that Cwenga did call her mother last Tuesday, 18 February, even though the call lasted only nine minutes. She said afterwards that she felt steadier. Next session, we agreed I would bring the question of what she actually wants from that relationship, not what she thinks she owes it.

I reminded her that caregiving splits people in exactly this way, and that the relief doesn't cancel out the love. She nodded, but I could tell she wasn't convinced yet. text:
I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on Thursday, the 14th of August, so I don't forget the details. I'm Rainer, 47 years old, and I live in Prenzlauer Berg here in Berlin, just off Kastanienallee. My GP is Dr. Hermann Vogt at the practice on Danziger Strasse, and I've been seeing him for about six years now.

The reason for the visit was the tightness in my chest that I'd been noticing on the stairs at work. I work at Brandt & Lindqvist GmbH in Mitte, where I've been a logistics coordinator for almost twelve years, so most of my day is spent on my feet or running between the warehouse and the office. My wife, Katrin, came along because she wanted to hear what the doctor said first-hand, which I was glad of, since I tend to forget half of what I'm told.

Dr. Vogt listened to my heart and lungs for a long time and then asked a lot of questions about my sleep, my diet and how much I've been drinking since the spring. He ordered a resting ECG, some blood work for cholesterol and blood sugar, and a referral to a cardiologist, Dr. Sabine Hoffmann, whose office is on Kantstrasse. The appointment with her is on the 26th of August at 9:40, so I've put it in the calendar and set two alarms.

He was calm about it, though he was clear that I should not ignore it. He asked me to cut back on salt and to walk for thirty minutes most days rather than taking the lift at work. He also said that if the pain comes on at rest, or spreads into my arm or jaw, I should call the emergency number straight away and not wait for the next appointment.

On the way home Katrin said I looked relieved, and I think I was. It's easier to face a problem when someone has given it a name and a plan. I'll send my blood test results to my email, rainer.meissner@gmx.de, once they come through, and I'll update this note after the cardiologist visit.

Rainer

text: I finally made it to Jaipur on 14 February after three days of crawling through traffic from Delhi. My driver, Lakshmi, had been insisting since Gurgaon that the Ajmer road was faster, and he was right, though I suspect he mostly wanted to show off his new GJ-05-TR-4471 Maruti. We stopped for chai at a roadside dhaba where the owner remembered my sister from a visit in 2019 and asked after her wedding. Honestly, the best part of the trip so far has been these small, unplanned conversations with strangers who treat you like family within ten minutes.

Thank you all for being here today. Standing up in front of so many people who loved the same person I did is harder than I expected, so please bear with me. I have known for weeks what I wanted to say, and somehow every version of it sounds too small.

What I keep coming back to is how she showed up. Not with grand gestures, but with a casual, dependable kindness. A cup of tea appearing when you had not even noticed you needed one. A phone call on a bad afternoon that was really just a way of saying, I'm thinking of you. She had a way of making people feel that their ordinary days were worth paying attention to, and that is a rarer gift than most of us realise until it is gone.

So today I am asking each of us to carry a little of that forward. Call the friend you have been meaning to ring. Make the tea. Notice the person quietly struggling in the corner of the room. She would not want a fuss made, but she would be glad to know that the way she lived is still being passed along, one ordinary kindness at a time. Thank you.

My name is Rohan, and I was lucky enough to be Dhruv's younger brother for thirty-four years. Dhruv passed away on the 14th of June, just three weeks after his sixty-first birthday. For most of his working life he was the Chief Accounts Officer at Bharat Textile Mills in Coimbatore, but if you asked anyone in Race Course Road what he was really known for, they would tell you about the Sunday chai he shared with the shopkeepers outside Lakshmi Stores. He never walked past a neighbour without asking after their children, their knees, their mother's health.

Dhruv taught me to ride a bicycle on the wide lanes behind our house, and he taught me that a good ledger and a good heart are not so different: both need to be kept honest every single day. He balanced everything he owed to others with a patience that embarrassed the rest of us. When my father fell ill, Dhruv drove him to the hospital every Tuesday for eleven months without once complaining about the traffic on Avinashi Road.

I am told that Dhruv's last words to his grandson were a reminder to finish his homework before the cricket match. That was so typical of him: the small, practical instruction given with love. Please keep his email, dhruv.raman@bmills.co.in, open a little longer if you are writing to us, because we will read every message. I've been coming to Mang Dodong's Carinderia on 47 Rizal Extension, Barangay San Roque, Cabanatuan City for almost six years now, and it never disappoints. Last Saturday, September 14, I stopped by after my shift at Pacific Harbor Logistics, where I work as a dispatch coordinator. It was my 34th birthday and my coworkers insisted on a proper celebration, so we ordered a whole tray of kare-kare, crispy pata, and garlic rice. The oxtail was tender, the peanut sauce was rich without being cloying, and the pata skin shattered the way it should. Mang Dodong himself came out to check on our table and even remembered that I prefer my bagoong on the side.

The only reason I'm docking a star is the wait. We sat for nearly forty minutes before our first dish came out, and the place was not that crowded. I understand that good food takes time, and the staff were apologetic, but a little communication about the delay would have gone a long way. The lady who runs the counter, Ate Vilma, was friendly and kept our drinks topped up while we waited, which I appreciated.

If you're in the area, make sure to try the sisig on a weekday when the kitchen isn't swamped. Follow their Facebook page at @mangdodongcarinderia for their daily menu and specials. Overall, a solid five-star experience marred only by the slow service.

June 14th. Athens is unbearably hot today, and I spent the whole afternoon at the ministry office in Syntagma trying to renew my residence paperwork. Orestis, the clerk behind the glass, was kind enough but insisted I bring my passport number written out in full, AB4471829, plus a photocopy of the ID card. Turning thirty-four in a few weeks makes these bureaucratic errands feel even more absurd, as if the government thinks I can still pass for someone younger and more patient.

After the office I walked down to Plaka with Eleni, who has been my closest friend since we shared a flat in Thessaloniki. We ate grilled octopus under a vine and argued about whether Crete or the Cyclades will win the summer. She keeps teasing me that Orestis only looked at my papers because I smiled at him, and maybe she is right. Her phone buzzed twice during dinner, a reminder of the tasks waiting for us both.

On the bus home I kept thinking about how much of my life is now written down in numbers and files. Tomorrow I will go back with the stamps, and hopefully that will be the end of it. I want to write something real this summer, not just forms. Maybe that starts with this diary.

I've been coming to this little bakery near the old market square for about a year now, and I finally felt I owed it a proper review. The place is tiny, with maybe four wooden tables and a counter that always smells of cinnamon and fresh rye. The staff are warm without being overbearing. On my last visit, the woman behind the counter remembered that I like my coffee black and didn't even need to ask.

The bread is the real draw. The sourdough has a crackly crust and an open, chewy crumb, and the poppy seed rolls are the best I've had outside of a family kitchen. Pastries sell out early, so if you want the apple turnovers, go before ten. Prices are fair for the quality, and the cash-only policy is a bit old-fashioned but nobody seems to mind.

My only complaint is the wait at lunchtime, when the queue spills out onto the pavement and the tables are hard to come by. Still, I'd recommend this place to anyone who wants honest food and a quiet corner to read. Ask for a seat by the window if you can get one. Go early, bring small change, and thank me later.

I have been going to Sharma Auto Care in Indiranagar for almost six years now, and I finally feel I should write something about them. My car is a 2014 Honda City, registration KA-03-MX-4417, and I have never once been made to feel like a number at this place. The workshop sits on a small lane just off 100 Feet Road, so parking is a bit tight, but the staff always wave you into a spot.

Last month my brake pads started squealing badly on the drive to the office. I called on a Tuesday morning and was told they could look at it that same afternoon. The service advisor, Rohan Kulkarni, who is the Service Manager at the workshop, walked me through the inspection report on a tablet, with photos of the worn pads and the scored disc. He did not push any extra work on me. He said the front discs were still within limits and only the pads needed replacing, and he showed me exactly why.

My wife, Meenakshi, had her own experience there in March when the AC stopped cooling. She says the technician, Imran, spent almost an hour tracing a small refrigerant leak and did not charge her for the diagnostic because the fault turned out to be a faulty compressor clutch under warranty. She still talks about it. Her cousin who lives near Koramangala has started bringing his Maruti there too, after hearing us talk about it at a family dinner.

The billing is transparent. Every invoice lists parts and labour separately, and they keep the old parts in a bag for you if you ask. Pricing is in line with or a little below what the authorised dealers charge, which is the main reason I keep coming back. I once got a bill wrong by a few hundred rupees and they corrected it within the hour without any argument.

The waiting area could use a better coffee machine and a few more chairs, but the Wi-Fi works and the tea is free. Appointments on weekdays are usually honoured, though Saturdays get crowded after about ten in the morning, so book ahead if you can.

Overall I would give Sharma Auto Care five stars without hesitation. Honest advice, fair prices and people who remember your name. If you live around Indiranagar or Domlur and need someone you can trust with your car, this is the place. I will be back in August for the scheduled service, and I expect nothing less.

Rosalind "Roz" Whitfield, 68, of the Eastwood Park neighborhood on Larkspur Avenue in Dayton, Ohio, died peacefully on August 14 at Miami Valley Hospital, surrounded by the family who loved her most. She is survived by her husband of forty-one years, Gerald, her two daughters, Megan and Tessa, and four grandchildren who knew her as the keeper of the cookie tin and the loudest voice at every ballgame.

Roz spent thirty-two years teaching third grade at Fairview Elementary School, where generations of students learned to read with her patience and her red pen. Many of her former students still write to say she was the first teacher who made them believe they were clever. She retired in 2012 but never really stopped teaching; she tutored neighborhood kids at her kitchen table on Tuesdays and Thursdays until this spring.

Her closest friend and colleague, Bernadette "Bernie" Kowalski, shared lunch with her every Friday for nearly three decades. "Roz could make a room laugh and then tell you exactly where you'd gone wrong in your fractions," Bernie said. "I will miss her every single Friday."

Roz was never without her golden retriever, Biscuit, who rode shotgun in her silver Buick with the license plate reading OH 4821 KLM and went with her on every errand around town. Biscuit now rests quietly at home with Gerald, who says the house feels far too still without the two of them bickering about the car radio.

A lifelong gardener, Roz tended roses along the front walk of Larkspur Avenue for more than thirty summers. Neighbors often stopped to admire them and left with a bundle of cut blooms and an invitation to come back next week. She also kept a small savings account at the credit union, number 77-203-9148, which she used mainly to fund school supply drives each August.

A memorial service will be held Saturday, August 23, at Fairview Community Church. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Fairview Elementary reading fund in Roz's name. She would have wanted every child to have a book in their hands and someone to believe in them.

text:
My name is Hannah, and I was lucky enough to be Grandad Lachlan's granddaughter for twenty-six years. Most of you knew him as the man who ran the hardware shop on Glebe Point Road for almost forty years, the one who could fix anything with a bit of wire and a lot of patience. He worked at Hardie & Sons Hardware until he retired, and he never once let anyone leave the counter without asking whether they had enough screws. He took that seriously.

When I was small, Lachlan would take me down to Callan Park every Saturday morning. We would walk the dog, a scruffy kelpie-cross named Biscuit who belonged to the whole street as much as to him. Biscuit never listened to a word he said, and Lachlan never minded. He told me once that the best things in life are the ones that don't do what you tell them, and then he laughed until he had to sit on the bench to catch his breath.

Lachlan was seventy-eight when he died on the ninth of November, at home, in the chair by the kitchen window where he could see the jacarandas. He had been turning sixty-three in his heart for about fifteen years, and he would have hated me saying he was old. He still climbed the ladder to clean the gutters until this past winter. He still argued with the weather forecast every single morning.

He taught me to plane a piece of timber until it felt like silk under my palm. He taught me that a crooked joint is only a lesson waiting to be measured again. And he taught me, mostly by example, that kindness is a practical thing. You show up with the right tool. You show up on time. You stay for the second cup of tea even when you have somewhere else to be.

So today I am asking you to do one small thing for him. Go and buy a few screws from someone who needs them. Walk a dog that isn't yours. Sit down on a bench in the sun and let someone else talk for a while. Lachlan would have liked that far more than any speech. Thank you all for coming to say goodbye to him with me.

text:
When people ask where I'm from, I usually say Haifa, though my family has moved around the country more than most. My name is Daniel, but everyone at home has called me Dani since I was small, and my grandmother still uses a version of it that only she can get away with. I grew up in a flat above a bakery on a street that smelled of cardamom and diesel every morning, and I learned early that a city can be both loud and tender at the same time.

My interest in engineering started in a far less glamorous place: the kitchen table, where my father kept a broken water heater in pieces for almost a month. I was nine. He let me hold the thermostat while he explained how the sensor talked to the valve. That was the first time I understood that a machine is just a conversation between parts that have to agree with each other. I have been asking that kind of question ever since.

The turning point came during my final year of school. On June 14th I was scheduled to sit for the practical examination in physics, and the week before, our lab was flooded after a pipe burst in the hallway above. Instead of panicking, I spent three nights rebuilding our group's circuit model from memory and from the notes I had taken during class. When the exam finally came, I was calmer than I had expected. I didn't ace it, but I learned that preparation is partly about what you do when the plan falls apart.

Since then I have volunteered at a community repair cafe in the Carmel neighbourhood, where neighbours bring in toasters, bicycles and radios that have stopped working. I am the one who opens the cases and explains to the owner what went wrong. Many of them are surprised that a seventeen-year-old can do this, and some of them come back every month just to talk. That is the part I value most: a repaired object is useful, but a repaired relationship between a person and their tools is something more.

I am applying to your programme because I want to study how systems fail and how people design around those failures. I want to work on infrastructure that serves ordinary households, the kind of boilers, pumps and grids that my family and my neighbours depend on without thinking. I hope to bring to your university the same habit I learned at that kitchen table: take the thing apart, ask how it talks to itself, and then put it back together so it works for the people who need it.

text:
Growing up outside a small market town in the west of Ireland, I learned early that the most useful skills are the ones nobody writes on a timetable. On Saturday mornings I worked the counter at my family's shop, weighing vegetables, reckoning change in my head and listening to the regulars talk about weather, hurling and whatever had gone wrong in the village that week. Those mornings taught me more about patience and about people than any classroom ever did.

When I was fifteen I started volunteering with a local meals programme that ran out of a church hall twice a week. My job was mostly unglamorous: stacking chairs, sorting donated tins, pouring tea for people who came in from the cold. Over time I found myself drawn to the quieter tables, where older men sat alone and wanted someone to listen. I came to understand that a good conversation can be as nourishing as the food, and that dignity is something you can either protect or quietly erode with a careless word.

These experiences shaped the question that now drives my interest in social policy. Why do some communities hold together through hardship while others fray? I have started to read about rural development, local governance and the economics of small enterprise, and I have noticed how often the answers depend on ordinary arrangements: who knows whom, who trusts whom, and who is willing to show up. I want to study this at a level where I can move from observation to evidence, and where I can test my assumptions against data and against the perspectives of people unlike myself.

I am aware that my experience is limited. I have not lived in a city, worked in a large institution or studied economics formally, and I expect that a university environment will challenge many of the conclusions I have drawn from a single corner of the country. That challenge is part of what attracts me. I want to be taught to doubt my own certainties and to build arguments that hold up beyond my own experience.

What I bring to a programme like this is a habit of paying attention: to the person at the counter, the one at the back of the hall, and the figures on the page. I am eager to turn that habit into rigorous work, to collaborate with classmates who see the world differently, and to contribute to a community of learners who care about how societies treat their most vulnerable members. I believe this is where I can grow most, and where I can begin to give back what I have been given.

My name is Alina Brooks, and I have spent the past eleven years building software that helps small clinics keep their scheduling and billing in order. Before that I was a nurse in Columbus, Ohio, and I still think the habits I learned on the ward, checking twice, writing things down, and listening carefully, shape everything I do as an engineer. People sometimes ask why I made the jump. The honest answer is that I kept seeing the same preventable problems: a missed follow-up, a duplicated chart, a claim sent to the wrong insurer. Those were not medical failures. They were software failures, and I wanted to be the one fixing them.

My path into the industry was not a straight line. I taught myself to code on night shifts, mostly with a battered laptop and a stack of library books. My first real project was a shift-handoff tool that a few colleagues begged me to build for them. It was messy, but it worked, and it taught me that the best requirements come from people standing next to the problem every day. Since then I have led teams at two health-technology companies and, more recently, co-founded a small firm that works only with independent practices. We are deliberately not chasing hospital systems. Our customers are often two or three doctors and a front-desk person who also does the payroll.

Outside of work, my life is quieter than people might expect. I run early in the morning, usually along the river, and I volunteer on the board of a community clinic that offers free screenings. I also share my home with Maple, a three-legged tabby who has opinions about every keyboard I own. She sits on my notes, my spreadsheets, and occasionally my pull requests. She has taught me more about patience than any management book.

I was invited to speak here partly because of the work we did on our most recent release. On February 14, my team shipped an update that cut average claim-submission time from nine days to under two. I remember that afternoon clearly, mostly because a clinic manager called to say she had finally gone home on time. That phone call meant more to me than any metric on the dashboard.

When I walk on stage, I hope to leave you with one idea: the most useful software often comes from listening to the people who will never write a line of code. If you take that home, the trip will have been worth it. Thank you for having me, and I look forward to the conversations that follow.

Hello everyone, and welcome back to the autumn term! I'm Amelia Hartley, Year 5 teacher here at Brackenfield Primary, and I've been asked to share a little update on our wild-flower project from the summer. Many of you will have seen the seed packets that came home with the children in July. Well, I'm delighted to report that the patch behind the playground has come up beautifully, and the bees have been very happy about it.

The project started with a simple idea. Last spring, a group of parents from the Willow Park area got together and asked whether we could turn the unused strip by the back fence into something useful. Along with Mrs Okafor from the PTA, I spent a rainy Saturday in March clearing bramble and old bricks. Our Year 5 pupils then did the planting, and I still smile when I think of Arjun pushing a wheelbarrow twice his size across the field.

Several people have asked how the children got on with the observation diaries. I was thrilled by the results. Every class kept a weekly log of what they spotted, from ladybirds and hoverflies to a surprisingly large family of snails. The best entries are now pinned in the entrance hall, so please pop in during drop-off to have a look. Parents with a camera are very welcome to take photos for the family album.

If you would like to follow the project, the school has a new page on our social media. Search for @BrackenfieldWildlife and you will find photos, short videos and a monthly update on how the patch is faring. We try to post every Friday, though I confess the bees keep getting in the way of my typing.

Looking ahead, we are planning a volunteer morning on Saturday 14th September, from nine until midday. We will be deadheading, weeding the path edges and putting up a new bird box. Coffee and biscuits will be provided by the PTA, and all helpers are welcome, including siblings. Please reply to the office by Thursday 5th September so we can arrange enough gloves and tools.

Thank you to everyone who has supported this project so far. It has been a joy to watch the children take real ownership of a space that is theirs. I look forward to seeing you at the volunteer morning, and do come and say hello if you pass the fence.

I told him I was fine, and I was fine enough to get through the next shift, but not much more than that.

Sending little voice notes to my old school friend Irene, who lives in Seville now and never lets a conversation end in silence. I wrote those down and felt a small, unfamiliar relief.

אורית, החברה הכי טובה שלי מהאוניברסיטה, התקשרה אתמול בערב. היא רצתה לתאם את יום ההולדת שלה, ב-14 באוגוסט, והזמינה אותי לארוחה בתל אביב. שמחתי לשמוע את הקול שלה, אבל אחרי השיחה הרגשתי שאני מתרחקת ממנה. אני לא יודעת אם זה בגללי או בגללה, ואני מפחדת לשאול.

היום אני צריכה להביא לוועדה את המסמכים שלי לחידוש ההיתר לעבודה. בתיק כתוב מספר תעודת הזהות שלי, 034871569, ושם הדבר נראה כמו פרט טכני, אבל כשאני מסתכלת עליו אני נזכרת שכל הדברים שלי מסודרים במספרים ובתיקיות. נועם אמר שזה חלק ממה שאני מנסה לשלוט בו, ושאולי כדאי לדבר על זה יותר.

בפגישה דיברנו גם על אמא. היא ביקשה שנתראה ב-22 באוגוסט, בדיוק אחרי השבת, ואני עדיין לא החלטתי אם אני הולכת. בכל פעם שאני חושבת על זה, הגוף שלי מתכווץ. נועם שאל אם אני מרגישה שאני צריכה הגנה מהמפגש, ולהפתעתי עניתי שכן.

החלטתי לנסות משהו קטן השבוע: לכתוב לעצמי מכתב קצר בכל בוקר, בלי לערוך. אולי זה יעזור לי לראות את הדפוסים. אני לא בטוחה שזה יעבוד, אבל לפחות זו פעולה אחת שאני לוקחת בידיים שלי.

אני רוצה לזכור שהפגישה הזו הייתה מאומצת, ושבכל זאת יצאתי ממנה עם משהו. בפעם הבאה אני רוצה לדבר עם נועם על אורית, ועל למה אני מרגישה שאני צריכה לבחור בין להיות קרובה אליה לבין לשמור על עצמי.

text:
I am Dieter Hallberg, and I have spent the last eleven years working at the intersection of hydrology and urban planning. I grew up in Passau, where the Danube and the Inn meet, and I think that early exposure to shifting water levels is what first pulled me toward this field. After finishing my secondary schooling at the Gymnasium am Ilzstadt, I studied civil engineering at the Technische Universität München, and later completed a doctorate on stormwater infiltration in dense districts.

My current position is as a senior researcher with a small planning consultancy in Leipzig, where most of my work concerns flood resilience for older neighbourhoods that were never designed for heavy rainfall. We have recently been piloting green roofs and permeable courtyards in the Plagwitz district, and the early monitoring data are more encouraging than I expected. I still spend a surprising amount of time on site, standing in wet boots and talking to residents, because the best ideas I have had came from those conversations rather than from models alone.

Outside the office I coach a youth rowing crew on the Weiße Elster on weekday evenings, a commitment that keeps me honest about the value of teamwork and early starts. I also volunteer with the Leipziger Stadtgrün initiative, helping to map unused urban land that could be converted into rain gardens. My partner, Marleen, often reminds me that I describe every project as though it were the most important one I have ever touched, and she is probably right.

I have been asked to speak at this conference on the subject of adaptive drainage design, and I am grateful for the invitation. The talk will draw on case studies from three German cities and will address both the technical constraints and the political difficulties of retrofitting infrastructure. I am particularly keen to hear from colleagues working in Scandinavia and the Netherlands, whose experience with water management is far more extensive than ours.

If you would like to follow my work, I post occasional updates under the handle @dhallberg_hydro on Mastodon, and I am happy to be contacted directly at dieter.hallberg@plagwitz-hydro.de. For matters requiring formal verification, such as accreditation for the speakers' list, my passport number is C4K9M2P71 and I can provide a copy on request. I look forward to meeting many of you in person.

text:
When I was seventeen, I spent the summer working as a junior pharmacy assistant at Lynch's Pharmacy in Tullamore, which gave me my first real glimpse of what healthcare looks like from the inside. My official title was 'dispensary assistant,' but in practice I spent most of my days restocking shelves, answering questions from older customers about their prescriptions, and learning to tell when someone needed more than a tablet. On the 14th of July, a woman in her seventies came in clutching a crumpled list of medications. She could not remember which tablets she had already taken that morning, and she was frightened. Our pharmacist, Mary Lynch, took the time to sit with her for twenty minutes, drawing up a simple chart. I watched how gently she spoke, and I realised that care is often just patience given freely.

That moment shaped the questions I now bring to my studies. I want to understand not only how drugs work but how people manage their own health when the systems around them are confusing. Ireland's rural communities face particular challenges here, with fewer GP surgeries and longer journeys to hospital. I have since volunteered with a local medication reminder programme, calling patients in the evenings to check they have their prescriptions. The work is quiet and unglamorous, yet it has taught me that good health outcomes depend as much on communication as on chemistry.

I am applying to your Bachelor of Science in Pharmacy because I want to build on that experience with rigorous scientific training. I hope to combine clinical knowledge with the human skills I first saw in that small shop in Tullamore, and to serve patients who, like the woman that July afternoon, need someone to explain things clearly and kindly.

The front desk asked for my passport number, which I thought was a little odd for a dentist, but they explained it was for their insurance verification system and I went along with it. The number on my passport is 548219376, in case anyone at the office is reading this and wondering why I'm sharing it.

The staff were friendly from the moment I walked in. Renata at the front desk remembered that my daughter had just started at Ridgeview Elementary and asked how she was settling in. That kind of small attention matters more to me than people realize. My husband Brandon, who works at Hollis Freight Logistics and has been a patient here for even longer than I have, always says the same thing: they treat you like a neighbor, not a number.

The actual procedure was quick. Dr. Ahmadi explained each step before doing it, which I appreciated since I tend to get anxious in the chair. She found the crack was superficial and sealed it the same day, so I didn't need the crown I was dreading. The hygienist, Mateo, was gentle and talked me through the cleaning without making me feel judged about how long it had been since my last visit, which, let's be honest, was longer than it should have been.

I did have one complaint. The wait time was about forty minutes past my appointment, which I only know because I checked my phone repeatedly. I was on my lunch break and had to call my office to say I'd be late. A text reminder about possible delays would have been helpful.

The billing was clear and fair, and the office manager, Keisha, walked me through the charges without any pressure to upgrade my plan. My next six-month checkup is booked for July 19 at 9:30 in the morning, which I'm already looking forward to, mostly because I know the drive is easy from our house on Alder Court.

Overall I'd give Maple Street Dental four stars. The care is excellent and the team is kind. Shorter waits would bring it to five. If you're in the area and need a dentist you can trust, I'd recommend them without hesitation.

When I was seventeen, I spent my summers working as a junior analyst at Bayanihan Agri Logistics Inc. in Iloilo City, a title that sounded far more impressive than the work itself. My job was to reconcile delivery manifests for rice shipments moving between Panay and Negros. Most days I sat beside Rowena Dizon, the warehouse supervisor who taught me that a spreadsheet error can delay a whole barangay's supply. Rowena never let me forget that numbers describe real families waiting for real sacks of rice.

One afternoon in May, a shipment came up short by forty bags. Rowena asked me to trace the discrepancy, and I spent two days cross-checking the driver logs, the gate records, and the vehicle registration on the truck, which was listed under plate number ABC 1234. The problem turned out to be a clerical mix-up in our own system, not theft. I still remember the relief in Rowena's voice when I told her, and the way she nodded and said, "Good. Now fix the process so it cannot happen again."

That summer taught me that careful work is a form of care. Back then I did not yet know I wanted to study economics, but I knew I wanted to build systems that people can trust. Applying to your university feels like the next step in that same direction: I want to learn the theory behind the logistics I have already seen fail and succeed on the ground.

Toch wil ik proberen de woorden te vinden die recht doen aan de vrouw die wij allemaal zo goed kenden, en die voor ons zoveel betekende.

Yvonne had een manier om mensen het gevoel te geven dat ze gezien werden. Of je nu kwam voor een kopje koffie, voor advies, of gewoon omdat je een slechte dag had, je ging altijd met een lichter hart weg. Ze luisterde echt. Ze onderbrak niet, ze oordeelde niet, en ze had altijd een vraag die je aan het denken zette. Ik heb dat van haar geleerd, en ik ben er elke dag dankbaar voor.

Als ik terugdenk aan de keukentafel waar zoveel verhalen werden verteld, dan zie ik haar lachen. Het was geen zachte lach. Het was een lach die je hele lijf deed schudden, vaak om iets wat ze net had gezegd en waar ze zelf het hardst om moest lachen. Ze kon ook zo eigenwijs zijn als het erop aankwam. Discussies met haar waren nooit saai, en soms verloor ik er, tot mijn grote ergernis, ook nog van.

Haar liefde voor de natuur was iets wat ze graag met ons deelde. Ze kende de namen van bijna elke vogel die voorbijvloog en ze kon uren op een bankje zitten, gewoon kijken naar het licht dat door de bomen viel. Ze zei altijd dat de herfst haar favoriete seizoen was, omdat alles dan even stilstaat voordat het weer opnieuw begint. Misschien is dat ook wel hoe ik haar nu zie: in een moment van rust, net voor iets nieuws.

Yvonne, we zullen je missen, elke dag opnieuw, in de kleine dingen en de grote momenten. Dank je voor alles wat je ons hebt gegeven. Rust nu maar, je hebt het verdiend.

I am Andreas Papadopoulos, and I have spent the last nineteen years working at the intersection of marine ecology and small-scale fisheries policy. I am thirty-eight years old, and I was born in Thessaloniki, though my family moved south to Patras when I was seven. Those early summers on the Gulf of Corinth, watching fishermen mend their nets at dawn, are the reason I chose this field. My first research grant, awarded in January 2009, funded a three-year survey of octopus populations along the Peloponnese coast, and it taught me that the most useful data often comes from the people who have worked those waters for generations.

Since then my work has focused on co-management: designing catch rules together with cooperatives rather than handing them down from Athens or Brussels. I currently lead a small team at the Hellenic Marine Research Centre, where we run monthly workshops in harbour towns across the Argolid. Andreas, as my colleagues sometimes call me, is a nickname I have never fully shaken off, and I have come to like it. It reminds me that the science is only ever one voice among many.

At this conference I will present our findings from the 2023 pilot programme, which reduced accidental bycatch of juvenile red mullet by roughly a third in two seasons. I am glad to share both the successes and the frustrations. I would especially welcome conversations with anyone working on similar partnerships in the Mediterranean, because I am convinced that the next breakthroughs will come from exchanging what has and has not worked on the water.

Today was the first time I said out loud that I am tired of being the person who holds everything together at work. Maya, my sister, called this afternoon while I was on the bus home. She said I sounded flat. I told her I was fine, which is the reflex I need to stop. She reminded me that she had sent me the link to that wellbeing course with the Mindful Leaders group, and I admitted I had not even opened it. She laughed, not unkindly, and said I should at least follow their account on Instagram, @mindfulledgeuk, which I did while she was still on the phone. Small wins.

Dr Okafor and I went over the paperwork again on Monday, the one I have to bring to my GP appointment on 19 March. I had to find my passport, which is number 512948371, because the clinic wanted identification on file for the referral. Holding it made the whole thing feel more official than I expected, and I got a bit weepy in the car park, which is embarrassing but also probably healthy.

We talked about the pattern: I say yes first, then resent it, then feel guilty for resenting it. Dr Okafor asked what would happen if I said no and the building did not fall down. I did not have a good answer. I am going to try one small no this week, maybe to the Friday report that nobody reads anyway. I wrote the draft reply to my manager, Graham, and I will send it tomorrow if my nerve holds.

If I am honest, the thing I am most scared of is that without the busyness I will have to sit with how lonely some of these months have been. If you go, give yourself a whole afternoon for Yanaka and resist the urge to rush. Pick a backstreet, follow it until it dead-ends, then turn around. Before leaving she sent the revised figures to rafael.santos@vasconcelos-log.com.br and copied Dona Lucia in accounts, just in case. Nina walked home under the jacarandas feeling tired but oddly proud. Rafael texted at midnight: 'Nina, you're a machine.' She laughed, put the phone face down, and fell asleep before she could answer.

Looking back, the moment that shaped me most was not a grand achievement but a quiet failure. I had spent months preparing for a robotics competition, convinced that the best design would win. When our prototype broke down in front of the judges, I felt the familiar urge to blame the materials, the schedule, or my teammates. Instead, I sat with the wreckage for a while and asked myself what I could actually learn from it.

What I learned was that I had been treating my own ideas as finished products rather than hypotheses. I had not tested the drivetrain under load, and I had dismissed a classmate's suggestion because it came from someone I assumed was less experienced. That realization changed how I work. Now I build in small increments, invite criticism early, and keep a running log of what fails and why. The habit has made me a better collaborator, and it has taught me to value a question as much as an answer.

I am drawn to engineering because it rewards this kind of honest iteration. I want to study systems that are messy, interdependent, and imperfect, and to contribute to solving problems where the first attempt is rarely the last. The failure at that competition was painful, but it gave me something a trophy never could: a clear sense of how I want to think and how I want to grow.

text:
Good morning, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Thomas Ashworth, and I was lucky enough to be Jim's son. Most of you knew him as Jimmy, which he insisted on right up until he was seventy-eight, when he finally let my daughter call him Grandad Jim and then pretended he hadn't enjoyed it.

Dad was born on the 14th of January 1947 at the Royal Infirmary in Leeds, and he never let us forget that it was snowing. He grew up at 22 Holbeck Avenue, Headingley, in a house where there was always someone at the kitchen table. He went to Leeds Grammar School, and he always said the only thing he learned there was how to fix a bicycle chain under a desk. He was not a scholar, but he was the cleverest man with his hands I have ever met.

He worked for thirty-one years at the same engineering firm, Harcourt & Lowe on Wellington Street, and he could tell you the serial number of every lathe in the place. When the firm closed, he took the redundancy money, bought a second-hand Vauxhall Cavalier with the registration plate KWR 4471, and drove it around the country for two summers. He called it his retirement, and I think it was the happiest I ever saw him.

Dad loved a good argument, a bad pun and a Saturday in the garden. He grew the most enormous runner beans and gave them away to anyone who stood still long enough. He would tell the same stories at every wedding and funeral, and somehow they got better each time. He never once let a cup of tea go cold if he could help it, and he always, always remembered your birthday, even when he had nothing to give you but a card and a terrible joke.

So I'll finish where he would have wanted me to. Dad, thank you for the bicycle chains, the runner beans and the endless patience. You were the best of us, and we will keep your kettle warm for you. Rest well, Jimmy.

I grew up in Duluth, Minnesota, where the lake shaped my sense of water as something to be respected and managed rather than simply enjoyed.

My path into engineering was not straight. I studied geology for two years before switching to civil engineering at the University of Wisconsin, mostly because I wanted to build things that people would use every day. My first real project was a retention basin in a neighbourhood that flooded every spring, and watching residents walk their children past it in the summer still feels like the best evidence I have that the work matters. Since then I have led design teams on drainage upgrades, green infrastructure pilots, and two bridge culvert replacements.

Over the last four years I have spent more time on community engagement than I expected. Public meetings are difficult, and I have learned that a diagram rarely persuades anyone on its own. What works is walking the site with people, listening to what they have already noticed, and treating local knowledge as data. That approach shaped the stormwater plan we delivered for the Eastside district last autumn, which was approved with unusually little opposition.

Outside the office I coach a youth robotics team on Saturday mornings and keep a small vegetable garden that is, by any honest measure, losing a long war with the deer. I am also an enthusiastic and sometimes overly earnest contributor to online discussions about infrastructure policy. You can find me on social media as @gare_builds_water, where I post photos from site visits and the occasional rant about culvert sizing.

I look forward to talking with you at the conference about resilient drainage, the economics of green infrastructure, and how cities can plan for heavier rainfall than their older systems were ever designed to handle. If you would like to continue the conversation afterwards, you can reach me directly at 612-555-0147. I am always happy to talk water, and I will probably bring too many slides.

Talk to people already doing the job, not just recruiters. And be prepared for the first three months to feel uncomfortable, because that discomfort usually means you're learning.

Dr. Haskell asked me what I wanted from those calls. I didn't have an answer, which annoyed me more than anything else. I think I want her to ask me something she doesn't already know the answer to. I want to be a person to her instead of a project.

What I did do this week: I went to the Thursday swim class at the community center, even though I stood at the edge of the pool for ten minutes before getting in. I talked to a woman named Renee afterward who said she also grew up in a town where everyone knew your business. We both laughed about it. Me cogió el teléfono Marta, la recepcionista, que me dio cita para esa misma tarde. El doctor Iñaki Benítez me atendió con una calma que agradezco, me explicó cada paso de la endodoncia y no me hizo sentir culpable por haber dejado pasar el dolor durante semanas.

Lo que más me gustó fue el seguimiento. Ya sé que hay clínicas más baratas en el centro, pero aquí pagas por un trato humano y por saber que alguien se acuerda de ti.

No todo es perfecto. La sala de espera es pequeña y en las horas punta hay que esperar un poco más de lo anunciado, y el aparcamiento de la zona es un desastre. Pero cuando lo comparo con lo que me pasó en mi anterior dentista, en la otra punta de la ciudad, no tengo ninguna queja seria.

I wanted to write down what happened at my appointment on October 14 so I don't forget anything when I talk to my family about it. My name is Tessa Lindqvist and I went to see Dr. Anand at the Brampton Civic Hospital family clinic, which is the same place my mom has been going for years. I had been having dizzy spells for about three weeks, mostly when I stand up quickly after working at my desk, and some mornings a dull headache that doesn't go away until lunch. I also mentioned that I've been sleeping badly since starting my second term at Western University.

Dr. Anand checked my blood pressure twice because the first reading was high, probably because I was nervous and had run from the parking lot. She asked a lot of questions about my diet, how much water I drink, and whether I've been using my laptop late at night. I told her I'm up until about one most nights studying, and that I skip breakfast on weekdays. She listened to my heart and lungs and looked in my ears, then sent me for bloodwork that same morning.

The lab results came back on October 21 and Dr. Anand called me herself, which I appreciated. My iron levels are a bit low and my vitamin D is under the healthy range. She thinks the dizziness is mostly from iron deficiency and not sleeping enough, so she prescribed an iron supplement to take with orange juice and asked me to come back in six weeks for a recheck. She also gave me a referral to a nutritionist, though I haven't booked that yet.

My partner, Marcus, drove me to the appointment and waited in the car, so I'm writing this partly to remind him what the plan is. He's been worried since I told him about the headaches, and I think it helped him to hear that it's probably something simple to fix. My sister Erin also asked me to keep her posted because she had similar anemia when she was in university, so I told her I'd send her the lab numbers.

For my own notes: take the iron tablet every morning, drink more water, eat breakfast even if it's just toast, try to be off screens by midnight, and book the nutritionist before the end of October. Next appointment is on November 25 at 10:30. If the dizziness gets worse before then, or I faint, I'm supposed to call the clinic right away or go to emergency. Account reference for the billing office is 40817-226, and my car registration is in the glovebox if I ever need it for the insurance paperwork.

text:
My name is Gilad, but my grandmother has called me Gigi since the day I was born, and the name has followed me through every classroom I have ever sat in. I am seventeen, and for most of my life I have measured myself against the people who grew up around me in our building at 14 Herzl Street in Haifa, where the stairwell smells of cardamom from the Iraqi family on the second floor and the view from our balcony stretches all the way to the port. That building taught me that a neighborhood is a set of small obligations: carrying groceries for the widow downstairs, repairing the broken gate with my cousin Yoni, and listening to stories on Friday evenings that I only half understood at the time.

The moment I started to think seriously about engineering came on October 9th, when our water pump failed during a heat wave and forty families were left without running water for three days. I spent those days with a multimeter and a library book on pumps, tracing the wiring with my uncle Avi until we found a corroded relay. The repair took twenty minutes. The understanding I gained over those three days took much longer, and it made me want to build systems that keep ordinary people safe and comfortable when something inevitably goes wrong.

I hope to study mechanical engineering because I want to work on exactly these problems, the ones that touch daily life in cities like mine. My teachers describe me as persistent and my neighbors describe me as useful, and I would like to become an engineer who is both. I believe a university that values hands-on learning and community responsibility would give me the tools to do that.

text:
I still think about the afternoon we spent in Haarlem last July, wandering the narrow streets behind the Grote Markt with no real plan. My sister Claudia had insisted we leave Amsterdam for a day, and she was right. We started at the Frans Hals Museum, where I stood in front of a portrait for almost ten minutes while Claudia laughed at me for being so quiet. Claudia works as a senior curator at the Rijksmuseum, so she spotted details I would have missed entirely, like the way the painter let the brushwork show in the lace collars. Her colleagues at the Rijksmuseum had warned her that Haarlem was too small to bother with, but I think they were wrong.

After the museum we crossed the old town toward the Spaarne river, stopping every few minutes for photos. Claudia kept checking her phone because a rota for the conservation team at the Rijksmuseum had to go out that evening, and she grumbled about it cheerfully. We found a little bakery on a side street where the owner, an older man with flour on his forearms, gave us two extra stroopwafels just because we asked him where the best view of the Bakenesser Gracht was. That kind of warmth is what I remember most about the Netherlands, more than any tulip field or canal house.

In the late afternoon we rented bikes, which is the only sensible way to see the countryside around the city. We rode out past the dunes toward Zandvoort, the wind pushing against us the whole way, and Claudia shouted that she would never forgive me if I let her fall behind. We stopped for chips with mayonnaise at a seaside kiosk, the sort of meal that tastes better than it has any right to after hours of cycling.

By the time we returned to the station, my legs were jelly and my camera battery was nearly empty. Claudia, who had memorised every train timetable on the trip, booked us onto the last direct service back to Amsterdam Centraal. We sat by the window and talked about our childhood in Leiden, where our mother used to take us to the botanical garden, and about the medical school our cousin had just started at Leiden University Medical Center. I fell asleep before the train reached Schiphol.

If you visit Haarlem in July, do yourself a favour: rent a bike, skip the first museum on your list if you must, and find that bakery. Claudia has promised to take me back next summer, and I have already started planning the route.

text:
I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to share that my father, Ryuji Matsuda, passed away peacefully at home in Kanazawa on the 14th of December, surrounded by the family he loved so fiercely. He was seventy-eight years old. Many of you knew him as the quiet man who never missed a Thursday at the Yanaka fish market, or as the teacher who spent thirty-one years at Nishi Kanazawa Junior High patiently explaining the difference between ellipsis and apostrophe to restless fourteen-year-olds.

Ryuji was born in Hakodate in 1946, the second of four children, to a family of fishmongers who had learned to read the tides before they learned to read books. He never lost that sense of the sea. Even in his final months, when he could no longer walk to the harbour, he asked me to describe the boats coming in each morning, and he would nod along as if he could see every hull. He often told me that the town where he was born had taught him patience, and the city where he raised us had taught him kindness.

After university in Sapporo he moved south to Kanazawa, where he met my mother, Hanako, at a tea house near the Higashi Chaya district in the spring of 1974. He pretended for a year that he had not fallen in love with her at first sight. She never believed him, and she teased him about it every anniversary until she passed in 2019. Their love was the kind that did not need to be loud, and I think that is the greatest thing I learned from him.

He was a man of small rituals. Every morning he brewed green tea in the same brown pot, every evening he listened to the radio broadcast of the baseball scores with his eyes closed, and every New Year's Eve he wrote a single line of haiku in a notebook, which he never showed anyone. Only after his death did we find the notebooks, forty years of them, tied with string on the shelf above his desk. We are still deciding what to do with them.

He is survived by his children, Keiko and Takeshi, and by three grandchildren who adored him. Those who wish to share memories are warmly invited to write to me directly or post them on his tribute page, which the family has set up under the handle @ryuji.matsuda.tribute. A memorial service will be held at Kōdai-ji temple on the 21st of December at ten in the morning. Please come if you can, and bring a story. He would have wanted us to tell them over tea.

With gratitude and love,
Keiko Matsuda

Tuesday 14 October

Rain again this morning, the kind that comes sideways off the Atlantic and gets into everything. I walked up to the bus stop on Harcourt Road with my hood up and my bag clutched against my chest, and by the time the 46A pulled in I was already regretting not taking the car. Mam would have told me so. She texts me every morning now, usually about the weather and whether I've eaten, and today she sent a photo of the kettle with the message "Put this on, you sound peaky on the phone." She is right, I did sound peaky. I've been sleeping badly since the move.

The new flat is at 27 Blackrock Gardens, Dublin 6, on the third floor, and the landlord is a retired teacher called Mr Keane who insists on calling me "Miss Brennan" as if I were fourteen. The building is old, the radiators clank like they're trying to get out, and the window in the back bedroom doesn't quite close. But the light in the kitchen in the afternoons is extraordinary, all gold across the worktop, and I've already started thinking of it as mine. Everyone in the family has a name for me. Mam calls me Oonagh, Dad calls me Oonie, and my brother, who has never once used my real name, calls me Nagger, which I have asked him repeatedly to stop doing.

Work was busy. The Hendricks report is due on the 22nd and Fergal from accounts keeps sending me emails with the subject line URGENT in capitals, as if I hadn't noticed. I replied to the last one with a single line: "Noted. Attached is the draft." I didn't add that the draft is actually finished and has been since Thursday. Sometimes I like to watch the emails pile up and then answer them all at once.

In the evening I finally called Ciara. We talked for almost two hours, mostly about her wedding planning and whether the venue in Kilkenny is worth the deposit. She asked if I'd joined any clubs yet and I said no, and she gave me the look even down the phone. She's sending me the link to the running group that meets on Saturdays in Phoenix Park. I said I would think about it. I probably will.

Before bed I wrote down the address and my email, oonagh.brennan@mailbox.ie, on the inside cover of this notebook, because I keep forgetting my own details when I fill in forms and it's embarrassing. Tomorrow I want to go to the market on Sunday, buy proper bread, and perhaps finally open the boxes in the hall. Goodnight, diary. The radiator is making its noise again.

Do you remember I told you about Pietro, the cousin who ran the bakery in Testaccio? Well, I finally went to see him last month, after almost three years of putting it off. I landed in Rome on the 4th of October with one suitcase and a passport number I must have written down a dozen times that week, PT9384071, because the airline kept asking for it. Pietro met me at the station with flour still on his shirt and hugged me so hard my ribs complained.

He took me up the narrow stairs of his building on Via Marmorata, and his wife Chiara had made cacio e pepe before I'd even put my bag down. We talked until nearly midnight about our grandmother's recipes and the old fight over the family house in Frosinone. Pietro kept calling me Pino, the childhood name nobody else uses anymore, and every time he said it I felt about nine years old again.

What I didn't expect was how easy it felt to be back. Testaccio still smells of bread and diesel in the mornings, and the woman at the corner stall still remembered my coffee order from when I was a teenager. I told Pietro I'm thinking of moving back for good, maybe next spring. He just laughed and said, 'Then you'd better learn the bus routes properly, Pino.' I think I will.

I still think about the morning Franco woke us up in Siargao, grinning like he had personally arranged the sunrise. He had been up since four with his surfboard, and by the time I stumbled out of our guesthouse on June 12, he had already talked two local fishermen into showing us their favourite break. We spent the first hour in the shallows, falling off boards and laughing so hard that the tide nearly carried my sunglasses out to sea. Franco's friend Marisol, a physiotherapist from Cebu who has been surfing since she was nine, watched us with the patience of someone who had seen a thousand beginners before us. She corrected my stance with two taps on the back and a single word: 'knees.'

Later that day we rode a tricycle across the island to Sohoton Cove, where the water turns a shade of green I didn't know existed. Franco insisted on bringing his camera, and he spent more time photographing his own reflection in the lagoon than the limestone cliffs. Everyone on the boat knew him as Kiko, a nickname his grandmother gave him when he was a toddler and that has never quite gone away. Between dives, he kept showing me videos of his dog back home in Davao, a scruffy mutt named Biscuit who, according to Franco, is the true ruler of the household. Biscuit is nearly fourteen now, and Franco's voice softened every time he mentioned him.

The following evening, we ate grilled squid and rice at a plastic-table stall in General Luna while Marisol kept reading out messages from the group chat. Someone had posted a blurry photo of us wiping out on our first wave, captioned with the handle @wavesandwanderlust_ph, and it had already collected more than two hundred likes. Franco pretended to be offended and then demanded a copy. We walked back along the dark road with our flip-flops in hand, listening to the crickets and the distant thump of a karaoke machine.

If you ever make it to Siargao, ask for Franco at the surf shop near the church. He will tell you the same stories I have told you here, and he will probably add a few more. Bring sunscreen, bring patience, and bring a little more courage than you think you need.

I still cannot quite believe that Melina Papadaki is gone. She was born in Kalamata on 14 April 1948, the second of four daughters, and she never let anyone forget that she was the one who had actually read the family's letters from Athens. For forty-one years she worked as a senior archivist at the Benaki Museum, and she spoke about old documents the way other people speak about their favourite football team. Many of us in the neighbourhood of Koukaki still remember her walking to the Saturday market on Veikou Street with a canvas bag and a sharp opinion about everything from olive oil prices to the new tram lines.

My own name is Nikos Vlachos, and I was her neighbour for almost twenty years, from the day I moved into the flat below hers on Dafni Street. She taught me to make spanakopita the way her mother did, though she insisted my pastry was always too thick. In the last months, when her eyesight began to fail, she asked me to read her the newspapers aloud every morning, and she would correct my pronunciation of every foreign name. She trusted me with the spare key and with her dog Tasos, and she never once asked me to be anyone other than myself.

Melina's funeral will be held on Thursday 23 April at the church of Agios Dimitrios at eleven in the morning. Friends who wish to share memories can write to me directly or post them on her page, @melina.archives.athens, which her grandchildren have promised to keep active. She is survived by her sisters Eleni and Sofia, her nephew Giorgos, and a great many people who owe her a book they never returned.

Today I want to write about the move, because my counsellor keeps asking me to name what I am actually grieving instead of calling it "just adjusting." Leaving the flat with the sticky balcony door, the bakery on the corner, and the friends who could drop everything for a late tea felt like shedding a skin I did not know I still had. Here, people are polite in a careful way. They say they will call and then they do not, and I have caught myself doing the same. I keep waiting for the moment when this place will feel like home, and I think that waiting is itself part of the problem.

What surprised me most this week was how angry I got over small things: a form that rejected my surname, a shopkeeper who pretended not to understand me, the way the light falls too early in the afternoon. My counsellor suggested that the anger is often grief wearing a louder coat. I wrote that down and then sat with it for a long time. It is easier to be furious at a bureaucrat than to admit I miss the version of myself who knew where everything was and who to ring when things went wrong.

I am trying a small experiment. Each morning I will write down one thing that is genuinely good here, even if it is only that the tea tastes different or that a stranger held a door without being asked. It feels a little forced, like a child being told to say sorry. But I notice I am starting to look for things rather than only waiting for them. That may be the first real step, even if I am not ready to call it progress yet.

Hey Rohan, I still can't believe I didn't tell you this over chai last week, so here it is in one long message. You know my cousin Vikram? The one who used to drive us to Lodhi Gardens every Sunday? Well, he's been having a rough time since the start of January. He got admitted to Fortis Hospital in Vasant Kunj on the 9th after collapsing at his office in Gurgaon. The doctors said it was his kidneys, and honestly, I was a mess for three days.

What I keep thinking about is how he never told anyone. My aunt only found out because she called him and he didn't pick up, so she went round to his flat in Malviya Nagar and found him on the floor. Can you imagine? I keep replaying that call in my head, wondering why we all let him drift like that. He always said he was fine, that it was just stress from work at Sharma & Associates.

The funny part is that Vikram was always the one bossing everyone around. At St. Columba's School he was the captain of the debating team, and he still talks about how we lost the inter-school finals because of a missing comma in some speech. Even now, from his hospital bed, he's grumbling about the food and asking me to bring him proper parathas from Old Delhi. So at least his sense of humour is intact.

He's been moved out of the ICU now, and the doctors say he can go home in about two weeks if his numbers keep improving. I've been giving him updates whenever I can, and my number is still 98114 32067 if you want to call me directly. Don't worry about visiting in the middle of your exams; just send him a voice note, he'll love it.

Anyway, that's the story. I'm exhausted but relieved. Honestly, I think this whole ordeal has made me realise how much we take people for granted. Call me when you get a free evening, okay? We need to plan that trip to Rishikesh we keep postponing.

Take care, and give my love to your mum.

Anjali Verma

Vilhelm Andersson grew up on Hammarby Allé in Stockholm, in a flat where the radiator clanked every morning at six and the windows looked over a small park with three birch trees. Most of what I know about patience I learned from watching my grandmother fix things in that flat: a leaking tap, a wobbly chair, the old wooden clock that stopped whenever someone slammed a door. She never hurried a repair. She listened to the problem first, then worked slowly until the object could carry its own weight again.

When I was fourteen I started volunteering at a repair café in Södermalm, once every other Saturday. Our customers brought in toasters, bicycles, lamps and, once, a violin with a cracked neck. Vilhelm, a retired electrician who ran the café, taught me that most broken things are not really broken; they are only waiting for someone to notice what has gone wrong. I spent my first months sorting screws and holding torches. By the end of the year I could diagnose a faulty kettle element on my own.

That experience pushed me toward engineering, but it also made me curious about why people throw things away so quickly. In February of my final school year I began a small survey of households in my building, asking how many appliances had been replaced in the previous twelve months and why. The answers were more varied than I expected. Many people said they did not know how to repair anything, while others said the parts were simply unavailable. I compiled the results into a short report and sent it to the municipal sustainability office, which invited me to present at a neighbourhood meeting on 14 February.

I am applying to your programme in sustainable product design because I want to work on the problem at the level where it begins: the design decisions that determine whether something can be fixed at all. Repair is not only a matter of skill; it depends on modular parts, clear manuals and access to spares. I want to learn how to build those qualities into products from the start.

If you would like to discuss my application or see the survey, you can reach me at vilhelm.andersson@example-mail.se. I would welcome the chance to tell you more about what I have learned at the workbench and in the community around it.

I've been putting off writing this for a week, mostly because my therapist asked me to and I didn't want to admit how much the Tuesday session stuck with me. So here goes. My name is Daniel and I live in Christchurch, though some days it feels like I've been living in a waiting room since the restructure at Kiwi Meridian Logistics. I'm still their Senior Analyst, which sounds more secure than it feels when half the team has been moved to contract roles.

On Tuesday I talked about my dad. He rang me on the 9th of July, just after lunch, and asked whether I'd sorted out the car rego yet. Ordinary stuff, but I spent the whole afternoon replaying the call. I kept thinking he sounded tired, and that I should have asked him how he was doing instead of rushing off to a meeting. My therapist, Marama, pointed out that I always end conversations with him by apologising for being busy, and asked what I'd be saying if I weren't afraid of being a burden.

I didn't have an answer in the room. I've been trying to find one since. Part of the problem is that I haven't told anyone at work how much the uncertainty is getting to me. When Sione from HR emailed about the new reporting structure, I read it three times and still couldn't tell whether my role was staying. I started drafting a reply and then deleted it because it sounded needy.

Marama suggested a small experiment. Each evening this week I'm meant to write down one thing I did for myself, however minor. On the first night I wrote that I went for a walk along the Estuary and didn't check my phone once. It felt almost silly, but it was the first time in a month my shoulders dropped.

I also called Dad back on the Thursday, from the car park outside the office, and asked him properly how he was. He laughed and said nobody had asked him that in years. We talked for forty minutes. I'm going to keep doing that, even if it feels awkward. Next session is on the 23rd, and I think I'll bring the list.

Even after forty years in Columbus, he would still say "back home" when he meant the small brick house on Elm Street where his mother taught piano. He carried that place with him: the stubbornness, the way he'd fix anything with a coffee can and a length of wire, and the habit of waving at every stranger who drove past him on a county road.

He kept a binder full of birthdays and anniversaries, and on February 14 he would send a card to every single one of us, even to the guy in receiving who never answered. If you want to reach out to our family, or share a story about Gerald, please write to gerald.holloway.memories@fastmail.com. We will read every one. Dad would want you to tell the stories that make you laugh first, and the ones that make you cry second. He always believed in that order.

Dr. Levi was patient and asked a lot of questions. She wanted to know when the pain started, whether it got worse at night, and if I had noticed any numbness in my legs. I told her it had come on after I started lifting heavy boxes at the warehouse, and that sitting for long periods made it much worse.

She examined me on the table, pressing along my spine and asking me to bend forward and to the side. I could feel the muscles tighten when she touched one particular spot. She said it looked like a strained muscle combined with some inflammation, and that it was not something that needed scans or anything invasive right now. She also checked my reflexes and my strength, and everything came back normal, which was a relief.

The treatment plan is fairly simple. I have been prescribed an anti-inflammatory medication to take with food for the next ten days, and I should stop if my stomach becomes upset. She recommended gentle walking every day, avoiding heavy lifting for at least two weeks, and using a heating pad in the evenings. She also gave me a referral for physiotherapy, and the clinic will call me to arrange the first session.

I asked whether I should be worried about the pain coming back, and she explained the warning signs to look out for. If I lose feeling in my legs, have trouble controlling my bladder, or the pain becomes sudden and severe, I should go straight to the emergency room without waiting for another appointment. She wrote all of this down on a printed sheet, which I found very helpful, since I tend to forget details once I leave a room.

I left the clinic feeling more reassured than I expected to. The visit was not long, but I felt listened to and I understood what was happening in my body. I will go back for a follow-up in four weeks if the pain has not improved, and I plan to keep a simple diary of how I feel each day so I can give her a clearer picture next time.

text:
Hello everyone, and welcome back to the new term! I am writing this piece for the newsletter as a bit of an introduction, since many of you have asked where I came from and why I joined us partway through the year. The short answer is that I moved here from another country with my family, and the longer answer is much more interesting than I expected it to be.

The first few weeks were a blur. Everything looked familiar and strange at the same time. The bread was different, the words on the shop signs were sometimes unexpected, and the way people greeted one another in the corridors took me a while to get used to. I remember standing in the playground during break, not knowing where to sit, and feeling quite small. Then someone waved me over, and that was the beginning of things getting easier.

What I have learned since then is that moving is less about leaving something behind and more about carrying a few things across with you. For me, it is music, a habit of reading before bed, and a stubborn love of long walks. I have discovered new things too: the sports clubs here are wonderful, the library has a surprisingly good collection of graphic novels, and the teachers have been patient with my questions, even the ones that seemed silly to me at the time.

I would like to thank everyone who has made this transition kinder than I feared. Whether you lent me a pencil, explained a joke I did not understand, or simply asked how my day was going, you made a difference. I have noticed that our school is full of people who are quick to include others, and I think that is something to be proud of.

If you are new this term, or if you have ever felt like the outsider in the room, please know that you are not alone. Come and say hello, join a club, or share your own story in the next edition of this newsletter. I would genuinely love to hear from you.

Thank you for reading, and I look forward to getting to know you all better over the coming months.

I am writing to file a claim for water damage to the ground floor of my home at Calle Alsina 1247, Villa Crespo, Buenos Aires, Argentina. My full name is Tomas Alejandro Quiroga. I was born in Rosario and have lived at this address for eleven years, along with my wife, Lucia, and our son, Mateo. I am 43 years old and have been self-employed as an architectural draftsman for most of my working life.

On the night of January 14, at approximately 11:40 p.m., I was awoken by a loud crack from the direction of the kitchen. When I went downstairs, I found water spreading across the tiled floor from beneath the sink cabinet. The supply line to the dishwasher had split at the fitting, and the pressure had been pushing water out steadily for some time. Lucia had already moved the rugs and was trying to mop up the worst of it with towels, but the water had reached the living room and was seeping under the wooden shelving unit along the east wall.

I shut off the main water valve in the utility room and called the emergency line of my insurer, Seguros Rio de la Plata, at about 11:55 p.m. The claims officer, Ana Belen Ortiz, took down the details and asked me to send photographs as soon as possible. Our neighbour, Hector Gimenez from number 1249, came over with a wet vacuum around midnight and helped us remove standing water from the hallway. Hector later confirmed to me that he had heard the commotion from his side of the wall.

The damage is extensive. The kitchen cabinet base, the dishwasher, and roughly eleven square metres of laminate flooring will need replacement. The wooden shelving unit has swollen and separated at the joints, and the drywall along the east wall shows staining up to about thirty centimetres. Mateo's school books and two of Lucia's sewing projects stored on the lower shelves were also ruined. I have attached a list of damaged items with estimated replacement costs, along with receipts where I still have them, and a plumber's report from Gasfitter Roberto Salas dated January 16 confirming that the fitting failed due to age rather than installation error.

I would be grateful if you could arrange for an assessor to visit the property as soon as your schedule allows, so that repairs can begin and the house can be dried properly before mould develops. Please contact me at tomas.quiroga@mailbox.com.ar or on 011 4555 0182 to confirm a time. I have kept all damaged materials until your assessor has inspected them.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

Tomas Alejandro Quiroga

text:
When my family left Porto for Toronto in the winter of my twelfth year, I believed the hardest part would be learning a new language. I was wrong. The language came slowly, but the silence of a city where nobody knew my grandmother's recipes or the name of the bakery on Rua das Flores was harder. My mother took a job at Brightwater Logistics in Mississauga, and my father, Tomas, began driving a delivery van for a small bakery on Dundas Street. I spent most afternoons with my cousin Inês, who had come over with us, and with Marco, a boy from my homeroom who taught me hockey and, in exchange, asked me to explain Portuguese football to him.

In January 14 of that first year, a blizzard closed the schools and my father could not leave the apartment. We played cards for six hours at the kitchen table while the radiator clanked. I remember thinking that this was what home could be: not the place itself but the people who stayed with you when everything outside had gone white. Tomas taught me to read the weather, and I taught him the word for saudade, which he said was untranslatable and then translated anyway.

Today I think of Porto differently. It is still the city where I was born, but Toronto is where I learned to be a person who asks questions in two languages. I want to study translation and public health because I have seen how much a single misunderstood word can cost a family in a clinic waiting room. My own story is a small one, but it taught me that meaning is always carried by people, and I want to be the one who carries it well.
Session with Dr Okafor on 14 March went better than I expected; I finally told her what Zara-Jo, my sister, calls me, "Zee", and how much it stung when Mum stopped using it.

If you're in the area and you have an older vehicle, call ahead, ask for the itemized estimate in writing, and make sure nothing gets added at pickup.
