3 luglio

Stamattina ho quasi perso il treno per Milano, di nuovo. Ottavio mi ha mandato un messaggio alle sei e mezza per ricordarmi della riunione con la Bianchi Logistica, e io ho risposto con un pollice alzato e poi mi sono riaddormentato. Quando finalmente sono arrivato in ufficio in via Marconi 14, Silvia mi ha guardato con quella faccia che dice tutto senza dire niente. Ho passato la giornata a sistemare i fogli del progetto nuovo e a cercare di non pensare alla telefonata di ieri sera.

La mamma ha chiamato alle sette, come sempre. Mi ha chiesto se mangio abbastanza e se ho sentito lo zio Franco, che è di nuovo in ospedale per il cuore. Le ho detto di sì a tutte e due le cose, anche se in realtà non ho sentito nessuno da settimane. Mio fratello Ottavino, che lei chiama ancora così nonostante abbia trentotto anni, le ha passato il telefono a metà conversazione e ha urlato che devo andare a trovarli a Pavia il prossimo weekend. Ho detto che ci penso.

Giovedì sera sono uscito con Silvia e Matteo nel quartiere Navigli, dove c'è quel posto con i tavolini fuori sull'acqua. Matteo ha raccontato per la ventesima volta la storia del suo capo che si è addormentato durante la presentazione davanti al cliente. Abbiamo riso fino alle lacrime. Silvia mi ha detto che secondo lei dovrei cambiare lavoro, che la Bianchi mi sfrutta. Non so se ha ragione, ma l'idea mi tiene sveglio la notte.

Oggi ho trovato per caso una vecchia fotografia nella borsa, quella dell'estate in cui io e Ottavio abbiamo guidato fino al lago di Como con la vecchia Panda rossa. Eravamo tutti e due magri e sorridenti, con il sole in faccia. Mi sono chiesto quando abbiamo smesso di fare cose così semplici. Forse quando ho iniziato a rispondere ai messaggi alle sei del mattino.

Domani il capo vuole vedere i numeri del secondo trimestre, il 9 luglio è la scadenza per il report finale. Devo chiudere tutto entro mercoledì. Ho già preparato il caffè per domattina e ho messo la sveglia alle sei e dieci, con la speranza che stavolta basti.

text:
I saw Dr. Mehra at the Sunrise Multispeciality Clinic in Pune on 14 November because the pain in my lower back had not gone away for three weeks. He asked me to lie on the examination couch, pressed along my spine, and then ordered an X-ray and a blood panel. My wife Sunita came with me and kept asking questions I had forgotten to ask, which annoyed me a little but was probably a good thing. The clinic receptionist, Ramesh, was very patient with my paperwork and even remembered my mobile number, 98234 17650, from my last visit in March.

Dr. Mehra says the X-ray shows mild wear in the L4-L5 disc, nothing alarming, and that most people my age have something similar. He wants me to stop lifting heavy bags of cement at the site, do the stretching routine he wrote down, and come back on 28 November with the blood report. He also told me to stop sitting for hours at my desk. I explained that my colleague Arvind Joshi and I have been trying to finish the Bandra project, so I cannot exactly take a break, and he just laughed and said I should try a standing desk. Sunita has already decided we will buy one this weekend.

On the way home we stopped at Chai Point near the station, which is my usual reward after any medical visit. My son Rohan called to ask if I was okay, and I told him I was fine, just getting old, which he says is what everyone says before they start complaining. My mother, whom everyone calls Bablu in the family, sent a message asking whether I had eaten, which is her way of checking on me. I am going to follow the exercises properly this time. I have promised Sunita and I have promised myself.

I am writing to describe the water damage that occurred in my flat on the third floor of a converted building in the centre of a French town, and to request that the claim be processed as soon as possible. On the morning in question I left for work as usual, having checked that all taps were closed and the washing machine had finished its cycle. When I returned in the early evening, the hallway floor was covered in standing water, and the water had already seeped under the bedroom door and into the parquet of the living room.

The source appeared to be a failed flexible hose connected to the washing machine in the small utility cupboard off the kitchen. The hose had split along a crimp, and the water had run for several hours before anything was noticed. The neighbours below reported a damp patch spreading across their ceiling, which is how the leak first came to light. I turned off the mains supply to the apartment straight away and called the building's caretaker, who arranged for a plumber to attend the same evening to isolate the appliance.

The damage is extensive. The engineered wood in the hallway and living room has lifted and warped and will need to be replaced throughout. The plasterboard on the kitchen wall behind the machine is saturated and has begun to crumble, and the skirting boards along two walls are beyond repair. Several pieces of furniture, including a sideboard and a bookcase, sat on the wet floor for hours and have swollen and delaminated. I have also lost a number of books and some electrical items that were stored on the lower shelves of the cupboard.

I have kept the failed hose, photographs of the affected rooms taken before any clearing took place, and the plumber's written report, which confirms the cause of the leak. I have also collected quotations from two local contractors for the flooring and plastering work, and I have listed each damaged item with its approximate age and value where I still hold a receipt. Copies of all these documents are enclosed with this description.

I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt of this claim and let me know whether any further evidence is required. I am happy to allow an assessor to visit the property at a time convenient to them, and I will make the affected rooms available for inspection. Please contact me if you need anything else to progress the matter.

Last month I took my car into Hanlon's Motor Works on the Old Mill Road in Drumcondra, Dublin, after the brakes started squealing every time I came up to the lights. My name is Kieran Dwyer and I've been a loyal customer of small garages for about fifteen years, so I'm not easily impressed.

The waiting area is small and the coffee machine is temperamental, so bring something to read, but nobody made me feel rushed.

If you live in Drumcondra or anywhere near it and need a reliable garage that won't upsell you, I'd recommend Hanlon's without hesitation. text:
Ilan Shapira here, writing from a café in the Florentin neighbourhood of Tel Aviv, where I have spent the better part of three mornings now. I arrived on the 4th of October with one backpack, a battered paperback and absolutely no plan, which I have decided is the correct way to start a trip in this country. The city wakes up slowly and then all at once. By nine the shutters on Shabazi Street are up, the smell of fresh za'atar bread drifts out of the bakeries, and somebody is always arguing cheerfully about football on the corner.

On my first full day I walked from the Carmel Market down to the port, stopping every fifteen metres to photograph another mural. The graffiti here is not decoration for tourists; it is a running conversation between neighbours, and you can read a whole year of local politics and birthdays on one wall if you slow down. I ate hummus so good that I briefly considered abandoning my flight home. Lunch was a plate of shakshuka eaten standing up, because every seat was taken by old men playing backgammon with ferocious concentration.

If you want to book a guided food walk, the operator I used is called Shuk Trails and their office number is 03-555-0148. Ask for Noa, who was patient with my appalling Hebrew and far too generous with her recommendations. She said the best falafel in the district is the one with the longest queue, and she was right. Ilan's advice to anyone planning a visit: go early, bring cash, and do not be shy about asking for a second pita.

The weekend brought a day trip to Jaffa, where the old stone alleys climb up from the sea in a way that makes your calves complain. I sat for an hour above the water watching fishermen mend their nets while the call to prayer from one mosque and the church bells from another drifted over the rooftops, and neither seemed to mind the other. It was the most peaceful hour of the whole trip, and I came close to missing my bus back to the city because of it.

By my last morning I had settled into a rhythm: coffee at the same counter, a short walk along the promenade, and a long goodbye to the cats who seemed to own the entire block. I leave on the 19th of October, slightly heavier and considerably less organised than I arrived. If you are reading this and wondering whether to go, the answer is yes. Write to me at ilan.shapira@travelnotes.co.il if you want my full list of places, and bring an appetite.

Growing up, I spent most of my weekends helping out at a small community kitchen run by volunteers who never seemed to tire, even on the coldest mornings. I started by peeling vegetables and stacking tins, but over time I found myself asking questions about why certain families came every week and others never did. That curiosity led me to read about food insecurity, and eventually to a conversation with one of the regular volunteers, a retired teacher who told me that the hardest part of the work was not the cooking but the quiet dignity required to make everyone feel welcome. Her words stayed with me long after the shift ended.

That experience taught me that good intentions are not enough without careful attention to the people being served. I began keeping a notebook of the small changes that made a difference, such as moving the queue indoors during rain or offering a choice of meals rather than a single portion. When I suggested some of these ideas to the coordinators, they listened, and several were adopted. I learned that listening is itself a form of service, and that the most useful contribution I could make was often to observe carefully before acting.

text:
Elena Ruiz Ocampo passed away peacefully at home in San Miguel de Allende on the night of December 14, surrounded by her children and a full kitchen of family. She was eighty-one years old. Born in Guanajuato in 1943, the second of six children, Elena grew up learning to bargain at the Mercado Hidalgo and to sing harmonies in the church choir. She never lost either habit.

For more than forty years Elena kept the books for the family hardware store on Calle Real, a job she described as "numbers with opinions." She knew every customer by name and most of their grandparents. When the store finally closed in 2006, she bought a small blue Nissan, plate number NLX-4471, and drove it everywhere she could justify, which was almost everywhere. Her grandchildren still tease her about the afternoon she parked it across two spaces outside the bank and informed the guard that it was none of his business.

Elena married Javier Ocampo in 1966 at the parish of San Rafael, and they raised three children together. After Javier's death in 1998 she remained the family's steady center, hosting Sunday lunches for twenty or more and keeping a ledger of birthdays that no one dared to question. She taught her great-grandchildren to play dominoes and to cheat at them gently.

Her dog, Tamalito, a scruffy brown mutt she adopted from a shelter in 2015, accompanied her on every walk through the Parque Juárez and was never far from her chair. The family asks that donations be made in her honor to the shelter where she found him.

Elena is survived by her children Mariana, Ricardo and Lucía; seven grandchildren; nine great-grandchildren; and her sister, Teresa, of Querétaro. A wake will be held on December 17 at the family home on Calle Mesones, followed by a Mass at San Rafael on December 18. Those who knew her will remember that she always had one more story and one more plate of food for whoever walked through the door.

Elena, we will keep the books balanced in your absence. Descansa en paz.

I am writing this with a heavy heart, because the person I loved most in the world has gone, and I find myself trying to put into words what that absence means. For more years than I can easily count, the voice on the other end of the line was the first thing I looked forward to in the morning. She had a way of making the ordinary feel worth noticing, whether it was the light over the hills in late afternoon or the stubborn ripeness of a fruit she had planted with her own hands. She believed that kindness was a practice rather than a feeling, and she practiced it every day, often in ways no one else would have thought to see.

She leaves behind a circle of people who were shaped by her generosity. Friends who arrived unannounced at her door always left with a meal, a warm word, or a practical solution to something that had seemed unsolvable. Those of us in the family learned from her that patience and humour are not opposites, and that a good laugh can carry you through the hardest rooms. She could be fierce when something was unjust, and tender when someone needed comfort, and she rarely confused the two.

I will remember her most in the small rituals: the cup of tea set down beside me without a word, the question asked at exactly the right moment, the way she hummed when she thought no one was listening. Those are the things I will carry forward. To everyone who sat with her, called her, or simply thought of her, thank you. text:
I still remember the first Tuesday of September when I walked into the Brunswick Community Pantry, clipboard in hand, and met Sophie Whitfield, the volunteer coordinator who would become my unofficial mentor. Sophie had been running the pantry for eleven years, and within an hour she had me sorting tinned tomatoes by expiry date and asking me questions about why the queue moved so slowly on Saturdays. I did not have good answers yet, but I started to notice things: the mothers who came early so their children could avoid the midday crowd, the older men who never asked for more than they needed, the way a single broken trolley could stall the entire line.

By the end of my first year I was helping Sophie draft a short survey for the families who used the pantry. Sophie asked me to write the introduction because, she said, my sentences were plain enough for people who did not speak much English at home to understand. We printed two hundred copies at the library on Sydney Road and handed them out over three weekends. The results surprised us. Most people wanted shorter opening hours on weekdays, not longer ones, because they could not take unpaid time off from work to queue.

Sophie is now the operations manager at Northside Food Relief, a title that sounds grander than the work actually is. She still answers the pantry's phone in the mornings, and she still gives out her direct line, 0412 558 214, to anyone who needs a referral. When I asked her why she never automated the calls, she laughed and said that a voice on the line was the whole point. I have thought about that answer many times since.

My own interest in public health grew out of those Saturdays. I became fascinated by the gap between what a policy promises and what a person experiences when they stand in a line for two hours. I want to study that gap formally, to learn the methods that let researchers measure it and the ethics that keep those measurements honest. Melbourne's Master of Public Health offers exactly the combination of epidemiology and community engagement I am looking for.

If you want to reach me about this essay, my email is sophie.marsh.study@gmail.com, which is a leftover from a nickname my family once gave me, and I check it every evening. I have written this essay as myself, Sarah, because the people I met at the pantry taught me that a name matters when you are asking someone to trust you.

Good evening, everyone. For those of you who don't know me, I'm Rafael Oliveira, Fernanda's older brother, and I have been sharing a bedroom, a bicycle, and a lot of bad advice with her since 1994. Tonight I get to make a speech about her, which she has been threatening to edit for three weeks.

When Fernanda was seventeen, she spent every Saturday morning at Cafe Brisa on Rua das Flores in Belo Horizonte, reading novels and pretending she wasn't waiting for the owner's son to bring her a second cappuccino. Nobody in our family ever figured out how she convinced the barista to let her run the cash register for a whole summer, but she did, and she was better at it than anyone. That was the first time I saw her decide something and simply make it happen.

Years later she became a Senior Data Analyst at Vanterra Logistica, where her colleagues describe her as the person who explains spreadsheets like they're gossip. She once spent a whole weekend building a dashboard for her team, then posted a photo of it on Instagram with the handle @fer.dadosbr, and somehow three hundred strangers wanted to know how she did it. She still hasn't figured out why that surprised her.

What I want you to know about Fernanda is that she never does anything halfway. When she trained for the Belo Horizonte half marathon, she woke at five every morning, ran past the same bakery until the owner waved at her, and finished with a time she refuses to tell me because I'm too competitive. She is the most disciplined person I know and also the one who will happily abandon a plan to rescue a stray dog on the way home.

Daniel, I have watched you learn to keep up with her. You don't just match her pace, you run beside her, and you let her be the one who sets the direction when she's excited and you're the one who reminds her to drink water. That balance is rarer than you think.

So please raise your glasses. To Fernanda and Daniel, to the mornings at Cafe Brisa, to the dashboards and the marathons and the stray dogs, and to a marriage that I already suspect will be the best project either of you has ever taken on. Saude!

My name is Rachel, and I was lucky enough to be Frank's daughter for forty-one years. Many of you knew him as the man who ran the hardware store on Delancey Street, or as the one who would talk your ear off about the Mets for an hour before he got around to asking how your mother was doing. He loved that store, and he loved the people who walked through its doors, even the ones who came in only to ask for a single washer and left with a lecture on plumbing.

Dad grew up in Dayton, Ohio, the second of four boys, and he never quite stopped being the kid who had to fix everything around the house. He studied engineering at Ohio State for two years before deciding that he would rather work with his hands and his neighbors than with blueprints. Mom always said that was the best decision he ever made, though he would tell you it was the day he met her at a church picnic. He stayed in touch with a few of his college friends right up until the end, and every Christmas card from them sat on the mantel for weeks.

He was never without his dog, Biscuit, a scruffy terrier who rode in the passenger seat of his old pickup every single morning. When Biscuit passed, Dad cried more than any of us expected, and then he went out and found a rescue puppy that looked nothing like her. He said a man ought to have something to come home to, and he meant it.

For the last three years, Dad lived in a small brick house on Maple Court, where the neighbors knew him by his wave and his tomatoes. He was proud of that garden, and he would hand out bags of them to anyone who stood still long enough. Even in his final months, when he was at Mercy General Hospital, he asked the nurses about their kids and remembered their names. One of them told me he was the most patient patient she had ever had.

I keep thinking about the last conversation we had, which was on December 14th, just a few days before he went into the hospital. We sat on his porch wrapped in old blankets and argued, as we always did, about whether the Browns could ever win a playoff game. He was wrong, of course. I told him so, and he laughed so hard he had to wipe his eyes. That is the Frank I want you to remember: stubborn, funny, generous, and always ready for one more conversation.

When I started my shift at Harbourline Logistics in Newcastle last October, I had no idea how much the job would teach me about responsibility. My title was Dispatch Coordinator, which sounded modest on paper, but I was the person who made sure forty trucks left the depot on time and that every driver knew where to go. Each morning I would check the fleet log, confirm the plates on the rostered vehicles, including the Toyota with registration 1QKX82 that always needed extra attention, and then call the drivers myself.

The work was not glamorous. Some mornings I was up at five, and on the worst days I ate my breakfast standing up at Brewhouse Corner before the first call came in. Lachlan, my supervisor, taught me that a good dispatcher listens as much as she speaks. When a driver told me a loading bay was blocked, I learned to believe them before the paperwork caught up. Over time the number of late departures dropped, and I began to feel that the schedule was partly mine to protect.

Looking back, that job showed me what I want to study. I want to understand how systems succeed or fail when people depend on them, and I want to be the kind of professional who notices small problems before they grow. Whatever I learn at university, I will carry the habits I built in that depot: checking twice, speaking up early, and remembering that behind every route is a person waiting for a delivery.

Friends and family, thank you for being here today to celebrate the life of Jack Thornton. For those who knew him as Jacko, and for those who only knew him as Jack, he was the same warm, stubborn, generous man who never let a bad day go unanswered with a good joke.

Jack grew up in Ballarat, the second of four boys, and he spent his earliest years riding a secondhand bike up and down Sturt Street until his mum finally banned him from the footpath. He carried that restlessness into Ballarat Grammar, where he was far better at the cricket nets than he ever was at maths, and where he met the friends who would stay with him for the next sixty years.

He went on to study engineering at the University of Melbourne, and then spent the better part of four decades designing water pumping systems for rural councils across Victoria. Ask any of his colleagues and they will tell you he could fix anything, and that he never once left a job site without thanking the people who had made the work possible. He was patient with apprentices, honest with clients, and fierce in defence of anyone he thought was being treated unfairly.

In his last years, Jack spent a long stretch at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, and the nurses there still talk about the crossword puzzles he left at their station and the way he asked after their children by name. He faced that hard season with the same dry humour he brought to everything else, insisting on a proper cup of tea every morning and refusing to let anyone treat him as fragile.

He was born on 14 October 1948, and for years he marked the day by driving his grandchildren out to the Lake Wendouree foreshore for fish and chips. Those trips will go on, in the way we keep the things he taught us. Jack, you were a good friend, a loving father and grandfather, and a man who made the world a little more practical and a great deal more fun.

Rest now, Jacko. We will take it from here.

I saw Dr Pieter Venter at the Mountain View Medical Centre in Durbanville this morning. I went in at 08:40 because I had been getting a dull ache in my lower back for about three weeks, and it was getting worse after long shifts at the office. My employer, Vantage Logistics Pty Ltd, has been understanding about the time off, but I wanted to get it checked before it became a bigger problem.

Dr Venter asked me a lot of questions about how I sit, whether I lift anything heavy, and whether the pain runs down my legs. It does not run down my legs, which he said was a good sign. He pressed on a few spots along my spine and asked me to bend forward and backward. The movement was stiff on the left side. He thinks it is muscular strain rather than anything structural, most likely from sitting at my desk with poor posture and carrying my laptop bag on one shoulder.

He wrote me a referral to a physiotherapist, Wendy Naidoo, who has rooms at 14 Bree Street in Durbanville. He wants to see me again on Thursday 26 February at 09:00 to check how things are going. I have written his number, 021 555 0148, on the back of my medical aid card, and I have set a reminder on my phone for the 26th.

September 14th. Rain all morning over the vineyards near Beaune, and I spent the first hour trying to coax Gaspard out from under the porch. He is a grey tabby with one torn ear and absolutely no interest in weather. Finally he gave in and trotted after me to the car, a dusty white Renault with plates reading DK-482-LM, which I still have to get cleaned before the inspection. Fernand from the bakery waved as I drove past, which made me smile. I keep thinking about how small this village is and how everyone knows the dog, the car, and the state of my laundry.

September 16th. Good news at last. The bank finally confirmed the transfer on account 40817-2295, so the repairs to the barn roof can start next week. I called the builder, Monsieur Thibault, and he promised to come by on Monday with a crew. I told him Gaspard would supervise, and he laughed, though I think he believed me. Francoise from next door brought over a tart with plums from her tree, and we sat outside talking until the light went orange.

September 19th. Gaspard got into the neighbour's chicken coop again this morning and came out looking very pleased with himself, feathers on his whiskers. I apologised on his behalf. Fernand says the cat is becoming a local legend. I am starting to think Fernand is right, and that I should stop trying to keep him inside. Tomorrow I drive into Dijon to pick up paint for the shutters. Quiet days, and I am grateful for them.

I've been coming to this place for about two years now and honestly it's the best coffee I've had in the area. The flat white is consistently good, the milk is steamed properly, and the staff remember how you like it, which is rare these days. The space is small but has a nice relaxed feel, with plenty of natural light in the mornings and a decent selection of pastries that sell out by mid-morning if you're late.

The only downside is the wait during the weekday rush. There's usually a line out the door between eight and nine, and the seating is limited, so if you're hoping to sit down with a laptop you'll want to go early or late. My name is Marek Nowak, and I was honoured when my cousin asked me to say a few words about Mikolaj, the brother I grew up with in the flats off Ulica Piotrkowska in Lodz. Some of you knew him as the quiet man who always got to the bakery before the queue formed. Others knew him as the loud one at weddings, insisting everyone dance. He was both, and he was always himself.

Mikolaj ran the little Kawiarnia Sokol on the corner for twenty-two years. Anyone who sat at the window there will remember the chipped blue cups and the way he would refuse to take money from students who were short. He used to say a cafe was just a kitchen with the door left open. I think that is the most honest thing I ever heard him say, and it was typical of him to make a serious point sound like a joke.

He was also a terrible patient. When his knee gave out, he spent more time arguing with the staff at the Przychodnia Lipowa than he did with his physiotherapist. Still, he kept going back, because he liked the nurses there and he liked being someone people looked forward to seeing. He collected people the way other men collect stamps.

He died on the 14th of January, a Tuesday, in his sleep, which he would have called a sensible way to go, though he would have grumbled about the timing. We were at the kitchen table on Ulica Zielona the night before, going over old photographs, and he laughed so hard at one of his own bad haircuts that he had to wipe his glasses.

If you want to honour him, go and have a coffee somewhere you usually would not. Talk to the person behind the counter. Let them tell you something about their week. That was how Mikolaj lived, and I think it is the best way to keep him close. Thank you all for coming, and for the years you gave him.

I've been going to Brennan's Hardware on the Quay in Limerick for about six years now, and I wanted to write something after my last visit because it really deserves it. I'm Jack, and I live just off the Ennis Road, so this shop is basically on my route every week. Last month I came in with a cracked tap washer that had been dripping into my kitchen sink for a fortnight, and I honestly expected to be sent off to buy a whole new mixer. Instead the man behind the counter, Seamus, took one look at it, found the exact replacement in a drawer I didn't even know was there, and talked me through fitting it in about two minutes.

What I appreciate most about this place is that nobody makes you feel daft for asking. I'm not handy, and I've asked some embarrassing questions over the years, like which way a light bulb screws in or whether I needed a particular sealant for the bathroom. Every time the staff have been patient and never once tried to upsell me on something I don't need. The prices are fair too, and they still do a proper paint-matching service, which the big chains in Dublin seem to have given up on.

The only real complaint I have is the parking. The spaces out front fill up by ten on a Saturday, and there's no real loading bay for anyone picking up lumber or bags of cement. I've had to double-park twice and been shouted at by a delivery driver once, so a bit more planning there would help. Their opening hours on the bank holiday weekend were also not clearly posted, and I drove over on the Monday to find the shutters down.

Despite that, I'd rate them five stars without hesitation. If you're in the Limerick area and need anything from garden hose fittings to a new door lock, this is where I'd send you. I've also started recommending them to my neighbours, and my dog Biscuit has even been given a treat by the owner, who clearly has a soft spot for animals.

If you have any feedback or want to get in touch about the parking issue, you can reach the shop directly at info@brennanshardware.ie, and I'd encourage you to do so. Good local businesses take this kind of feedback seriously, and I think they'd want to know. Thanks to everyone there for making a simple Tuesday errand so much easier than it had any right to be.

April 3rd. Woke up early again, which is becoming a bad habit. Brenda's cousin called from Scranton last night to say the old house on Linden Street finally sold, and I found myself sitting on the back step for an hour afterward, thinking about the summers we spent there. Scranton is where I was born, in a hospital that doesn't even exist anymore, and somehow that feels like it matters more now than it did a year ago. I keep telling myself that a place is just a place, but then I catch a smell of cut grass and I'm nine years old again.

Went to the bakery on Fifth this morning for a loaf of rye, and the woman behind the counter asked if I was still writing that blog. I laughed and said not really, but she said she'd seen my posts about the garden and wondered if I'd ever start a new one. I told her I'm thinking about it. Honestly, I've been posting less since the winter, mostly because I don't know what I want to say anymore. Brenda says I should just post whatever comes to mind, even if it's only a photo of the tomato seedlings. Maybe she's right. My handle is still @bethsgardenlog if anyone wants to find me there, though I haven't checked the notifications in weeks.

April 9th. Rain all week. Brenda and I finally sat down and talked about the trip to Ohio in June, and it turns out we want completely different things from it. She wants to see every museum and historic site along the way; I just want to sleep in a tent by a lake and not look at my phone. We ended up arguing about it over dinner, which was silly, and then laughing about how we both always assume the other one will give in. We agreed to split the itinerary down the middle. It's a small victory but I'll take it.

April 14th. Got a letter from my mother's old friend Gloria, who still lives in Scranton and who remembers everything. She enclosed a photo of me at maybe six, standing in front of the church on Adams Avenue with a popsicle melting down my wrist. I stared at it for a long time. Some days I feel like I've lost the thread of who I was before everything got complicated, and then a picture like that shows up and reminds me that the kid in it was already herself, already curious and a little stubborn.

April 22nd. Planted the tomatoes today, finally. The soil was still cold but the sun came out in the afternoon and I sat in the dirt with my hands full of compost and felt, for the first time in months, like something was growing that I actually chose. Brenda brought me lemonade and sat next to me without saying much, which was exactly right. I think I'll post a photo tonight. Just one, just the seedlings, nothing else.

I should have listened to the woman at the car hire desk in Shannon when she tapped the form and said, "Mind the lanes, love, they're narrower than they look." I didn't, and by the second roundabout outside Ennis my heart was hammering. Still, nothing beats the moment the Burren opens up in front of you: grey limestone pavements stretching to the sea, wildflowers pushing out of the cracks as if the rock were only a thin coat. I pulled into a lay-by, sat on the bonnet with a flask of tea, and let the wind do the talking.

The real surprise of the trip was Galway. I'd booked a room above a pub on Shop Street, which sounds grander than it is, but the window looked straight down onto buskers and a fiddle player who kept going until nearly midnight. My host, Máire, runs the place with her brother Eoin and insisted on giving me the good towels. Her breakfast spread was generous enough to see me through a day of walking the Long Walk along the Corrib, where the swans had clearly decided the path belonged to them.

From there I drove the coast road toward Clifden, past Connemara's bog and the lakes that glow after rain. I stopped in a village whose name I still can't pronounce, bought a bar of smoked salmon from a tiny shop, and ate it on a stone wall while a farmer's dog inspected my boots. Small kindnesses like that stick with you far longer than the scenery.

If you go, book accommodation early for June, since the festivals start filling the towns quickly. I learned that the hard way, sleeping in the car for one night near Westport. Keep your phone charged, too: the signal drops out completely on the back roads. For bookings I used the email I'd set up for the trip, mmorrison.travels@gmail.com, which was handy when I needed to rearrange the Aran Islands ferry.

Looking back, the best parts were the unplanned ones: a pint with strangers in a snug, a detour when the rain cleared, the moment the cliffs of Moher came into view and nobody on the path spoke for a full minute. Ireland rewards people who slow down. I'm already planning the return trip, and this time I'll trust the woman at the car hire desk.

Thomas Reed Calloway was the kind of man who could fix anything with a socket wrench and a little patience, and he was never once in a hurry to leave a neighbor's kitchen. For fifty-eight years he lived at 214 Maple Hollow Drive in Dayton, Ohio, the house he and Linda bought in March of 1989 with more ambition than cash. Everyone on that block knew him as Tommy, a name his mother gave him and nobody else ever managed to shake loose. He coached Little League for nineteen seasons, taught every kid on the street how to throw a curveball badly, and always remembered your birthday, even when you were forty.

Those of us who called him Dad, Uncle Tom, or just Tommy knew the other side of him too. He was stubborn about the wrong things and generous about the right ones. When my son broke his arm at the lake, Tom drove four hours through the night without being asked twice. He kept a battered notebook of everyone's phone numbers, including his own, which he insisted on writing as (937) 555-0148 so we could always reach him. If you ever need to talk about him, or want to share a photo from those summers, you can still find him in our family group chat or on Instagram at @tomcallowayfixit.

So today, as we say goodbye, I ask that you remember him the way he remembered us. Call an old friend. Fix the thing that's been bothering you. Show up early and stay late. Tommy would have hated a fuss, so let's give him the quiet, honest kind of love he always gave to everyone else.

June 9

It's almost midnight and the apartment is finally quiet. Ilan Dekel left his shoes by the door again, so I've been stepping around them all evening. I'm writing this at the kitchen table because if I sit on the couch I will fall asleep mid-sentence.

Today was one of those days where everything went sideways from the start. The car, my little silver Hyundai, plate 47-219-83, made that grinding noise on the way to work, so I dropped it at the garage on Herzl Street and took the bus. The bus was packed. Someone's speaker was playing old Mizrahi pop the whole way down Ibn Gabirol, and I stood there the entire time holding a bag of groceries that was threatening to split open.

At the office, my manager Yoram Stern called a meeting at ten, which is never good news. I'm still the Senior Analyst at Meridian Lakeside Technologies, and he wanted to talk about the Q3 budget review. Honestly I think he just wanted to say he'd spoken to everyone. I came out of it with three new tasks and a headache. Ilan laughed when I told him, but he's the one who gets to work from home on Thursdays, so he doesn't get a vote.

In the evening I finally sat down to answer the messages I'd been ignoring. My cousin Tamar posted photos from the Galilee trip, and I commented on them, then realised I had tagged the wrong person and had to delete it. She sent me a laughing emoji and a link to a bakery in Haifa that apparently makes the best sufganiyot in June, which doesn't make sense but I'm going to check it anyway. I also saw that the group account we run for the neighbourhood garden, @rosh_ha_ayin_garden, has a new follower request from someone I don't recognise, so I'll deal with that tomorrow.

On the 16th we have the family dinner in Beersheba, which means another long drive and another argument about who is responsible for the salads. Ilan says he'll bring the wine if I promise to stop bringing up the car. I think that's a fair trade. Tomorrow is a new day, and hopefully the garage will call before lunch to say the car is fixed.

Good night, diary.

I'm thrilled to share that I've started a new role as Senior Product Analyst at Lumière Logistique in Lyon, and I wanted to take a moment to reflect on the journey that brought me here.

For almost six years I worked at a mid-sized software firm in Bordeaux, where I learned more about user research than I ever expected to. When the team restructured last autumn, I knew it was time to look for something that would challenge me in new ways. Lyon has been on my list for a while, mostly because of the food, I'll admit, but also because the city has a growing tech and logistics scene that felt like the right place to build the next chapter.

The interview process was longer than I anticipated. I had three rounds across two weeks, and the final one was a case study that I genuinely enjoyed. On March 14, I got the call from Camille Lefèvre, the hiring manager, and I think I said "oui" before she'd finished her sentence. Bruno, my partner, is still teasing me about it.

A lot of people have asked how I managed the move, and honestly the biggest help was my network. My former colleague Bastien put me in touch with two people at Lumière, and one of them, Inès, walked me through the team culture in a way that made the decision much easier. I'm grateful for every coffee call and every honest conversation.

One small thing that made the transition feel real: our apartment comes with a balcony, and Mochi, our grey cat, has already claimed it as her office. If you need to reach me for anything about the new role, you can write to bruno.garnier@lumiere-logistique.fr or call +33 4 72 55 18 90 during office hours.

For those who don't know me, I'm Marcus, Kevin's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words about the man who has been my best friend since we were kids running around our grandmother's backyard in Dayton, Ohio. When Kevin was six, he decided he was going to be a firefighter. When he was twelve, he decided he was going to be an architect. By the time he was twenty, he had settled on being a nurse, which surprised all of us, but nobody who has seen him with a scared kid in a hospital bed is ever surprised again.

I want to tell you about the day Kevin called me from the airport, back in April of 2019, after he had flown home for the funeral of our uncle. He had his passport in one hand and his phone in the other, and he said, "Marcus, I don't know how to do this part." I said, "Just come home." He did. He has been coming home to people who love him ever since, and tonight he is coming home to Hannah, who I have never seen so happy. Kevin, you were always the one who made the hard things look simple. If anyone needs to reach me about the toast or the seating chart, my number is 555-204-7731, though I'm told Hannah's mother has already claimed that role.

Hannah, welcome to the family. You have given my brother a steadiness I didn't know he was missing, and you have shown all of us what patience and laughter look like together. Please raise your glasses with me. To Kevin and Hannah, may your years together be as warm as this room tonight.

When I was seventeen I spent three summers as a volunteer at St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney, mostly pushing trolleys and sorting linen, but eventually I was trusted to sit with patients while the nurses did their rounds. One of them, a retired postal worker named Edward Pryce, taught me more about listening than any textbook could. He told me stories about delivering mail through the Blue Mountains in the 1960s, and he always asked how my own week had gone before he would say a word about his pain.

That experience pushed me toward a Bachelor of Health Sciences at the University of Queensland, where I have spent the past year as a peer tutor for first-year anatomy. I have come to see teaching as another form of listening: working out what a confused student actually needs to hear. Since March I have also worked two days a week as a Community Engagement Coordinator at Brisbane Youth Health Network, where my job title sounds grander than my daily routine, which is mostly updating the group's Instagram account (@ellie.hopes.ahead) and running Tuesday information sessions for teenagers who are nervous about their first doctor's visit.

What I want from a graduate program in public health is a chance to connect those threads. I want to understand how a single conversation at a bedside can scale into policy that reaches a whole suburb. Edward once told me that the mail always got through, even when the roads did not. I would like to build systems that carry that same kind of reliability to people who are easily overlooked. Ellie Hopkins, applying from Brisbane, is ready to start learning how.

I completed my undergraduate degree in civil engineering at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in 2009. The years there were demanding, but they gave me a rigorous foundation in materials science and seismic analysis, which has proved essential in a country that lives with earthquakes as a fact of life. Afterwards I worked for three years on hospital refurbishment projects, including the seismic upgrade of the wing at Papageorgiou General Hospital, a project that convinced me the most meaningful engineering often happens in buildings people depend on every day.

In my current role at a small consultancy, I lead a team of six engineers reviewing older residential stock across northern Greece. Our work focuses on affordable reinforcement methods that residents can actually finance, and we have now assessed more than two hundred buildings. I am proud that several of our recommendations have been adopted by municipal housing programmes, though I remain cautious about declaring any project finished until the concrete has cured and the families have moved back in.

Outside of work I am an enthusiastic, if not particularly skilled, amateur cook. I am writing this obituary for my mother, Carol Ann Whitfield, who died peacefully at home in Columbus, Ohio, on December 9, after a long illness that she faced with the same quiet courage she brought to everything else. She was 74.

Mom spent thirty-one years at Midwest Mutual Insurance Company, where she rose from a claims clerk in 1978 to Senior Claims Manager, the title she held when she retired in 2009. Her colleagues often said that she could calm an angry policyholder faster than anyone in the building, and she took real pride in treating every file as if it were about someone she knew. After she retired, she still got calls from former coworkers asking how to handle a difficult case, and she always found time to answer.

She was born in Dayton to Harold and Eleanor Brandt, and she grew up believing that a good meal and a hard day's work were the two surest ways to show love. She married my father, Thomas Whitfield, in 1971, and together they raised my brother and me in a small house on the east side of Columbus. Sunday dinners were non-negotiable, and her pot roast became legendary among our friends. She kept a handwritten recipe box that now sits on my kitchen counter, and I am still learning to make the things in it.

Carol loved gardening, crossword puzzles finished in pen, and long phone calls with her sisters. She was a devoted member of St. Brigid's Parish, where she volunteered for the food pantry every Thursday for more than twenty years. She never sought recognition for any of it, though the pantry's volunteers still speak of her with affection.

She is survived by her husband of fifty-three years, Thomas; her son, Daniel; her daughter-in-law, Rebecca; and three grandchildren who adored her. She is also survived by her sister, Margaret Lowell. She was preceded in death by her parents and her brother, Richard.

A memorial service will be held at St. Brigid's on Saturday, December 20, at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Columbus Community Food Bank. Those who wish to share memories may write to me at carol.whitfield.family@gmail.com. I will read every message to my father, who has asked to hear them all.

I've been going to Greenleaf Auto Care on Halsted Street for about six years now, and I finally sat down to write this because my experience last week was genuinely impressive. My brother-in-law Gordon Pruitt recommended them after his truck was misdiagnosed at a chain shop across town, so I went in skeptical. I came in with a grinding noise from my front brakes and a check engine light that had been blinking since the spring.

The service advisor, a woman named Dana Whitfield, listened to the whole story without rushing me. She explained that the grinding was not just worn pads but a warped rotor, and she showed me the old pads on the counter so I could see the difference for myself. Nobody has ever done that for me before. The quote was itemized, and when I asked whether the check engine light could wait, she was honest that it could, but she also told me exactly what to watch for.

The work itself took a little over three hours, which was faster than the estimate they gave me. The shop called me at my office twice to update me, and once they texted a photo of the new rotors. I had a question about the invoice afterward and emailed the front desk at service@greenleafautocare.com. Someone replied within the hour with a clear breakdown, which I appreciated since I'm a stickler for paperwork.

My daughter Maya, who is 34 and works as a nurse at St. Vincent's, drove over with me because her car has the same engine and she wanted to see how the mechanics handled the diagnostic. She was impressed by how patient the technicians were when she asked questions, and she has already booked her own oil change for next month.

The waiting area is clean, the coffee is decent, and there's a kids' corner with books that kept my grandson busy. Prices are fair for the area. They are not the cheapest in town, and I'd say that's a reasonable trade for work done right the first time.

If you're in the neighborhood and need honest service, I'd recommend Greenleaf without hesitation. Five stars from me, and I'll be back.

I finally made it to the Pacific Northwest this January, three years after I first put it on my list. I'm Vanessa, thirty-four, and I work as a nurse at St. Brendan's Medical Center in Spokane, so getting away for ten days felt like a small miracle. My sister Rhonda flew in from Chicago to join me, and we rented a silver Subaru with the plate 7KQM-421 because the rental agency only had one left in our price range. We picked up the keys on January 9th, the morning after my shift ended, still half-asleep and buzzing on bad airport coffee.

Our first stop was Port Angeles, where the ferry crossing out of Seattle had been delayed by fog. Vanessa Miller, that's me, had never seen the Olympic Peninsula in winter, and the snow on the mountains looked like frosting someone had piped on in a hurry. We walked the waterfront with our hoods up while a few gulls argued over a bag of fries. Rhonda kept calling it the most beautiful, grey, chilly day she'd ever had, and I think she meant it.

We spent the next two days near Lake Crescent, staying in a small cabin that allowed pets, which is how we ended up with Biscuit, a shaggy terrier belonging to the owner, Mr. Halvorsen. Biscuit followed us around like we were long-lost family. Vanessa, Rhonda and Biscuit went on a trail along the water on January 12th, and the lake was so still it looked like polished glass until a wind pushed ripples across it.

On our last full day we drove to the coast, and I couldn't resist posting a photo to our family group chat. My cousin Derek, who works at Brightline Logistics in Tacoma, replied within minutes asking whether we'd gotten a glimpse of the sea lions at Ruby Beach. We had, and they were enormous and loud and utterly unbothered by us.

I'd recommend this trip to anyone who needs a reset. Pack layers, bring a thermos, and don't plan too tightly. Our flight home left on January 18th, and I already miss the smell of cedar and the sound of rain on the cabin roof.

I still can't believe how much ground we covered in Jerusalem on our first full day. My name is Felix Harwood and I'd been planning this trip for months, but nothing prepares you for the Old City at seven in the morning, when the lanes are empty and the bells start up. My old college friend Rafi Dolev met me at Jaffa Gate, and he insisted on being called "Raf" by everyone, even the shopkeepers who only knew him as Rafi. He had booked us a guide, but then spent the whole walk correcting her on the history of the Armenian Quarter.

We ended the morning at Café Ruth on Agrippas Street, which Raf swore was the best shakshuka in the city. He was right. The owner, a woman named Ruthie Amsalem, remembered him from a visit three years ago and brought us an extra plate of pita without being asked. Later that afternoon I stumbled into a small clinic near Mahane Yehuda after a bad sunburn, and the nurse there, Dana, patched me up with more kindness than I expected from a stranger.

If you go in April, bring layers and comfortable shoes. The weather swings from warm sun to sudden cool wind, and the hills will punish flip-flops. I'd also recommend booking Café Ruth early, because by nine on a Saturday the queue stretches halfway down the street. Raf is already threatening to make me come back next April so he can show me the Galilee properly.

My name is Noa Ben-Ami, and I am the younger sister of Nadav. I stand here today with a heavy heart, but also with a great deal of gratitude for the forty-one years we shared. Nadav was born on September 14, 1983, in a small hospital in Haifa, and from the moment he arrived he made it clear that he would do things his own way. He was stubborn, funny, and impossibly generous, the kind of man who would give away his last shekel and then borrow a coffee from you to make the point.

For the last nine years Nadav lived in Be'er Sheva, in a little apartment on Yehuda Halevi Street, number 12, where the afternoon light came through the kitchen window and made the whole place feel like a Sunday. He loved that city. He used to say that Be'er Sheva had the desert's honesty, and that people there told you exactly what they thought, which suited him perfectly. Every Friday he would call our mother from that kitchen table, and I could hear the kettle whistling in the background while they argued about nothing at all.

Nadav was a carpenter, and he believed that a well-made chair could hold a family together. He built the table at which many of you have eaten, and he would never let anyone leave his workshop without a glass of tea and a story. Those of you who knew him through his work know that he never cut a corner, and that he was happiest when he could hand someone a finished piece and watch their face change.

Some of you have written to me since his passing, and I have been moved by how many people kept his email address in their contacts so they could send him photographs of their children, their gardens, their newly painted doors. His address was nadav.benami@ariel-woodworks.co.il, and I have promised his friends that I will keep checking it for a while, in case one more message comes in that makes me laugh the way he always made me laugh.

Nadav, you were the most alive person I have ever known. Thank you for the workshop, the tea, the stories, and for teaching me that a life can be measured by the people it holds up. Rest now, my brother. We will carry the table from here.

Oskar, my landlord's nephew, helped me carry the boxes up four flights on the eighteenth of August, and I swear the stairs got longer with every trip.

The first few weeks were rough. My German is fine for ordering bread and asking for directions, but when people speak fast at the Amt I just nod and hope for the best. I spent almost a whole morning at the Bürgeramt trying to register my address, and the woman behind the counter was patient but also clearly done with me by the end. Oskar, the one from the stairs, sort of adopted me after that. He took me to the Kneipe on the corner where the owner now calls me "der Neue" and slides me free Mate.

So yeah, it's not the glossy Berlin story I half expected, but I'm getting there. Write back soon and tell me how Hannover is treating you. And if you ever visit, you have a bed on my floor, cat included, though I can't promise it'll let you sleep.

Session notes to myself, July 14. I keep circling back to what Chetan said after the wedding in Pune: that I always act like my worth depends on being useful to everyone. Ananya, my closest friend from Christ College days, texted me that same week asking if I could help her sister with applications, and I said yes before I'd even checked my calendar. I am Zoe Halvorsen, and I have spent the last twelve years working at the intersection of civic data and public health. I currently serve as Senior Epidemiology Analyst at Brightwater Health Partners in Tacoma, Washington, where I lead a small team that tracks emergency department visits across six counties. Before joining Brightwater, I completed my doctoral work at the University of Oregon, and my dissertation examined how heat waves affect hospital admissions among older adults living alone.

I grew up in Duluth, Minnesota, the daughter of a commercial fisherman and a school librarian. Those two influences still shape how I work. From my father I learned that patterns in the water tell you something true even when the instruments disagree, and from my mother I learned that a dataset is only useful if the people it describes can understand it. Most of my projects now try to honor both lessons by pairing rigorous modeling with plain-language reports that community groups can actually use.

My most rewarding recent work began on December 14, 2022, when I was appointed to the Washington State Winter Preparedness Advisory Panel. The panel asked me to review how cold-weather shelter capacity was being reported across the state. Over the following eight months we identified reporting gaps in three rural counties and proposed a shared template that has since been adopted by eleven agencies. I was proud to see how quickly a practical fix could travel once people trusted the numbers behind it.

Outside the office I coach a youth robotics team at the Lakeview Community Center, a commitment that keeps me grounded and reminds me why accurate information matters to young people as much as to policymakers. I also volunteer as a reviewer for the Pacific Northwest Journal of Population Health, where I try to encourage early-career researchers to publish their work even when their findings are modest.

I would welcome the chance to talk with colleagues about translating surveillance data into action. If you wish to reach me before the conference, you may call my office at (253) 555-0147 or write to zoe.halvorsen@brightwaterhp.org. I look forward to meeting many of you in person and hearing about the work you are doing.

Right, you asked what happened with Dad's flat, so here it is properly. My name is Thomas Whitfield-Ross, though nobody outside the family bothers with the double-barrel, and the phone number I gave the solicitor is 07734 219 856 if you ever need to reach me about it. I'm writing this at the kitchen table in Leeds with a cold tea, because I didn't want to say it all on the phone again.

Katherine, my sister, had been the one dealing with Dad since the spring. She'd call me from the car park of the Brunswick Street Cafe, which is where she always went to get out of the house, and she'd sound like she'd been crying into a napkin. I told her to stop being the hero. Honestly, I was useless. I kept saying I'd come up at the weekend and then finding a reason not to.

On the ninth of May we had the meeting with the care coordinator at the clinic on Harrowgate Road. Tom from the practice had booked the room, and Kath turned up with a folder so thick it looked like a bad script. I remember thinking, she's got all this sorted and I've got nothing. She just looked at me and said, "Tommy, you can take the bills, I'll take the bathroom," and I didn't argue because she was right.

The bit that really got to me came a few days later. Dad, who hadn't remembered my wife's name for a month, asked Kath whether she'd been to the gym that morning, and she laughed so hard she had to sit down on the stairs. We both did. It was the first time in ages we'd laughed about anything together.

So that's where things stand. The flat goes on the market in June, Kath is staying at the house until the paperwork clears, and I'm finally driving up every other weekend. You don't have to say anything wise about it. Just tell me you'll ring me on the Sunday, because I'll need someone to tell me I'm doing alright.

Helena has told me that she heard a loud bang from the kitchen at about half past nine, followed by water running through the ceiling of the dining room. By the time she got downstairs, the floor was already covered and the ceiling plaster in the corner had started to come down.

Helena phoned me immediately, and I rang our emergency plumber, who attended within two hours. He identified a failed compression joint on the pipework running behind the kitchen units, which had apparently been weakening for some time. He isolated the supply and made the pipe safe, but by then the water had travelled into the adjoining rooms. Bramble was shut in the utility room for her own safety while the work was done, and she was distressed by the noise and the commotion.

I have since obtained the plumber's invoice and a written report, both of which I have enclosed. The damage includes the kitchen flooring, the lower sections of two fitted units, plasterboard and skim coat in the dining room, and a section of the living room carpet. Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Cormac, Ailbhe's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words tonight, which for someone who once talked his way out of a parking ticket by reciting the Irish constitution is either an honour or a warning.

When Ailbhe told us she was moving to Toronto three years ago, I'll be honest, Mum cried in the car park at Dunnes. We thought we'd lose her to a different time zone and a different accent. What we got instead was a sister who learned to drive on the wrong side of the road in the snow, who started working at Brightwater Analytics on Bay Street, and who somehow turned a rented one-bedroom at 418 Carlisle Avenue into the best hosting spot in the whole city. Half of you in this room have slept on that couch.

Ailbhe, you have always been the one who keeps the rest of us together. When Mum had her hip done last winter, it was you on the phone every single night, and when I said I couldn't manage the trip over, you sent me a plane ticket with a note that said "stop being a eejit." So thank you for that, and for everything since.

Now, Ciaran. I'd like to say I was worried about you, but I'd be lying. From the first time you came to Sunday dinner, you sat at the table like you'd been there for years. You asked Dad about the boat he restores, you let Nessa beat you at cards, and you were the only man I've ever met who would happily spend an hour talking to our dog, Biscuit, about nothing at all. Biscuit approved immediately, which for a dog who growls at the postman is saying something.

You two have built a life that is kind, funny and a little bit stubborn, which is exactly how it should be. Ciaran, you make her laugh until she snorts, and Ailbhe, you give him the nerve to try things he'd never have attempted alone. Most of all, you both make people feel welcome.

So please raise your glasses. To Ailbhe and Ciaran, to the next adventure, and to whoever ends up on the couch at Carlisle Avenue next. Sláinte!

Hi all, first time posting here so bear with me. I'm a 34 year old nurse based in Leeds and I've been stuck on a decision for about three weeks now. I work nights on the cardiac ward at St James's Hospital and the rota has been brutal since the start of the year. My manager, Gillian, has offered me a move to days if I agree to take on a band 6 charge role, but I'm honestly not sure I'm ready for the responsibility.

Some background. I trained at Leeds Beckett about ten years ago and I've been qualified ever since. I love the clinical side, the patients, the teamwork on a good shift. What wears me down is the sleep debt. I've had two near misses on the road home after nights, and that scared me more than I want to admit. My partner Nathan keeps telling me to just take the offer, but he doesn't see what goes on during a shift when things go wrong.

The thing that's making it harder is that I already had a meeting with HR on 14 April to talk through options, and they said I'd need to give an answer by the end of the month. I've been going back and forth on whether I should ask for a few more weeks, or whether that just looks indecisive. Has anyone here moved from nights into a charge role? How did you handle the transition, and did you find the extra admin overwhelming?

I've also been looking at whether a clinical educator post might suit me better, which would keep me off the wards most of the time but still in patient care. I checked a few adverts on NHS Jobs and the one for the Leeds Teaching Hospitals trust looked interesting, though I'm not sure how competitive those are. I request a full refund or an immediate replacement delivered within five business days, along with reimbursement for the spoiled groceries, which totals $86.40. Please respond in writing to frank.delaney@mailbox-example.com or call me at 555-214-7782 by June 28.

Sincerely,

Frank Delaney

Hey Marcus, I still can't stop thinking about what happened with Sloane last weekend. You know how she's always been the calm one, the one who never panics? Well, she called me Saturday night from the hospital parking lot, sounding like someone I'd never heard before. Her car had been towed from outside the ER and she didn't even know where they'd taken it. I drove over with her spare key that I'd been keeping since college, and I kept telling myself it was going to be fine. I'm Jordan Ellis Carver, and I've never been so glad to be the one with the spare key.

Sloane was fine, mostly. Her mom had a fall on February 9th, and nobody in the family had been ready for how fast things would move after that. Sloane spent the next three days shuttling between Cedar Rapids and her mom's place in Dubuque, living on gas station coffee and half-finished sandwiches. Every time I asked how she was holding up she said "I'm okay, Jordie," which is what she's said since we were nine, and which means the exact opposite. So I cleared my schedule and started driving up on weekends.

What I keep coming back to is how quietly she carried all of it. She never asked me for help, and I had to offer it three times before she let me take anything off her plate. I think she's finally starting to breathe again, and I'm writing this to you because I need someone to tell me I did the right thing by showing up. Call me when you get a minute, okay? I owe you a long dinner.

To my new colleagues at Northgate: I'm coming in to listen first. When I was nine, my grandmother taught me that a good question is worth more than a fast answer. We lived in a small apartment in Belo Horizonte, and every afternoon she would sit with me at the kitchen table while the rain tapped on the window. My name is Kaique Albuquerque Mendes, and I have spent most of my life asking why things work the way they do. Some of those questions led me to a broken radio, some to a neighbor's stalled car, and eventually to the physics textbooks my cousin left behind when he moved to Curitiba.

The question that truly shaped me arrived in my second year of secondary school, when our science teacher, Professora Lúcia, asked the class why the sky is blue. Most of my classmates gave the answer from the textbook. I went home and spent three weeks building a crude spectrometer out of a cardboard box, a CD fragment and a flashlight. It was not elegant, but when I held a prism-shaped sheet of glass to the light and saw the colors spread across the wall, I understood something that no diagram had ever made clear to me. I wrote up my results and sent them to Professora Lúcia, who replied with three pages of notes and a suggestion that I apply to the regional science fair.

That experience taught me that curiosity without patience is only a mood. Patience is what turned my cardboard box into a small but honest investigation. Since then I have volunteered at a community library in Contagem, where I help younger students with mathematics on Saturday mornings. I have learned that explaining an idea clearly is often harder than discovering it, and that the two skills feed each other.

My family has never had much money, and I know that a university education is a privilege my grandmother did not have. When I think about my future, I want to study engineering so that I can design tools that make everyday problems easier to solve for people like the ones I grew up with. My passport and national ID documents are ready for the exchange program I hope to join, and I have already written to the admissions office at kaique.mendes.2009@example-mail.com to ask about the interview schedule.

My dog, Pipoca, has taught me something as well. He waits patiently by the door every evening, certain that I will return, and he never asks for an explanation of why I was late. I hope to bring that same steady loyalty to my studies and to the people I serve. I am ready to keep asking questions, and I am ready to work hard to find the answers.

I'm writing this down so I don't forget what Dr Keane told me at my appointment on Tuesday 12 August at the Riverside Medical Centre in Limerick. My name is Darragh Brennan and I'd been having a dull ache in my lower back for about three weeks, mostly after long shifts at the warehouse. I had also been waking up with tingling in my right foot, which is what finally made me book the appointment instead of just taking ibuprofen and hoping for the best.

Dr Keane asked a lot of questions about when the pain started, whether anything made it worse, and whether I'd had any numbness in my groin or problems with the bathroom. I said no to all of that, which she seemed pleased about. She had me lie on the bed and lift each leg, then pressed along my spine and asked me to bend forward and sideways. The reflexes in my knees and ankle were normal, and she said the foot tingling was most likely a pinched nerve from how I've been sleeping on the sofa.

She was clear that this is a muscular and nerve issue and not anything serious, but she wants me to take it properly seriously. I've been given a referral letter for physiotherapy at the Shannon Physio Clinic, and the receptionist, Sinéad, said they could fit me in from the end of August if I ring on Monday. I need to ring them and ask about a weekend slot because of my shifts. My car is a 2015 Skoda with registration 151-L-4482, which I mention only because the physio clinic asked for it when I rang to confirm my details.

Dr Keane also wants me to do a short exercise routine every morning: a gentle knee-to-chest stretch, a cat-cow movement, and a walk for twenty minutes if I can manage it. If the tingling spreads, if my leg gets weaker, or if I lose any control of my bladder or bowel, I'm to go straight to the emergency department at University Hospital Limerick and not wait for the physio appointment. Friends and family, thank you for being here today to honour Kiran Halloran. Many of you knew her as the woman who could fix anything with a roll of tape and a stubborn look, and some of you knew her as the one who always remembered your birthday. I am Maeve, her eldest, and I have been trying all week to find the right words for a person who never needed many of them.

Kiran was born in Leeds in the winter of 1952, the second of four children, and she never let anyone forget that she was the one who got things done. When she moved to Valencia in 1989, she did it with two suitcases, a secondhand Vespa, and a letter of introduction she had written herself. Within a year she knew every baker on Calle Ruzafa by name and had talked the whole street into planting geraniums along the balconies.

My father, Tomas, always said she was the only person he ever met who could argue with a bus driver and make him laugh at the same time. They were married for forty-one years. She kept a notebook of his bad jokes, which she read aloud at every anniversary, and he pretended to hate it every single time.

In her last years she lived at 14 Carrer de Ruzafa, Apartment 3B, Valencia, where the neighbours checked on her daily and she checked on them back. She sent out a monthly newsletter, handwritten, about the state of the building's roof and the state of the local politics. Several of you received them. Keep them. They are better than any biography.

Kiran, you taught us that kindness is a practical thing, that you show up with soup and a spare key and you do not make a fuss about it. We will miss your voice on the phone, your opinions on everything, and your terrible sense of direction on the Metro. Rest now. We have the roof under control.

genre: personal story told to a friend
text:
Okay, so you won't believe what happened to me last Thursday. I was driving back from my shift at Riverside Memorial Hospital, and it was already past eleven. I'm thirty-four now and I still think I can handle anything on four hours of sleep, which, clearly, I can't. Anyway, I stopped at the Shell on Harmon Avenue to grab a coffee and some gum, and when I got back to my car the driver's side window was smashed and my bag was gone. Gone. My laptop, my charger, the textbook I borrowed from Ashworth College for my nursing exam in September, all of it.

I called the police from the parking lot and an officer named Officer Delgado came out in about twenty minutes. He was really kind about it. He asked me to spell my name, Amara Lockhart, and then he asked again, slower, because apparently I was mumbling. He said the store camera might have caught the guy, so I should check back with them in a few days. I told him I'd come in on Monday. I also had to call the bank and freeze my cards, which took forever because the automated system kept asking me to confirm my date of birth, and I kept getting it wrong because I was shaking.

The weirdest part? When I finally got home, my roommate Jules had left a note on the fridge that said, "Don't panic, but your mom called twice." So of course I spent the rest of the night thinking someone had died. Turns out she just wanted to remind me about my cousin's wedding. I cried for about ten minutes straight, mostly from relief. So yeah, that's my week. Call me tomorrow? I need to vent about it properly and I'd love a glass of wine that isn't from a gas station.

When I was nine, my grandmother taught me that every bread in Jerusalem has a story, and I have spent the years since trying to find out which ones are true. My name is Carmel Adler, and I grew up in a third-floor apartment in Haifa where the windows faced the port. My mother worked nights at the hospital on Mount Carmel, so most of my afternoons were spent with my grandmother in her kitchen, kneading dough while she talked about the Yemenite bakers she knew as a girl.

That kitchen is where my interest in oral history began. In the spring of my junior year I started recording her memories on an old phone, transcribing them late at night, and sharing short excerpts on my account, @carmel.kneads, which grew slowly to about four hundred followers, mostly bakers and food historians in Tel Aviv and Amman. Many of them wrote to me about recipes their families had lost. Carmel, one message read, you are doing what our parents never had time for. That sentence changed how I thought about my project.

On May 14 I presented my first complete collection to our school's history club, twelve interviews from six neighbourhoods. I want to study social history at university because I believe a family's kitchen is an archive, and I want to learn the methods that let me read it responsibly. I hope to bring that same care to the communities I document, and to keep asking my grandmother's question: who taught the bread to the people who baked it?

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ryan Okafor-Blake, Dana's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words before we raise our glasses. Some of you have heard me tell the story of how Dana, at age six, decided she was going to be a veterinarian and then spent the next three years bringing home every injured sparrow on Maple Crescent. Tonight I want to talk about the Dana I've known since the day she was born in Kingston, Ontario, on a snowy morning in January, the kind where the hospital parking lot is a sheet of ice and our dad drove like he was in a rally.

Dana has always been the one who shows up. When I moved back to Ottawa after my divorce, she was the one who drove over with a box of takeout and a stack of old board games and didn't leave until we'd finished three rounds of Scrabble. She's the one who remembers the name of every server at the Bluebird Cafe on Princess Street, and who still, after eleven years, sends a birthday card to her first ever client at the Riverside Animal Clinic. If you've ever needed help, Dana is already on her way with a plan, a snack, and a spare set of car keys.

So, Jordan, I want you to know what you've got. You've got someone who listens to the quiet parts, who will argue with you about the best pizza in town and then secretly order the one you like. Dear Babcia,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold hasn't been too hard on your knees this season. I keep thinking about the evenings we spent together at your kitchen table, the radio murmuring in the background while you rolled out dough with that old wooden pin. I have never managed to make pierogi the way you did, though I have tried more than once. Mine always come out a little too thick and a little too lopsided, and I can hear you laughing gently at them from wherever you are in my memory.

Things here have been busy. The new job keeps me on my feet from morning until late afternoon, and I often come home tired enough to fall asleep on the sofa before I have even eaten. Still, there are good moments. A colleague who has been very kind to me invited me to a small gathering last week, and I found myself talking about the stories you used to tell me about the village and the people who lived there long ago. It surprised me how much of it I still remember, word for word, the way you told it.

I have been thinking a lot about the time you taught me to sit quietly and simply listen to the wind moving through the trees. You said that people rush through life because they forget to pay attention to small things. I try to remember that now, especially on the long walks I take after work when the leaves start turning. The colours are beautiful this time of year, and I wish you could see them with me.

I also wanted to tell you that I have been learning more about the traditions you carried with you. I bought a book of old recipes and folk songs, and I have started copying the handwritten notes you once left in the margins of your own cookbook. Reading your careful handwriting makes me feel close to you, even across all this distance. Some of the words are faded now, but I can still picture your hands moving as you wrote them.

Please take care of yourself through the coming months. Keep your scarf close and your tea warm, and do not hesitate to call me if you need anything at all. I will try to visit as soon as I can arrange some time off, and I promise to bring a bag of the good sweets you always liked, even if I have to hide them from you until after dinner.

With all my love and gratitude,

Your grandchild
