Last May I finally made the drive west from Dublin, and I can say without exaggeration that the Burren was worth every mile. My name is Aidan Keogh, I'm 34, and I work as a surveyor for Corrigan Geotech in Kilkenny, so landscapes are usually something I measure rather than admire. That afternoon I forgot the clipboard entirely. The limestone pavements stretched out in grey slabs, cracked into clints and grikes, and tiny wildflowers, mountain avens and orchids, were pushing up through the gaps like they had something to prove.

I stayed two nights in Ballyvaughan, in a small guesthouse run by a woman who knew every walking route in the parish. She gave me a printed map, circled three trails, and told me to avoid the coastal path after rain. I followed her advice on the second morning and walked up toward Mullaghmore with a flask of tea and a sandwich I'd bought from the village shop. Nobody else was on the hill until almost noon. If you want to plan something similar, my details are on the booking form, but honestly just email me at aidan.keogh@corrigangeotech.ie with questions. I'll gladly tell you where the best tea is.

Keep your passport handy when you cross over from the north, though: the guesthouse asked for my passport number (P1234567) at check-in, and it's worth having it ready on the ferry from Rosslare too. When people ask me why I want to study environmental engineering at the University of Waterloo, I usually start with the creek behind my house. My name is Benjamin Okafor-Lindqvist, and I have lived at 418 Larkspur Avenue in the Westmount neighbourhood of Kitchener since I was six. Every spring, the water in Schneider Creek rises over the footbridge and carries away the same plastic bottles, and every spring I wondered why nobody fixed it. Ben, my neighbour and closest friend, got tired of hearing me complain about it and suggested we stop complaining and start counting.

So in February of Grade 11, Ben and I started a small project. We walked the length of the creek every Saturday with two buckets, a notebook, and a clipboard. By the end of the month we had logged over four hundred pieces of litter, most of it within two blocks of the storm drain outlet. Ben, who is far better with spreadsheets than I am, built a simple map showing where the debris clustered. Our teacher, Ms. Halvorsen, saw the map and asked if we would present it at the school science fair. We did, and it ended up being the only project that the city's conservation officer stopped to ask questions about.

That conversation changed how I think about my future. The officer explained that the creek problem was not really about litter at all. It was about runoff from parking lots and roofs that carried oil, salt, and fertilizer straight into the water system, and the city had only recently begun to model it. I asked whether anyone was building those models, and she said the people doing it were engineers who understood both hydrology and policy. I had never considered that engineering could be a way to listen to a neighbourhood as well as to build things in it.

Since then I have stayed in touch with the conservation office and have volunteered on two stormwater surveys. I have also kept the project alive on social media under the handle @schneidercreekwatch, where I post photos, monthly tallies, and the occasional update on the footbridge repair the city finally approved last autumn. The account has about nine hundred followers, most of them neighbours who now text me when they see someone dumping yard waste near the water.

I want to study at Waterloo because its water and environmental programs combine field research with the kind of community work I have already started. I would like to learn how to design the systems that keep creeks like Schneider from becoming dumping grounds, and to do it with people who live beside them. If admissions has questions about my application, I can be reached at 519-555-0148, and I would welcome the chance to talk about the creek, the buckets, and the models that will one day help keep it clean.

Many of you knew her as a neighbour, a colleague, a friend at the market or someone who could always be counted on to bring soup when life got hard. She had a way of making every guest feel expected, as though the house had been waiting all week just for them. Her kitchen was never quiet. There was always the clatter of pans, someone laughing at the table, and the smell of garlic and fresh basil drifting out into the courtyard.

She taught me that patience is a form of love. She would sit for hours with a difficult plant, a stubborn sauce or a child who would not stop crying, and she never once rushed any of them. When I was younger I thought her calm was simply who she was. Only later did I understand how much effort it took, and how often she chose kindness when it would have been easier to choose anything else.

So today, let us not only grieve what we have lost. Let us carry forward the small things she gave us: a warm welcome, a seat at the table, and the willingness to slow down for the people who matter. If you find yourself cooking for someone this week, think of her. That is how I will keep her close, and I hope you will too.

text:
When I think about why I want to study environmental science, I remember the summer I spent helping at a community garden on the edge of town. Nobody there had a degree in anything related to soil or water, but every person in that garden knew exactly how the land behaved after a hard rain and how the first frost changed the plants. That knowledge was practical, shared freely, and passed from one neighbour to the next. It taught me that science is not only something that happens in laboratories; it is also something people carry in their hands and their habits.

What I found most striking was how often the questions we asked each other ended in uncertainty. Why were the tomatoes splitting this year? Was the drainage ditch along the fence slowing the runoff, or just moving the problem somewhere else? Our answers were rarely clean. We tested, we argued, we changed one thing at a time and watched carefully. I came to value that patience. I want to learn the methods that turn these everyday observations into evidence that can guide decisions about water quality, farmland and the wider ecosystems that depend on them.

My own path has not been a straight line. I began my schooling expecting to pursue medicine, and I still admire the people who do. Over time, though, I noticed that my attention kept drifting outside, toward rivers, wetlands and the slow processes that shape them. Taking a introductory geology course and then an ecology seminar gave me language for those interests. I started reading research papers for pleasure, which surprised me, and I began to see that the careful, unglamorous work of monitoring a single watershed can matter as much as any dramatic discovery.

I am also aware that environmental problems do not respect boundaries between disciplines. Solving them requires chemists who understand contaminants, engineers who can design filtration, economists who can weigh costs, and community members who know what the land has meant to them over generations. I want to be the kind of scientist who listens across those divides. Working with people who have a different relationship to a place has already changed how I ask questions, and I hope to deepen that habit in a university setting that values collaboration.

Every autumn, the garden I worked in is cleared and the beds are covered for winter. The soil rests, and so, in its way, does the community that tends it. I think often of that rhythm when I imagine my future work: periods of intense effort followed by reflection, and a steady commitment to understanding the places we share. I am ready to bring that commitment to your program, and I look forward to learning from the researchers, classmates and local communities who will help me grow into the scientist I hope to become.

When people ask me where I come from, I usually say Haifa, but the truth is more specific. I grew up on Yefe Nof Street in the Hadar neighbourhood, in a third-floor apartment where the balcony looked down on a falafel stand that my family considered a second kitchen. My grandmother, whom everyone calls Bubbi Rachel, taught me to read Hebrew newspapers at that same balcony table, insisting that headlines were the fastest way to understand a city's moods.

My full name is Maya Levkovich, but on the bus and at the corner shop I have always been just Mimi. The nickname stuck when I was four, after my cousin failed to pronounce my name and I decided the mistake was better. It is the name my teachers at Gordon Secondary School still use, and it is the name I want to carry into the classroom of a journalism program. On October 14, 2023, I wrote my first published piece for the school paper, an account of the neighbourhood's bakery closing after forty years. That article taught me that small local stories can explain larger changes.

I am applying because I want to tell stories like that with more rigour and reach. I have spent two summers interning with a community radio station, and I have learned that listening is the core skill of reporting. Hadar taught me to pay attention to the people who are often overlooked, and I hope your program will help me turn that attention into work that matters beyond my own street.

Thank you all for being here today. Many of you knew Donald as Don, and some of you knew him as Dad, Pop, or just the bloke who always had a spare sausage for you at the barbie. I'm his eldest, Margaret, and I've been asked to say a few words on behalf of the family. It's been a hard week, but it has also been a week of stories, and I want to share a few of them.

Don spent thirty-four years at the Port Adelaide depot, and he never once let anyone forget that the best tea in the state was made in the tin shed out the back. He taught me to drive in his old Holden on the back roads near Mount Barker, and he taught me patience, which I am still working on. When my son Liam was born, Dad drove up from Adelaide before the sun came up and sat in the hospital car park for an hour because he didn't want to wake anyone. That was Don. Quiet, steady, and always there.

If you want to write to us, or share a photo or a memory, please send it to donald.fraser.family@outlook.com and my brother Peter will gather everything up for the family album. We would love to hear from you. Dad always said a good funeral was one where people kept talking after the sausages ran out, so please, stay a while, have a cuppa, and keep telling stories about him.

When I first walked into the Brisbane Youth Mentoring Hub in March, I had no idea that the coordinator, Wendy Okafor, would become the person who shaped my understanding of what leadership really means. Wendy had been running the program for nine years, and she treated every volunteer like a future colleague. I was seventeen, anxious about everything, and convinced I had nothing useful to offer. Wendy simply asked me what I was good at and then gave me a group of eleven students to support. Over the following months I learned that the most valuable thing I could do was listen.

The hardest moment came in July, when one of the students, a quiet boy named Tomas, stopped attending sessions. Wendy and I drove out to his house in Logan together. His grandmother, Lydia, answered the door and explained that Tomas had been caring for his younger brother while their mother worked double shifts. Wendy did not lecture anyone. She sat at the kitchen table and asked questions, and by the end of the afternoon we had arranged for the family to access a free after-school program at the local library. Watching her work reminded me that compassion and competence are not opposites.

That experience pushed me toward studying social work. I want to build the kind of systems that catch students like Tomas before they fall through the cracks. My mum, Wanda, a nurse at Princess Alexandra Hospital, has always told me that caring for people is a practical skill as well as a feeling. I now believe she is right, and I am ready to learn the rest.

I have always believed that the most important lessons are learned in ordinary places. For me, that place is Bluebird Coffee on Alder Street in Tacoma, where I spent three mornings a week during my junior year working the espresso bar. My name is Brianna Okafor, and I have been reflecting for months on what those early shifts taught me about responsibility, patience and listening.

I remember my first real test vividly. It was December 9th, the week before finals, and the line stretched past the bookshelf by seven o'clock. A regular named Mr. Halvorsen was furious because his order had been mixed up twice. Instead of apologizing and remaking his drink in a panic, I asked him to tell me exactly what he wanted. He laughed, told me about his late wife's habit of ordering a cortado after church, and by the end of the conversation he had become my most loyal customer. That morning taught me that a problem is often just a story waiting to be heard.

Before I started at Bluebird, I thought of myself as a quiet student who preferred working alone. Those mornings changed that. I learned to run a team of four during the rush, to keep track of inventory on a clipboard when the register failed, and to call our supplier when the milk delivery was late. Each small task required me to step out of my own head and think about what the people around me needed.

This is why I am applying to your public health program. I want to study how communities make decisions about their own wellbeing, and I want to work on the kinds of questions that a coffee bar teaches you to ask: who is being served, who is being missed, and what would make the next morning better. I have already begun speaking with a community clinic on Pacific Avenue about a volunteer intake project, and I hope to bring the same listening habits I developed at Bluebird into that work.

If you would like to confirm any details of my application or my references, you can reach my former manager, Lucas Pereira, at (253) 555-0148. He has watched me grow from someone who dreaded the morning rush into someone who looks forward to it. I hope to carry that same steadiness into your classrooms and into the communities I will serve after graduation.

Lorraine is also a generous mentor. Several of the junior analysts who joined the team had their first real experience of month-end reporting under her guidance, and two have since been promoted. Ó Ceallaigh was his family name and he wore it with pride, teaching all of us the Irish words for the places and people we loved.

text: When I first moved to Lisbon from Chicago back in 2016, Wendy was the only person who answered my messages on the 14th of December, and she still does, at wendy.hale@lisbonmail.pt. Tonight I'm honored to raise a glass to her and to everything she has built with Ryan.

The first thing that hits you in Lagos is the noise, and I mean that in the best way. Horns blare, vendors call out their wares over the traffic, and somewhere a generator hums so steadily you stop noticing it after a day. I spent most of my first morning just standing at the edge of a busy market, trying to take it all in while a woman balancing a tray of plantain on her head laughed at me for gawking. Nobody minded. People here are quick to share a joke and even quicker to point you toward the best jollof you will ever eat.

What surprised me most was how much of the country's life happens outdoors. Evenings are for sitting on plastic chairs outside a bukka, sharing grilled fish and cold drinks while the street slowly fills up with music and conversation. Travel between cities can be slow and unpredictable, so I learned to build in extra time, keep a little cash on hand, and accept that the plan will change at least twice. The friendly strangers who helped me find the right bus at every stop made those detours feel like part of the adventure rather than a setback.

If you go, pack light clothing, a good hat, and more patience than you think you need. Bring a sense of humour too. The roads, the heat and the crowds will test you, but the warmth of the people and the sheer energy of the place make it one of the most rewarding trips I have ever taken. I left already planning my return, with a suitcase full of fabric and a head full of rhythms I still catch myself humming.

We finally made it to Galway this December, and I have to say the city lived up to every bit of hype. I'm Aoife, 34, and I've called Limerick home my whole life, so it was a treat to be the visitor for once. My sister Niamh tagged along and insisted we start at the Latin Quarter before anything else. We wandered the cobbled lanes, ducked into a pub with live fiddle music, and ended up at the Salthill promenade on the 14th just as the sun dipped into the bay. If you're planning a winter trip, pack a proper coat, because the wind off the Atlantic is no joke.

My mind kept drifting back to a conversation I had with my sister months ago, where she said I always apologise before I've even finished asking for something. I laughed at the time. Okay, you're not going to believe what happened to me at the Bluebell Coffee House on Thursday. I'd popped in on my way back from the surgery in Leeds, mostly because I needed something hot and a bit of peace before dealing with the bank. Eleanor was behind the counter, the same lovely woman who always remembers I take oat milk, and she asked if I'd heard about the flat on Hyde Park Road. I hadn't. Apparently the landlord has been trying to push out the older tenants since spring, and half the street is furious. I sat there with my flat white going cold, listening to her go on, and honestly I felt like I'd walked into the middle of a soap opera.

What really got me, though, was the notice board by the door. Someone had pinned up a handwritten sheet asking for signatures for a tenants' meeting on 14 June at the church hall. Under it was a phone number and an email, something like tenantsleeds.watch@gmail.com, and a little note saying Eleanor was collecting names. I thought that was brilliant. Nobody in this city seems to organise anything anymore, so seeing neighbours actually take the lead made me want to help out.

So I've put my name down, Ellie, and I'm dragging you along to the meeting with me. Don't argue. You've complained about our rent for three years, so this is your chance to stop grumbling and start doing something. Meet me outside the Bluebell at six on the Saturday before, and we'll walk over together. Bring your mum's lemon cake if she'll let you have it, because I've promised the organisers we'd bring biscuits and I am useless at baking.

I keep coming back to the same moment from last week, the one where I stood in the kitchen with the kettle half-filled and realised I had no idea what I was waiting for. Not the tea. Something else. My therapist asked me to write this down instead of carrying it around in my head, so here I am, at the table with the window open a crack because the house gets stuffy in the evenings this time of year.

Her question was simple: what did I feel when I came home from work on Tuesday? I said tired, and then I said nothing, and she waited, the way she does, until I found the word underneath. Empty. Not sad exactly. Just hollow, as if the day had taken something out of me and nothing had been put back. I think I have been running on that hollowness for a while and calling it being busy.

What I am trying to notice is how often I apologise in my head before anyone has even asked me for anything. I rehearse explanations for why I was late, why I did not reply, why I need a quiet evening. Most of the time nobody is cross with me. The worry is almost entirely my own invention, and that is both a relief and a little embarrassing to admit.

We talked about boundaries, which always sounds tidy in a session and feels messy in practice. I agreed to try one small thing this week: to leave my phone in the hall after six o'clock and see what happens. I expect the first evening to feel like missing a limb. I hope by the third it will feel more like rest.

There is a line she said that I wrote on the back of my hand so I would not lose it: you are allowed to take up space without earning it first. I do not believe it yet. But I am writing it here so that some future version of me, reading this back, can see that I was at least willing to hear it.

Tomorrow I will try the phone in the hall. Tonight I will finish the tea, which has gone cold, and sit with the hollowness for a minute without rushing to fill it.

Growing up in Eldoret, I learned early that a good answer to a hard question is often a question of its own. My grandmother, Mama Esther Chebet, taught me this while we shelled beans on her verandah. She ran a small clinic out of her home for years, and every patient who came to her gate was greeted by name before anything else happened. I watched her listen more than she spoke, and I began to understand that medicine starts with attention.

That understanding took a sharper shape when I volunteered at Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital during my final year of secondary school. I was assigned to the maternity ward, where I recorded blood pressures and tried to keep track of which mothers had already been seen. One December morning, a young woman arrived with a bundle and no one to explain her symptoms but herself. I spent nearly an hour with her, using the little Kiswahili I had and the chart my supervisor allowed me to read. Her case was handled by the nurses, but the hour was mine, and it taught me what Mama Esther had been showing me all along.

I want to study public health because the gap between what clinics know and what communities can access is where most of my family's stories begin and end. Before I apply, I have been calling the district office to confirm outreach schedules, and the line I was given, 0722 418 306, has become my most useful lesson in persistence. I hope a university like yours will give me the tools to close that gap, and the community to keep asking better questions.

I sat in the car park for almost twenty minutes after the session today before I could bring myself to drive home. My therapist asked me to notice where the feeling lived in my body, and it was in my chest, tight and heavy, like I was holding my breath without realising. We talked about the pattern again: how I apologise before I've even said anything, how I rehearse conversations so many times that the real one feels like a performance I've already given. I hate that I still do it, even though I can name it now.

This week I tried something small. When I caught myself drafting an apology to my sister for something she hadn't even been upset about, I stopped and wrote down what I actually wanted to say instead. It was far less dramatic than I expected. I wanted to tell her I missed our old walks and that I felt a bit left out of her new routine. Writing it down didn't fix anything, but it made the feeling smaller, like I'd set it on the table where I could see it.

I keep coming back to the idea that I am allowed to take up space without earning it first. It sounds obvious when I write it down, and yet I didn't believe it at all this morning. I'm going to try to remember the tightness in my chest as information rather than as a verdict. Next session, I want to bring the list of things I wrote down and see whether we can work out which ones are worth saying out loud.

Dear Nan,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the new hip is behaving itself. Mum says you've been doing your exercises every morning with the radio on, which I think is marvellous. I'm writing because I've finally got some news worth sharing, and I wanted to tell you properly rather than in a rushed phone call.

Wilfred and I have decided to move back up north. We've found a little terraced house in Harrogate with a proper back garden, so you'll have to come and inspect the runner beans when you visit. The move is booked for the 14th of January, which is a dreadful time to be shifting boxes about, but the landlord was keen and we didn't want to lose the place.

You'll be pleased to hear I've already found a new local haunt. There's a cafe on the corner of the high street called Bramble & Crumb, run by a lovely woman called Hannah who remembers how I take my tea. Her scones are nearly as good as yours, which is the highest compliment I can give anyone. Wilfred has been sneaking in there every Saturday to try the flapjacks, and I've told him he's going to be a very round man by spring if he carries on.

I've also signed up at the leisure centre on Cold Bath Road, mostly because the swimming pool is warm and the lady at reception, Marjorie, insisted I'd love the aqua classes. I went along on the 9th and I'm not ashamed to say I was the oldest one in the water apart from the instructor, who is Wilf's cousin's husband, of all things. Small world, as you always say.

Anyway, I'm rambling. What I really wanted to ask is whether you'd be up for coming to stay for a long weekend once we're settled. Wilfred has asked me to say he'll make you his famous shepherd's pie, though I suspect he's been practising on the neighbours. Ring me on Sunday evening when the rates are cheaper and tell me what you think.

Love always,

Winnie

We gathered today to remember Nikodem Wiśniewski, whom everyone in Kraków knew as Nikuś, a name he kept from his grandmother and never quite outgrew. He was born on 14 February 1951 in a small flat near the Wawel, and he spent almost his whole life in that same city, walking its streets with a notebook in his coat pocket and a story ready for anyone who stopped to listen. Nikodem taught history at a school on Floriańska for thirty-one years, and generations of students remember his habit of closing the textbook and simply talking.

In his last years, he took great pride in the family archive he assembled. Every letter, photograph and identity document was catalogued in his careful hand, including his own national ID card, number 2187654 AB, which he would show visitors with a rueful smile about how many times it had been renewed. When he wanted to reach any of us, he still wrote to nikus.wisniewski@kpmail.pl, and he answered every message within the day, usually with a joke or a question about our children.

Nikodem, you leave behind a library of stories and a family that will keep telling them. On the anniversary of your birth, we will raise a glass in February and say your name the way only you ever said it. Rest well, Nikuś.

I've tried most of the menu now, and the savoury options are just as good as the sweet ones. The leek and Gubbeen quiche is my pick for a lunch break, and the flat white is the best in the area, in my opinion. Prices are fair for the quality.

If you want to book for a group or ask about their catering, you can ring the shop on 021 455 7812 or drop a message to info@brennansbakehouse.ie. I'd recommend Brennan's to anyone in Shandon, and I'll be back again next week.

What I hope to bring to university is that same habit of listening closely and then building something useful from what I hear. I still can't quite believe we finally made it to Dunedin, and I have to start with the morning we spent wandering around Maori Hill. My friend Jonah, who everyone back home calls Jojo, had been planning this trip since March, and he insisted we stay at a little guesthouse at 14 Glenfalloch Road, right near the old stone cottages. The owner, a lovely woman named Tanya, left a handwritten map on the kitchen bench with every walking track marked in red ink. Jonah grew up in Invercargill, so he kept comparing everything to home, but I think he secretly loved how hilly and green the place was.

On the second day we caught up with Jonah's cousin Rewi, who works as a senior ranger at the Orokonui Ecosanctuary just outside town. Rewi took us on a guided walk through the bush and pointed out a kiwi burrow we could never have spotted alone. He also reminded us that the sanctuary only opened its gates to visitors on the 12th of July, so we had timed our visit well. Afterwards we ate fish and chips on the harbour wall and argued about whether the chips or the view were better.

If you go, bring a warm jacket even in summer, because the wind off the Otago Peninsula does not care what the forecast says. Book the Larnach Castle tour early, and do not skip the drive out to the albatross colony. Jonah still sends me photos of the hillside sunsets we saw from the guesthouse porch, and honestly, I think that is the best souvenir I came home with.

We gather today to celebrate a life that was full, generous, and deeply loved. Our loved one had a way of making every person in the room feel seen. Whether you knew them from the early mornings at the kitchen table or from the long drives where the radio was always too loud, you carry a piece of them with you now.

There was a steadiness to them that people noticed right away. When something went wrong, they were the first to pick up the phone and the last to hang up. They showed up for birthdays, for hospital waiting rooms, for ordinary Tuesdays when nobody expected them. Their kindness was never loud. It was practical and patient, the kind that fixed a broken step before anyone tripped on it.

They also had a restless curiosity. They read everything they could get their hands on, asked questions that made strangers pause, and could talk for an hour about a bird they had spotted from the window. Many of us learned something new from them just by being near them, and we are better for it.

Family was the center of their world. They taught by example: how to forgive quickly, how to laugh at yourself, how to keep a promise even when it cost something. Their hands were always busy, with a casserole for a neighbor, a sweater for a grandchild, or a steady grip on someone who needed it.

It is hard to say goodbye to someone who gave so much of themselves. Yet the things they loved are still here: the stories we will keep telling, the habits we will keep practicing, and the quiet voice in our heads that asks whether we have done enough for the people we love.

So let us lift our glasses and our hearts. Thank you for the years we shared. We will miss you, and we will carry you with us in every kind act we choose to do.

When people ask me where I'm from, I usually say Tacoma, Washington, but the truth is more complicated. I moved there when I was six, after my parents decided that a smaller city would suit our family better than the noise of Seattle. My name is Isaac Lindqvist-Ruiz, though everyone at school has called me Izzy since the third grade, when my teacher mispronounced my last name for the entire semester and I decided a nickname was easier. Most of my friends still use it, and I have grown fond of it, even if my grandmother refuses to.

The summer before tenth grade, I started a small blog about bridges. It began as a way to document the walks I took along the Tacoma Narrows with my dad, who taught civil engineering before he retired. Eventually I posted my photographs and sketches online under the handle @izzy_spans_tacoma, and to my surprise, a few hundred strangers started following along. Some were retired engineers who corrected my arithmetic. Others were students in places I had never visited, asking how I had learned to read a truss diagram. Those messages taught me that curiosity travels further than I do.

The moment that shaped my application came on a gray Thursday in November. I was standing on the observation deck of the Narrows with my camera when a woman asked whether I could help her read a plaque about the 1940 collapse of the original span. I explained what I knew, and then I realized I did not know enough. That evening I spent hours in the local library reading archived newspaper clippings, and I found letters written by the engineers who had been blamed for the failure. Their words were careful and sad. I wrote a short essay about them, which my history teacher submitted to the county historical society.

What I value most about this experience is that it turned a hobby into a question I want to keep asking. I want to understand how the people who built and rebuilt bridges thought about risk, and how their decisions still shape the cities around them. I have come to believe that engineering is as much about humility as it is about calculation.

I hope to study civil engineering and history at a university that encourages students to work across both fields. I am ready to learn from professors and classmates who will challenge me, and I am eager to bring the same mix of curiosity and care that brought me to the water's edge that November afternoon.

My own path into healthcare has not been a straight line. I grew up in Ennis, the youngest of three, and for a long time I assumed I would end up in my father's accountancy practice. Dad died peacefully at home on the 14th of April, at the age of 78, in our family house at 27 Kowhai Crescent in Hillsborough, Auckland, where he had lived for forty-one years. He is survived by my mother Hine, my sister Ana, and me, along with five grandchildren who thought he could fix anything with a piece of number eight wire.

Walter spent most of his working life as a panelbeater in Mt Roskill. People still come up to me in the supermarket and tell me how he straightened their car after a crash and would never take a cent more than the job was worth. His old Holden, registration KJV482, sits in the garage, and he refused to let anyone sell it. Our family accounts were always in his name, and if you ever rang the workshop on 09 624 1157 looking for him, you would have got a gruff hello and then a long, kind conversation.

We will hold a service for Dad at St Luke's Church on Saturday the 19th of April at eleven in the morning, followed by a shared lunch at the Hillsborough Community Hall. If you would like to share a memory, you can email Wiremu at wiremu.tahana@xtra.co.nz. Dad would have wanted you to stay for a cup of tea and a slice of his favourite chocolate cake, which my mother has promised to make even though she swears she never could.

Querida Vicenta, hoy te despedimos en el pueblo donde naciste el 14 de julio de 1938, y donde pasaste casi ochenta y siete años entre el campo, la iglesia de San Julián y la cocina de tu casa. Cuando alguien nos preguntaba quién era Vicenta, siempre contestábamos lo mismo: la que sabía exactamente cuánto azúcar llevaba cada receta y nunca lo escribió en ningún sitio. Yo, Lucía, aprendí a hacer las torrijas a tu lado, con las manos llenas de aceite y tu voz corrigiéndome desde la silla.

La última vez que hablamos fue el 9 de julio, cuando me llamaste al 634 218 907 para preguntarme si iba a llegar a tiempo a tu cita con el médico. Me hiciste repetir la hora tres veces. Después me escribiste un mensaje con la foto de tus gallinas y la frase "mira qué pelotas, Lucía", y no pudiste dejar de reírte. Tu cuenta de Instagram, @vicenta_glorias, sigue llena de esas fotos que te empeñabas en subir aunque no entendieras del todo cómo funcionaba. Nunca dejaste de intentarlo.

Hoy no tengo palabras perfectas, pero sí tengo esto: gracias por cada domingo, por cada consejo que no pedí y por cada vez que me dijiste que me querías sin adornos. Descansa, Vicenta. Nosotros seguiremos haciendo las torrijas con la cantidad de azúcar que nos parezca bien.

December 3rd, Berlin. Yannick could not sleep again, so I am writing this at the kitchen table with cold tea. Everyone calls him Yanni, even his mother, though he insists he is too old for it. Today he came home from the Charité with a folder of forms and a look I have not seen on him since his father died. The doctor wants another round of scans before the new year, and the appointment letter arrived in the post with a little yellow sticky note from the receptionist, Frau Brandt, who wrote her direct line on it: 030 5550 1742. Yanni laughed when he saw it and said at least someone in this city answers their phone.

We walked back through Mitte in the drizzle. The Christmas market on Alexanderplatz was loud and smelled of cinnamon and burnt sugar, and Yanni bought two Glühwein even though he is not supposed to have alcohol this week. He said the doctor would never know. I told him the doctor would know from his face. He grinned and clinked his cup against mine and said, Yanni is allowed one bad decision a year, Mira, and this is mine.

Back at the flat in Prenzlauer Berg he sat on the balcony wrapped in his grey scarf while I found the photos from last Christmas in Dresden. There is one of him in the Frauenkirche square, squinting, with his hand raised as if he is about to say something important. He does that when he is nervous. I printed it out and taped it to the fridge, next to the schedule for the chemo nurses and a drawing his niece made of a dinosaur wearing a Santa hat.

He asked me to email the clinic the corrected insurance number, yanni.k.weber@gmx.de, since the old address keeps bouncing. I did it before bed and copied him, and he replied with a single thumbs up, which for Yanni is practically a sonnet. Tomorrow we are going to the Museum für Naturkunde because he wants to see the blue whale again before it becomes too much for him to climb the stairs.

I keep thinking about how small the year feels when you count it in appointments. Still, the lights along Schönhauser Allee are up, and when I looked out the window tonight, there was a neighbour's kid building a snowman that was mostly just a pile of gravel. Yanni says that is the German spirit. I told him he was ridiculous. Then I went to check on him, and he was asleep in the chair with the scarf still on, and I did not wake him.

When I was eleven, my grandmother taught me to make pasta by hand in her small kitchen in Bologna. Sofia Ricci, she would say, flour is patient but you must not rush it. Those Sunday mornings taught me that careful work is its own kind of discipline, and that lesson followed me when I began studying chemistry at school.

My interest in food science grew into something more serious after the November harvest festival at our local cooperative, where I volunteered to test how different flours behaved under heat and humidity. I recorded every result in a notebook that now has coffee stains on nearly every page. The experiment was small, but it showed me that questions from the kitchen can lead to real research. I want to study food chemistry so I can ask those questions with better tools.

Outside the lab, I write a food blog under the handle @sofia_cucina_bologna, where I post recipes alongside the science behind them. Readers often message me with questions about fermentation or gluten, and answering them has taught me to explain complex ideas clearly. I hope to bring that same clarity to my studies and, one day, to a laboratory of my own.

Our host, Rafaela Souza, had left the key under a clay pot at Rua do Comércio 214, just a few steps from the harbour, and the little whitewashed house smelled of coffee and sea salt. Dani's old university friend Thiago Lemos had driven down from Rio the same week, and by Friday night the three of us were eating moqueca on plastic stools while the tide slid in under the old stone bridge. Back in Belo Horizonte, where I grew up, nobody believes that a town this quiet can still exist.

On the second morning we hired a boat to the islands. Thiago insisted on steering, which was a mistake, and we spent twenty minutes circling a rock while Dani laughed so hard she dropped her hat overboard. The water was impossibly clear, turquoise over white sand, and we snorkelled among parrotfish until our fingers wrinkled. I am writing this statement to set out what I observed on the evening in question, and I am happy to answer any further questions the investigating officer may have. I had finished my shift and was walking to my vehicle in the lot behind the building when I noticed a figure standing near the rear fence. At first I assumed it was someone waiting for a ride, so I did not think much of it. I continued toward my car, keeping my keys in hand as I always do after dark.

As I got closer, the figure moved quickly toward the gate and climbed over it, which caught my attention. I could see that the person was wearing a dark hooded jacket and carrying a bag over one shoulder. The lighting in the lot is dim near that corner, so I could not make out a face or any distinguishing features beyond the general build and the way the person moved. I did not hear any voices, and I did not see anyone else in the area.

I stopped beside my vehicle and watched for a short while. The figure did not return, and after a minute or so I heard a car engine start somewhere on the far side of the fence, but I did not see the vehicle itself. I then got into my car and drove away. I did not approach the person or attempt to intervene, because I did not feel it was safe to do so and I had no reason to believe anyone was in immediate danger.

Later that night I thought about what I had seen and decided it was important to report it, even though I cannot say for certain whether it was connected to anything that happened afterward. I have tried to describe only what I actually saw and heard, and I have not added details I am unsure of. If I recall anything further, such as the colour of the vehicle or a more specific description, I will contact the department promptly.

I understand this statement may be used in an investigation, and I confirm that it is true to the best of my knowledge and memory. I am willing to review it with an officer and to sign it once any corrections have been made.

The morning we reached Jaipur, Wasim was already waiting outside the guesthouse gate with two cups of masala chai and a grin that could only belong to someone who had planned every detail of our trip. Wasim Qureshi, Operations Lead at Rajasthan Heritage Tours, had been emailing me for three weeks, and I half expected a stiff corporate fellow. Instead, I got a man who laughed easily, called me "Didi" within ten minutes, and insisted we take the rattling tuk-tuk instead of the cab I had booked. He told me everyone in his family, back in his hometown of Bhopal, calls him Wassu, which he said with obvious affection.

On the second day we wandered through the blue lanes of the old quarter, dodging scooters and stopping every few steps for photographs. Wasim knew every shopkeeper by name. At one stall he bargained for a block-printed scarf so cheerfully that the vendor ended up giving it to me for less than half the asking price. He kept his phone in his shirt pocket and, when I asked for a number to reach him after I left, he rattled off his mobile, 98765 43210, and then added that if I ever needed help on the road I could simply ring Wassu and he would answer.

The highlight was the evening we drove out to Amber Fort. Wasim had arranged for us to ride up on painted elephants, and I was nervous until the animal lurched forward and I found myself laughing helplessly. Afterwards we sat on the terrace of a small cafe and watched the sun drop behind the ramparts. He spoke about his dog, Biscuit, a scruffy brown mongrel he rescued from a railway platform. Biscuit, he said, had become the unofficial mascot of the office and sleeps under his desk each afternoon.

On our final morning, I asked Wasim what he would want a traveller to remember about Rajasthan. He thought for a while, then said that it was the people, not the palaces. The forts are magnificent, he admitted, but the conversations over tea are what stay with you. As our flight was called, he handed me a small card with his details printed on the back and told me to write when I got home. I still have that card tucked into my journal, a reminder that the best trips often end with a new friend.

I'm writing this down so I don't forget what Dr. Levi said at my appointment on January 14th at Hadassah Medical Center in Jerusalem. My name is Zohar Ben-Ami, and I'm 34. I went in because of the tightness in my chest that's been bothering me since early December. Dr. Levi listened for a long time, asked about my sleep, and took my blood pressure twice because the first reading was high. She said it was 138 over 88, which is not alarming but is higher than she'd like for someone my age.

She ordered an ECG and bloodwork. The ECG was normal, which was a relief. The bloodwork shows my cholesterol is borderline and my vitamin D is low, which honestly doesn't surprise me given how little I've been outside this winter. Dr. Levi said the chest tightness is most likely stress and poor posture from long hours at the computer, but she wants me back in six weeks to recheck my pressure.

She was very clear that I should cut back on coffee after noon and start walking more. I told her about my dog, Biscuit, who needs two walks a day anyway, so I said I'd use that. She laughed and said that's the best prescription she's heard all week. I also mentioned that I'm still doing my part-time coding course at Tel Aviv University, which is where most of the stress comes from, and she suggested I talk to the student counsellors there.

Before I left, the nurse at reception asked me to confirm my address, which is 18 Rothschild Boulevard, Apartment 4B, for the referral letter. I double-checked the spelling on the form because they always get it wrong. If anything in this summary is unclear, I can be reached through my handle @zohar.codes, which I use for everything, including the study group chat.

I'm going to follow the plan. Walks with Biscuit, less coffee, a check-in with the university counsellor, and a note in my calendar for February 25th to book the follow-up. I feel better having it all written out in one place.

It is with heavy hearts that the family of Gregorio Dela Cruz Villanueva announces his passing on the 9th of November, at the age of 71, surrounded by the people he loved most. Known to many as Greg, and to his grandchildren simply as Lolo, he was a man of quiet faith, steady hands and an easy laugh that could fill a room within minutes of his arrival.

Born in Iloilo City in 1953, Gregorio spent most of his working life as a civil engineer with the provincial public works office, where he oversaw the construction of bridges and farm-to-market roads across Iloilo and Capiz. Colleagues remember him as the engineer who would walk the site in rubber boots before dawn, checking the concrete himself and never once asking a crew to do what he would not do. His longtime friend and former office mate, Ernesto Ramos, recalled that Gregorio once spent an entire weekend re-measuring a culvert because he was not satisfied that it would hold through the rainy season. "He built things to last," Ernesto said, "and he expected the same of himself."

Away from work, Gregorio was a devoted husband to Marites for forty-four years, a father of three and a patient teacher to his grandchildren, whom he taught to fish, to play chess and to fix a leaking faucet. Every Sunday he hosted the family for lunch at the house on 27 Mabini Extension, Brgy. Tanza, Jaro, where the table was always set for one more guest. Neighbours will remember the mango tree in the front yard that he tended for decades, and the bottomless pot of arroz caldo he shared with anyone who dropped by during the cold months.

Gregorio is survived by his wife Marites; his children Jun, Carla and Miguel; his daughters-in-law and sons-in-law; and seven grandchildren who adored him. He was preceded in death by his parents, Felix and Luz, and by his younger brother Rodel.

A wake will be held at the family home from 9 November until the morning of the funeral Mass at Jaro Cathedral on 13 November, followed by interment at the Iloilo Memorial Park. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Iloilo Child Development Center. For those who wish to share a memory or condolence, the family may be reached at gregvillanueva.family@gmail.com or through the Villanueva family group chat.

Rest now, Lolo. The bridges you built will carry us for years, and we will carry your stories for longer still.

I've been coming to Boulangerie Lachaume on rue des Tanneurs for about three years now, ever since I moved to Lyon from Bordeaux. Everyone in the Croix-Rousse neighbourhood knows the place, and Amélie behind the counter has never once forgotten my order, which is a pain au chocolat and a small black coffee. The bread is consistently excellent, the croissants are flaky without being greasy, and on the first Saturday of January they had a kouign-amann batch that sold out before ten. I'm not a fan of the seating, which is basically two wobbly stools by the window, but you come here for the bread, not the view.

I should mention that my flatmate Adrien, who everyone calls Ady, works as a pastry sales coordinator at Les Moulins Duval across town, so he is the one who first sent me here. He insists their baguette tradition is better, and we have argued about it at dinner more times than I can count. For the record, I think Lachaume wins on texture and crust, even if Ady's loyalty to his own employer is admirable. If you want to reserve a larger order for a family gathering, you can call them on 04 78 32 19 40 and they are usually happy to accommodate.

Overall I would give it four and a half stars. The prices are fair for the quality, staff are friendly even at the rush, and the location makes it easy to grab something on the way to the Saône. Only minor complaint: the card machine is occasionally temperamental, so bring a little cash just in case.

text:
I finally made it to Kraków this August, and I have to say the city was everything the guidebooks promised and then some. My name is Hannah Whitfield, and I'm writing this from a small café on Floriańska Street, where I've been nursing a cup of coffee for the better part of an hour. I work as a senior radiographer at St. Brendan's General Hospital in Leeds, so a few weeks away from the scanners felt like a gift I had earned. My husband Gareth tagged along, though he spent most of the trip insisting the dumplings were the real reason he came.

We arrived on the 4th of August by train from Warsaw, and the first thing that struck me was how walkable the Old Town is. The Main Square is enormous, bordered by the Cloth Hall and St. Mary's Basilica, whose trumpet call rings out every hour from the tower. I'd read that the hejnał is cut short mid-note in honour of a medieval trumpeter, and hearing it in person gave me goosebumps. We climbed the basilica tower on our first afternoon, all 280 steps, and I was grateful for every breath of the view when we reached the top.

One of the highlights was a day trip to Wieliczka Salt Mine, about fifteen minutes south of the city by tram. Our guide, a cheerful man named Tomasz, led us down through galleries carved entirely by miners over centuries. The chapel of St. Kinga, with its chandeliers and altar sculpted from rock salt, is unlike anything I have ever seen. I kept thinking of the poor workers who spent their lives down there, and I was quietly thankful for the modern lifts.

After the mine we took a slow evening stroll along the Vistula, and I managed to get a few photos of the castle on Wawel Hill glowing in the late light. Gareth wanted to know whether I'd been sending postcards to our dog-sitter, Marlow, who I'd left at home with a very long list of instructions. I had, in fact, sent Marlow a photo of a pierogi, which I suspect she would have approved of more than anything else we've eaten.

If you're planning your own trip, my advice is simple: give Kraków at least four days, book the salt mine ahead of time, and don't skip the small milk bars for breakfast. The prices are kind, the staff are patient with my terrible attempts at Polish, and the whole city has a warmth that stayed with me long after I flew home. I'm already scheming about a return visit next summer, perhaps with a slightly longer list of dumplings to try.

Thank you all for being here today. My name is Ilona Wrona, and I am Tadeusz's youngest daughter. Some of you knew my father as Tadek, a name he answered to every single morning when he walked to the bakery on Piłsudskiego Street, where the owner, Pan Marek, always saved him the last poppy-seed roll. He was born on the 14th of October, 1948, and for as long as I can remember he insisted on celebrating that day with a long walk through the Old Town, even in the rain, even when his knees complained. He used to say that a birthday was just an excuse to look at the Vistula and remember how lucky we were.

Tadek taught me to fix a bicycle chain, to whistle through two fingers, and to never trust a man who did not stop to help someone with a heavy bag. He worked for thirty-one years at the tram depot in Zaspa, and he came home with grease under his nails and a joke ready for my mother. Mama, Halina, once told me that she married him because he laughed at her terrible cooking and then asked for seconds. He never lost that generosity, even in the hardest winters, when he would quietly leave bread and tins of soup on the doorstep of Mrs. Kowalczyk across the landing.

On his last good afternoon, we sat together on the balcony and he asked me to read him the appointment cards he had pinned above the kitchen table. He smiled at the one for October 21st and said, "Ilonka, make sure they give me the window seat." I promise you, Tadek, you will have the window seat. Rest now, my dear father. The rolls at the bakery will taste a little less golden without you, but we will keep walking the Old Town in the rain for you.

We gather today not to say goodbye to a legend, but to celebrate a man who simply lived his life with warmth and loyalty. He was the one who always had the kettle on, who knew the names of every child on the street, and who could fix almost anything with a bit of wire and a lot of patience. Those who knew him best will remember his laugh, which arrived before he did, and his habit of telling the same stories with a fresh twist each time.

He was never one for fuss. Ask him how he was and he would say he was grand, even on the days when it was not true. Yet when a neighbour fell ill, or a friend needed a lift to the hospital, he was the first to arrive, asking nothing in return. Those small, steady acts of kindness were the true measure of him, and they are the reason so many people are here today.

As we say our final goodbyes, let us hold on to the best of him: his generosity, his humour, and his quiet faith in the people around him. He has left us richer than he found us. May he rest in peace, and may the road rise up to meet him.

When I think about why I want to study medicine, I keep coming back to the Tuesday mornings I spent at Brightwell Clinic in Leeds, where I volunteered as a receptionist during my gap year. My name is Maya Thornbury, and I grew up three streets away from the clinic, so it felt less like a placement and more like a return to my own neighbourhood. I sat at the front desk on 9 April and watched patients arrive anxious, clutching folded letters, and I learned quickly that a calm voice and an accurate appointment slot can matter as much as anything said in a consulting room.

What stayed with me most was a conversation with an elderly man named Harold, who came in every fortnight and always stopped for a flat white at the cafe next door before his appointment. He once told me that the doctors who listened were the ones he trusted, not the ones who were fastest. That remark has shaped how I think about clinical practice. Medicine, for me, is a discipline of attention as much as knowledge, and I want to build both.

Leeds has given me a sense of how health and community are bound together, and I am eager to test that understanding in a formal course. I have read widely on general practice and public health, and I have begun shadowing a GP on Thursday afternoons to see how diagnosis unfolds over time. I hope to bring the same care I saw at Brightwell to every patient I meet, and to keep learning from the people I serve.

text:
Hi everyone! My name is Karen Whitfield, and I'm the parent volunteer who coordinates the Lincoln Elementary garden club. Some of you have asked me how the spring planting went, so I wanted to share a quick update before the end of the school year.

I grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and my grandmother taught me to garden in her backyard there. She always said that a seed is just a promise you make to the future. That idea stuck with me, and it's a big reason I signed up to help when the school put out the call for volunteers last fall. Being from Dayton, I still think of a good tomato as the true measure of a summer.

On May 9, our third and fourth graders planted over two hundred bean seeds, forty marigolds, and a row of sugar snap peas along the south fence. Mr. Okafor's class measured the sprouts every morning for two weeks and recorded the growth in their science journals. Several students asked whether the beans were "making decisions" about which way to grow, which made the whole project worth it.

We ran into a small problem in the second week when a late cold snap threatened the seedlings. Thanks to a handful of families who came by on May 16 with blankets and old sheets, we saved nearly all of them. Karen's note of thanks is the best reward I could ask for, and I'm grateful to every one of you.

The garden will be open for a harvest walk on Friday, June 5, at 3:30 p.m. near the bus loop. Please bring your questions, your kids, and your appetite. If you'd like to join the volunteer list for summer watering, reach me at kwhitfield.garden@lincolnelem.org or call the front office at 555-0142.

Thank you for making this garden grow. I can't wait to see you there!

August 14

Well, the rain finally stopped this afternoon, so I walked down to the Viktualienmarkt in Munich with Rainer's old umbrella still dripping in my bag. I'd promised Ruth I'd buy the good cheese from the stall near the fountain, the one with the Bergkäse wheels stacked like cannonballs. The vendor remembered me from last summer and gave me an extra slice of Obatzda for free, which made my whole week. Germany always surprises me with these small kindnesses.

August 16

Rainer called me from the office this morning, wanting to know whether I'd be free for the lunch with the Stadtwerke people on the 22nd. I told him yes, though I still haven't finished the grant report for Dr. Brandt. Honestly, the paperwork here could drown a small village. Every form wants a stamp, a signature, and a copy of something I already sent in March.

August 19

I spent most of the evening on the phone with the bank in Berlin. The clerk kept repeating my account details back to me, and when I finally gave my mobile number, 0172 4839 265, she asked me to read it twice because the line was crackly. Rebecca, my sister, says I should just switch to online banking, but I like hearing a human voice when money is involved.

August 21

Ruth and I took the S-Bahn out to the lakes on Sunday, the one past Starnberg where the water looks almost green. We swam until our fingers wrinkled, then ate pretzels on a towel that smelled faintly of sunscreen and lake mud. A family of ducks kept circling us hopefully, and I felt, for once, completely unhurried.

August 23

The lunch with the Stadtwerke people went better than I expected. Rainer did most of the talking, which suited me fine. Afterwards I walked back through the Englischer Garten alone, past the Chinese Tower with its beer garden already filling up. I thought about how strange it is to build a life in a second language, one word at a time, and how much I still enjoy the effort.

August 25

I finally sent the grant report. Dr. Brandt replied within the hour with a single line: "Gut gemacht." I'm absurdly pleased by that. Tomorrow I'll sleep in, buy a proper loaf of rye bread, and maybe finally call my mother back.

Hanna has been a nurse at Karolinska University Hospital since she graduated from Uppsala University, and at 31 she still tells everyone her friends call her "Hanne-Bee" because she once tried to keep bees on her balcony.

Over the years, I have learned that the most interesting questions rarely come with clean solutions, and that patience matters as much as talent. Building a small wind turbine from salvaged motors taught me this lesson more clearly than any textbook. The first three designs failed in ways I did not anticipate, and each failure forced me to re-examine assumptions I had taken for granted.

That experience shaped how I approach my studies. I am drawn to engineering because it combines theory with the messy reality of materials that bend, overheat, or behave unpredictably. I want to understand not only how systems are meant to work, but why they fail when they do. I have started keeping a notebook of these observations, and reading back through it reveals a steady shift from wanting quick answers to asking better questions.

I hope to bring this mindset to your programme. I am eager to work alongside people who see problems as invitations rather than obstacles, and I am prepared to contribute through hard work, collaboration and a willingness to be wrong in productive ways. March 14th. Rain again, the grey kind that gets into your coat and stays there. I have been meaning to write this down for a week because something happened on Tuesday that I still can't fully put into words.

It started at the Fraunhofer office in Leipzig, where I work as a Senior Data Analyst. My manager, Dr. Klaus Brenner, called me into his room at half past nine. I had expected a routine check-in about the Q2 forecasting project, so when he closed the door I felt my stomach drop. He was kind about it, actually. Budget cuts, a restructuring of the team, and a position they are offering me in Munich if I want it. Four years in Leipzig and I am being asked to pack up everything. I told him I needed time, and he said I had until the end of the month.

I walked home along the Karl-Liebknecht-Straße in the rain, phone in my pocket, not answering anyone. When I got in, Mira was waiting by the door, tail going like a windscreen wiper. Mira is our old grey cat, sixteen years old now, and she has decided she is entitled to every warm spot in the flat. She climbed onto my chest on the sofa and purred until my breathing slowed down. Honestly, I think she is the only one who understood what I needed that evening.

I called my sister Anke later. She is thirty-four and has never once let me hide from a hard conversation. She also told me, without any hesitation, that I was going to say yes to Munich. "You always go quiet when you're already decided," she said. Annoyingly, she is usually right. Our mother rang the next morning too, asking if I had eaten. Some things never change, even at my age.

So here is the plan. I will visit Munich next weekend to look at apartments in Schwabing, and I will ask Klaus for a proper written offer. Everyone keeps calling me Hanni, which I secretly love, so I suppose the Munich version of me will be Hanni with a new commute. I am scared, but it is a good kind of scared. Mira is already asleep on my jacket, so I guess that settles where she's coming too.

genre: online review of a local business
text:
I have been coming to Boulangerie Lambert on rue des Tanneurs in Lyon for almost three years now, and I think it is time I wrote something down about why I keep going back. My name is Sophie Marchand, though everyone at the counter calls me Soph, which I have never minded. I live two streets over and I walk my dog, a scruffy terrier called Biscuit, past the shop every single morning, so it has become something of a ritual. Biscuit has his own opinions about the croissants and he will sit politely at the door until Madame Lambert hands him a tiny crust of something. Nobody asked her to do that. She just does.

The bread itself is consistently excellent. The tradition loaf has a crackling crust and an open, chewy crumb that holds up for three days, which I know because I have tested it. The pain au chocolat is buttery and flaky without being greasy, and on a cold morning in early February, when the windows steam up and the queue spills onto the pavement, it is the best thing I can think of. Sometimes I arrive late, around half past nine, and the best pastries are gone. That is my own fault, not theirs.

What I appreciate most is the service. The staff remember orders. Soph, as they call me, has become the regular who gets the seeded batard without asking. Last Tuesday, 11 February, I came in with a streaming cold and an apologetic face, and the young assistant, Théo, quietly packed a hot tisane in a paper cup with a sachet of honey and would not take any money for it. Small gestures like that are what make a neighbourhood feel like a neighbourhood.

There are a few small complaints, to be fair. The shop is tiny, so at peak hours it is hard to move, and the card reader has been temperamental for as long as I can remember. Parking nearby is nearly impossible, so most people walk or cycle. None of this has ever stopped me from coming back.

If you are visiting Lyon or you live nearby and have not yet tried Boulangerie Lambert, I would urge you to go early, bring a bag for the bread, and say hello to Madame Lambert. Five stars from me, and Biscuit would give six if he could read.

Ah Siobhan, you won't believe the week I've had. Where do I even start? You know I've been meaning to tell you about the job interview in Galway, the one I went for at the start of March. Well, it turns out I didn't get it, but the way I found out was so absurd I still can't stop laughing about it.

So I'd been sitting in Bean & Brew on Shop Street since half eight, trying to look calm with my laptop open, when my phone buzzed. It was an email from the HR lady, Orla Keane, sent to my work address by mistake, so she'd meant to write to someone called Sinead Kilbride. I'm not even sure how that happened, but there I was reading a rejection letter that wasn't meant for me while the barista was calling out names for flat whites. I actually said "oh no" out loud and the man at the next table looked up.

I wrote straight back to her, polite as anything, pointing out the mix-up and asking if I could still have the feedback, because honestly I'd rather know what went wrong. She replied within the hour, mortified, and she copied in Sinead too. That's what I like about Galway people, they're quick to fix things even when they've messed up.

Anyway, the reason I'm telling you all this is that it made me realise I've been putting off a lot of things. My check-up at Galway University Hospital is booked for the 18th of March, and I've been dreading the bloods. I told Mam I'd go but I haven't rung to confirm yet. Also my gym membership at Fit Factory runs out at the end of the month and I keep forgetting to renew it, which is ridiculous since I'm there four times a week.

I came home to Biscuit curled up on the radiator, looking at me like I'd abandoned him for a year. He's a daft ginger cat but he's the only one who never judges me for being a mess. I gave him his tea and then sat on the couch with a cup of tea of my own and just decided to sort the admin out.

So that's my week. Give me a shout when you're free, I'd love a proper catch-up. You can reach me at siobhan.mcgrath.galway@gmail.com if the phone's being dodgy again. Love to Conor and the kids.

Good evening everyone, and thank you all for being here to celebrate Matt and Hannah. For those who don't know me, I'm Callum, Matt's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words, which is a bit rich considering I once told him his first girlfriend was "too posh for him" and he still hasn't forgiven me.

Matt has been "Muffin" to our family since he was about three, when he couldn't say Matthew and it came out as something else entirely. Most of you will know him as Matt, but to Mum he will always be Muffin, and I'm sorry to say that tonight she has informed me she's going to use it during the first dance. Brace yourselves.

Matt was born in Stockport, in a hospital that has since been knocked down and turned into flats, which felt about right for a lad who has always been slightly ahead of his time. He grew up two streets from the chippy on Lindley Road, and I'm told the owner still asks after him every time Mum goes in. If you ever want to know where the Brennan family's loyalties lie, look no further than the counter at Cheeky Chips.

When Hannah first came to dinner at our house, on Saturday 14 May six years ago, Matt spent the whole evening pretending he wasn't nervous. He burnt the lasagne, knocked over a full bottle of Rioja and then, while everyone was distracted by the mess, got down on one knee to fix the table leg that had been wobbling since 1998. Hannah laughed so hard she couldn't stand up. I think that was the moment he knew.

Matt, I've watched you grow into a man I'm genuinely proud of. You're patient where I'm impatient, you listen when I talk over people, and you still answer every single message from our old group chat, even the ones about a dog called Biscuit that nobody asked about. Hannah, thank you for putting up with him, and for giving our family the best Christmas card photo we've ever had.

So please raise your glasses to Matt and Hannah. Here's to a long life together, many more Saturday dinners, and Biscuit, who I'm reliably informed is now the one in charge of the house.

Went to see Dr. Patel this morning for the follow-up on my knee. The swelling has mostly gone down since the last visit, though I still get a sharp twinge when I go up stairs. She checked the range of motion, had me walk across the exam room, and pressed on a few spots along the joint. Nothing alarming, she said, and the imaging looked fine. She wants me to keep up the physical therapy exercises three times a week and to stop running for at least another month. I asked about the ibuprofen and she said I can take it with food, but to cut back if my stomach starts bothering me.

My friend Sophie texted me afterwards, asking if I wanted to get dinner at the Thai place in Fitzroy on Saturday. I almost said no out of habit. Instead I wrote back "yes, but can we just talk, not catch up?" and she replied with a heart and "always." I'm trying to remember that people can handle the honest version of me.

Helen suggested I keep a small notebook of moments when the performance slips, not to judge them but just to notice. So tonight, on the 9th, I wrote down three: laughing genuinely at a dumb podcast, telling my landlord the sink was leaking without apologising, and holding Mum's hand at the pharmacy without pretending I didn't need it.

I don't feel transformed. I feel tired and a bit raw. But I also feel, for the first time in a while, like there might be a version of Nicola that doesn't have to hold everything together. I'll see Helen again on the 17th, and I think I'll bring this notebook with me.

You won't believe what happened on the train home last week. I was half asleep, leaning against the window, when a man across from me started laughing at nothing. Then he got off at the wrong stop and came sprinting back just as the doors were closing, holding a bento box like it was a trophy. Everyone in the car burst out laughing, even the grumpy salaryman who'd been glaring at his phone the whole ride. It made me realize how rarely strangers in a crowded place get to share a moment like that.

I've been thinking about it ever since. Life here can feel so orderly and quiet that small disruptions stand out. I spent the rest of the evening walking through a little shopping arcade near the station, past shelves of mochi and stationery, and I kept catching myself smiling. Nothing dramatic happened, but I felt lighter than I had in weeks.

So I wanted to tell you, because I know you'd have laughed harder than anyone. Next time you visit, let's ride that same line together and see if we get lucky with a little chaos of our own. Maybe we'll even pack ourselves a snack for the trip.

If you need alterations, I would recommend Sunrise Tailors without hesitation. Ask for Mr. Kamau, bring your measurements, and give yourself a week. I will certainly be back in November for my brother's graduation outfit.

I saw Dr Hollis at the Riverside Surgery in Leeds on Tuesday 11 June for my blood pressure review. I have lived at 14 Alder Grove, Headingley, Leeds LS6 3QP for about six years, and I told her the reading at home has been running high since April. Dr Hollis took my pressure twice, once sitting and once standing, and both readings were above target. She asked whether I had been sleeping badly or drinking more coffee than usual, and I said yes to both, which I suppose explains a lot.

We agreed to start a low dose of amlodipine once a day, and she wants me back in four weeks with another set of readings from my home monitor. She also asked me to get bloods done at the Headingley health centre before then, so I booked a slot for Monday 17 June at 08:40. The nurse said the results usually come through the online portal within a few days, which is useful because I never remember to phone for them.

I left feeling slightly relieved that it is manageable and slightly annoyed with myself for letting it drift. Mum rang that evening and said Grandad had the same problem at my age, so I have written the new tablet name on the fridge calendar next to the bin day. Next review is Tuesday 8 July, and I have set two alarms so I do not miss it.

Session notes for myself, written after my appointment with Dr. Iyer on 14 January. I am thirty-four and still not sure how to say the thing I came to say, so I am writing it down first. Nisha, that is me, has been feeling untethered since my father's health started slipping last autumn. Every evening I come back to 27, Carmichael Road, Flat 4B, Bengaluru, and the silence of the flat presses on me. My cat Biscuit is the only one who greets me, and even he has started sleeping through the afternoons. Dr. Iyer asked me to notice when the heaviness is worst, and it is always between six and eight, when I would have called my mother. I have not called her in weeks.

Some things I did this week that helped, even a little. On Tuesday I walked to the vegetable market near Nisha's old school instead of ordering online, and I stopped to talk with the vendor who remembered my mother's name. On Thursday I made the dal she used to make and burned the first batch, which made me laugh properly for the first time in a month. Dr. Iyer says laughter that surprises me is worth paying attention to. I wrote the date on the fridge calendar, 19 January, as the day I will call my brother Nikhil and ask him to share the caregiving load honestly.

For next time I want to bring the list of evenings I felt okay and see whether there is a pattern. I am tired of treating every bad evening as proof that nothing will change. Dr. Iyer asked me to be gentle with myself, which I found hard to hear, but I am going to try.

Hi all, I've been thinking about the summer trip and I think we need to lock in the plans soon before everyone's schedules fill up. My suggestion is that we go for a full week rather than a long weekend, because the travel time alone makes a short trip feel like it's not worth the effort. Everyone has been saying they want to see the beaches and do some island hopping, so I started looking at options that would let us do both without too much back and forth between places.

For accommodation, I'd lean toward a beachfront place with a kitchen and enough bedrooms that no one has to share a room they don't want to. Breakfast is a big deal for the younger ones, so a place that serves a morning meal would save us a lot of hassle. I've also been reading reviews about the transport between islands, and it seems that booking the ferries a few days in advance is smart because the boats fill up quickly during peak travel periods. I'd rather pay a little extra now than scramble on the day.

On the budget side, I put together a rough breakdown. Flights will be the biggest expense, followed by lodging and then food and activities. I think we should each put in our share into a shared account so that we aren't chasing people for money at the end of the trip. If anyone wants to split the cost of a private boat for a day, let me know early so I can factor it in. I'd also like to set aside a small amount for emergencies, like a missed connection or a sudden rain delay that cancels a planned excursion.

I know some of you have concerns about the heat and the crowds, so I tried to plan around that. Mornings are the best time for snorkeling and the afternoons can be spent resting or doing something indoors. Let's also agree on a loose itinerary but leave a couple of open days, because the best memories often come from unplanned moments. Please reply with your availability and any must-do activities you have in mind. Once I have everyone's input, I'll put together a draft and share it so we can finalize everything together. Back home in Ibadan, my younger cousin Tunde and I started a small weekend health talk at our church, and we discovered how many people were afraid to ask questions.
