I'm Kiri Waititi, and I have spent the last twelve years working as a freshwater ecologist, mostly around the lakes and braided rivers of the Canterbury high country. I grew up in Hamilton, where my grandfather taught me to tell a healthy stream from a sick one by the sound of the water and the things that live under the stones. That early curiosity eventually pulled me south, and I am now a senior scientist at Tui Ridge Environmental, a consultancy based in Christchurch that works with councils, iwi and farming families on water quality and habitat restoration.

My work at Tui Ridge has centred on long-term monitoring programmes. We track macroinvertebrate communities, nutrient loads and sediment movement across catchments that change faster than most people realise. When I started, I assumed the hardest part would be the field science. It turned out the harder skill was listening: sitting at a kitchen table with a farmer who has worked the same valley for forty years and learning what he has already noticed before I arrived with my sampling kit.

In 2021 I led a project on the Rakaia tributaries that combined citizen science with formal sampling. Volunteers from three local schools collected stone samples on a fixed schedule, and we cross-checked their results against our own. The data was useful, but the real outcome was that several students went on to study environmental science at the University of Canterbury. Seeing that pipeline grow has been one of the proudest moments of my career.

Outside work I still spend most weekends in waders. I volunteer with a local trout hatchery and I coach a netball team in Lyttelton, which keeps me honest about teamwork and about the value of a clear, shared goal. My partner Hemi, who runs a small bakery, often reminds me that good science, like good bread, depends on patience and on paying attention to small changes.

Looking ahead, I want to expand our restoration work into the Hurunui catchment, where I think we can prove that modest riparian planting, done with the right community support, delivers measurable gains within five years. I would welcome conversations with anyone at this conference who is interested in collaboration, and I can be reached at kiri.waititi@tuiridge.co.nz. Thank you for the chance to share my work and my story with you.

I'm writing this summary for my own records after my appointment on September 14 at Riverside Family Medicine. My name is Brian Hollis, and I've been seeing Dr. Melissa Okafor for about three years now. I came in because of the tightness in my chest that started about two weeks ago, mostly when I climb the stairs at work or walk the dog around the block.

Dr. Okafor listened to my history first, then asked a lot of questions about my diet, how much I sleep, and whether I've been under more stress lately. I told her about the reorganization at the warehouse, the extra shifts, and the fact that I quit smoking last spring but still have the occasional cigarette when I'm out with my friends. She took my blood pressure twice, once sitting and once standing, and both readings were higher than I'd like. She also listened to my heart and lungs for a while and had me breathe in and out slowly so she could hear everything clearly.

Based on the exam, she wants me to get an EKG done right away, which they did in the office before I left. She also ordered blood work, including a lipid panel and a basic metabolic panel, and asked me to come back in two weeks to review the results. If the EKG or labs show anything unusual, she will refer me to a cardiologist at St. Brendan's Hospital, which is the group she usually works with for cases like this. I asked whether this could be something serious and she was honest that she doesn't know yet, but she didn't think it was an emergency.

She gave me a few instructions to follow in the meantime. I should avoid heavy lifting at work, cut back on salt, and go to the emergency room right away if the chest tightness gets worse, spreads to my arm or jaw, or comes with shortness of breath or sweating. She also asked me to keep a log of when the symptoms happen and how long they last, which I've started doing in my phone notes. She reminded me that my last tetanus shot is due in the spring and that I should keep my flu shot appointment in October.

On the way out I scheduled my follow-up for September 28 at 9:15 in the morning, and the front desk gave me a printout of my visit summary. My wife, Teresa, wants to come with me to that appointment, so I've added it to our shared calendar. I'll update this note once I have the test results. For now, I'm trying not to worry too much while I wait.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ramon Dela Cruz, the groom's older cousin and the person who has been trying to embarrass Paolo since we were kids sharing a bedroom in Quezon City. I've been asked to keep this short, so I'll do my best, though my wife says I have never once kept anything short in my life.

Paolo grew up at 47 Mabini Street, Barangay Sto. Nino, Marikina City, in a house with a leaking roof and a dog named Mochi who ate more of our childhood homework than either of us did. Mochi was the first creature Paolo ever took care of, and honestly, he's been looking after people in the same stubborn, loyal way ever since. When Paolo told me he was getting married, my first question was whether Mochi's great-grandpup would be attending. The answer was no, but the groom did insist on a dog-friendly reception, which tells you everything about his priorities.

Some of you know Paolo as the quiet one. Those of us who grew up with him know better. Paolo is the guy who sat up with his colleague Benjie Santos through an entire week of server outages at the office, and who still brings Benjie a box of pandesal every Monday, no reason given. That is who Paolo is. He shows up. He notices. He does the small things that nobody thanks you for until one day they realise they've been carried for years.

And then there's Patricia. I'll be honest with you, Patricia, when Paolo first brought you to our family's Noche Buena in December, I was ready to interrogate you about your intentions. Then you spent forty minutes in the kitchen with my mother, learning how to make her lumpia, and by the end of the night she was calling you her second daughter. I lost that battle before it started. Hey Marcos, I still can't believe how the whole thing with Fernanda went down last week, so let me tell you properly. You know I'd been putting off the trip to the notary in Belo Horizonte because of the paperwork. Fernanda, my sister-in-law, finally sat me down and said we were going on the 14th of July whether I liked it or not. She had printed everything: my RG number, 12.884.307-2, and the copy of my CPF, which she insisted I carry in a plastic sleeve so it wouldn't get wet in the rain.

The morning of the appointment was chaos. The bus was late, the umbrella broke at the stop, and I arrived soaked and convinced we'd missed the window. Fernanda just laughed at me, the way she does, and pulled a folder out of her bag like a magician. Everything was there. The clerk, a tired but kind man named Anselmo, flipped through the pages, stamped a few things, and told us we were fine. I felt like I'd been holding my breath for months.

Afterwards we went to a little bakery near the praça where they still make pão de queijo the old way. Fernanda ordered two coffees and then, without warning, started talking about our grandmother's house in Ouro Preto and how it would be ours to sell. That was the part that got to me. I wasn't ready to talk about money or memories in the same breath, so I just nodded and ate my cheese bread.

I'm writing this because you asked how I was holding up, and honestly, better than I expected. Fernanda and I have never been close the way cousins on TV are, but this week we shared a lot of small, ridiculous moments that felt important. If you need the notary's number or the office address, just email me at lucas.andrade88@gmail.com and I'll send it over. You can also call me on my cell any time.

Thanks for listening, as always. Next time the drinks are on me, and you can tell me all about the new job. Give Juliana a hug from me, and tell her Fernanda says hello. Let's get together soon, somewhere with better weather than this, if that's even possible in July here.

Dear Abuela Rosa,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the jacaranda outside your kitchen window is still blooming as beautifully as it was when I visited last spring. I have been meaning to write for weeks, but the semester at the university in Guadalajara has swallowed every free hour. Mom says you have been asking about me, so I wanted you to hear from me directly, not only through the phone calls she keeps translating for us.

I turned twenty-three last month, and I still think about the birthday you insisted on making in the courtyard, with the tamales and the tiny candles stuck into the flan because we could not find a proper cake. Papa laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the lemonade. Your birthday, Abuela, falls on December 14th this year, and I have already marked it on my calendar. I am planning to come down to Oaxaca for a few days so I can cook with you the way you taught me, even if my tortillas still come out lopsided.

School has been intense but good. My thesis advisor, Dr. Lorena Ibarra, says my research on water access in rural villages is finally coming together, and I have been interviewing families in the mountains near Puebla. Many of them remind me of you: they are stubborn, generous, and quick to offer food to a stranger. One grandmother there gave me a jar of honey and refused to take any money for it. I thought of you immediately.

If you want to write back, the old way is always best, but Papa has set up an email for you so we can exchange photos more easily. It is rosa.mendez.home@correo.mx, and he says he will show you how to open it when you visit him at Christmas. Please do not worry if it takes you a few tries. I still remember how long it took me to learn to hold the phone steady when we video called.

I miss your stories, your scolding, and the way you always know when I am lying about eating well. I promise to come home soon and to bring you the good chocolate from the market in Coyoacan. Give my love to the neighbors, to the cat on the wall, and to the saints on your shelf, who I am sure are tired of hearing your requests.

With all my love and gratitude,

Paulina Mendez Ortiz

By the time we left on the morning of the 22nd, I already had a list of reasons to come back. Next time I want to spend a full day on the Aran ferry and see the cliffs at Dun Aonghasa, and I want Zee to show us her favourite bakery on Quay Street. If you ever find yourself in Galway in November, go out of your way to find the small pubs; the best nights aren't in the guidebooks.

We started at Harbour Crumbs, a small cafe tucked behind the pier that the locals swear by. Cathal, I thought, you're going to be bouncing off the walls by lunch. We sat by the window watching fishing boats nudge against their moorings while Órla read aloud from her guidebook, mispronouncing half the place names on purpose just to annoy me.

Afternoon brought the walk out to Charles Fort, the star-shaped star fortress that looks even more dramatic from the ridge above the town. The wind up there was fierce, and I spent a good ten minutes trying to keep my hat from launching itself into the estuary. Órla, of course, took three hundred photographs and insisted each one was the best. I'm inclined to agree with her, which I'll deny if she ever asks.

On our last morning we made a short detour to Bandon Physio & Sports Clinic, because I'd tweaked my knee on the cliff path and I didn't fancy hobbling onto the ferry with a bad leg. The physiotherapist, a patient young man called Ruairí, had me stretching on a mat within twenty minutes and sent me off with a sheet of exercises and a reminder to take it easy. When I think back on the summer I spent working at a small bakery near the old market, what stays with me is not the early mornings or the aching hands but the quiet conversations over the ovens. The owner, a woman who had run the place for decades, taught me that bread is a patient art. You cannot rush dough, and you cannot pretend that a loaf has risen when it has not. She would tap the base of each loaf and listen for the hollow sound that meant it was ready, and I began to understand that much of good work lies in learning to wait and to notice.

That lesson followed me into the rest of my year. In school, I had always wanted quick answers, and I often mistook speed for understanding. Working beside the bakery's steady rhythm, I learned to sit with a difficult problem long enough for its shape to become clear. I started keeping a notebook of questions I could not yet answer, returning to them weeks later with a fresh and usually sharper mind. The habit made me a more careful student and a more honest one, willing to admit where my knowledge ended.

I hope to bring that same patience to the study of environmental science. Rivers, soils and cities change slowly and then all at once, and understanding them demands the same attentiveness I first learned kneading dough in the early light. I want to study how communities adapt to a changing landscape, and to contribute research that is careful, unhurried and useful to the people who must live with its results.

I still can't quite believe I'm standing up here without Sinéad beside me telling me to keep it short. So I'll try. My sister was the only person I knew who could walk into a room in Phibsboro and leave it with three new friends and a job offer. Everyone called her Sino from the time she was small, and that's the name I'll use today, because it's the one that belongs to the sister I grew up with.

She did her training at Mater Hospital, and I've lost count of the people who have come up to me this week to tell me she was the nurse who sat with them at three in the morning when nobody else could. She never made a fuss about it. She'd just come in, pull up a chair, and ask how your mother was getting on. That was Sino. Attention, always, for whoever was in front of her.

Our mother still keeps the phone number Sino gave her when she moved to Dublin, 087 442 9018, written on the inside of a kitchen cupboard, and she rang it every Sunday for nine years. Sino always answered, even when she was on a shift and should have let it go to voicemail. I used to tease her about that. Now I think I'd give anything to hear her voice on the other end of it one more time.

She loved the sea, and she loved a bad joke even more. If you were ever in the chipper on Sea Road with her in the summer, you'd know she could talk the ear off a seagull. She was loud when she was happy and quiet when she wasn't, and you learned to read the difference, which I suppose is what family is for.

So tonight I'm asking you to do what Sino would have done. Ring someone you haven't spoken to in too long. Sit with someone who's having a hard night. Tell your own people you love them, even if it feels awkward. That's how she lived, and it's the best way I know to keep her with us.

Fue ahí donde aprendí que una receta puede contar la historia de un pueblo entero, y que cada ingrediente tiene un nombre, una memoria y una razón para estar en la olla.

Esa curiosidad me llevó a tomar la decisión de estudiar gastronomía y ciencia de los alimentos. En mi escuela preparatoria organicé un proyecto con mi compañera Lucía Benítez, que estudiaba química conmigo, para documentar cómo cambia el sabor del mole cuando se usan chiles secos de distintas regiones. Pasamos semanas en la cocina de mi casa, con mi perro Tlaloc sentado junto a la estufa esperando que cayera algún pedazo de pollo, y terminamos presentando nuestros resultados en un congreso estatal el 14 de septiembre de este año.

Quiero entrar a su programa porque busco unir lo que aprendí en la cocina de mi abuela con el rigor de la investigación científica. Sé que la gastronomía mexicana necesita personas que la estudien con método y que la defiendan con datos, y creo que puedo aportar esa mirada desde mi experiencia. Estoy lista para aprender, equivocarme en el laboratorio y volver a intentarlo, como lo hago cada vez que pongo a hervir una olla de mole.

I am writing this notice with a heavy heart to say goodbye to my brother Nigel, who died peacefully on 14 February at the Royal Infirmary in Leeds, surrounded by those who loved him. Nigel was born in 1952 and grew up on Clarendon Road in Headingley, where our mother still talks about the noise of him and his mates kicking a ball against the garden wall until dark. Everyone who knew him called him Nobby, a name he wore with pride from his schooldays at Roundhay Grammar onwards, and I don't think I ever heard him answer to anything else.

From Roundhay he went on to the University of Leeds to study engineering, and he never really stopped being an engineer. He could fix a boiler, a bicycle or a broken heart, usually without being asked and almost always with a cup of tea in his hand. For thirty-one years he worked for a small firm in Wakefield that built bridges and then, in his retirement, he kept building things for the rest of us: a greenhouse for Mum, a bird table for the neighbours and a rather crooked shed that is still standing at the bottom of my garden.

Nigel was the sort of man who remembered birthdays, anniversaries and the names of your dogs. He sang loudly and badly in the Headingley Male Voice Choir for nearly twenty years, and he never once let the lack of talent stop him from enjoying every rehearsal. He was patient with his grandchildren, forgiving with his friends and fiercely loyal to Leeds United, even through the lean seasons when the rest of us would have given up.

In his final weeks he was cared for with great kindness by the nurses on Ward 27, who grew very fond of his sense of humour and his endless questions about their shifts. He spoke often of the house on Clarendon Road and of the Sunday walks along the Meanwood Valley, and I hope he knew how much he was loved there too.

Nigel leaves his wife Margaret, his children Sarah and Tom, five grandchildren, and me, his little sister, who will miss him every single day. The funeral will take place at St Chad's Church on 24 February, and friends are warmly invited to join us afterwards for tea and far too many biscuits. Nobby, you were the best of us, and we will keep building in your honour.

He was 74. Many of you knew him as Aki-san, a name he carried proudly through the bakery he ran for thirty-one years on the corner of Motomachi Street, and it is the name I will always hear when I think of him.

Dad grew up in Shizuoka and studied agriculture at Shizuoka University, where he met my mother, Yoko, at a student dance in 1971. He often told us that he had only gone because a friend owed him a favour, and he would laugh every time, because that favour turned into fifty-three years of marriage. He believed in hard work, early mornings and telling the truth even when it was inconvenient. He taught me to knead dough by feel rather than by the clock, a lesson I still try to follow.

For the last decade Dad was a regular at Kissa Maruyama, the small coffee house near the station, where he read the newspaper aloud to anyone who would listen. He also attended the morning sessions at Fitness Kamo three days a week, insisting that a man in his seventies needed to keep his legs strong for the hills of his beloved Enshu region. The staff at both places have asked us to say how much they will miss his stories and his terrible puns.

Our family dog, Kuma, a patient old shiba mix, will be lost without his evening walks, and I know Dad would want me to mention him. Dad's last errand before he fell ill was to drive his silver Toyota Corolla, registration 33-41 Shi 8216, to the vet for Kuma's checkup. He cared for every living thing around him with the same quiet devotion.

A private family ceremony will be held on November 14th at Hamamatsu Shinto Shrine. In lieu of flowers, we kindly ask that donations be made to the Shizuoka Prefectural Cancer Research Fund, a cause Dad supported quietly for many years. Thank you to everyone who visited him in hospital and sent messages of comfort.

Dad, you will be missed every single day. Rest well, Aki-san.

My interest in engineering began not in a classroom but on a crowded bus. The vehicle stalled at the same intersection almost every day, and I started timing the lights, counting the passengers, and sketching how the traffic flow could be improved. What began as idle curiosity turned into a sustained habit of asking why systems fail and how they might be redesigned. I eventually wrote a short proposal to the local transit office, which was politely acknowledged but never implemented. The disappointment taught me that good ideas need persistence, clear communication, and people willing to listen.

That lesson shaped my work in the robotics club at school. Our team struggled for months with a sensor that gave inconsistent readings whenever the room got warm. Rather than simply replacing the part, I proposed calibrating the system against temperature changes and documenting every trial. The process was tedious, and several teammates doubted it would work. When the robot finally navigated the course without error, I felt a satisfaction that no grade had ever given me. It also reinforced my belief that careful measurement matters as much as inspiration.

Beyond engineering, I have found meaning in tutoring younger students who feel discouraged by mathematics. Many of them arrive convinced they are simply bad at numbers. I try to show them that confusion is a normal step toward understanding, and that a problem can be broken into smaller pieces. On Tuesday 12 March my car was struck while parked outside our flat on Harrowgate Road, Leeds, and I'm attaching the photos I posted on my Twitter account @freddie_drives88 along with my sister Fiona's written statement as a witness.

I'll admit I almost skipped Byron Bay altogether, but my friend Vivienne insisted we stop for a week on our way up the coast, and I'm so glad she did. We rented a little weatherboard place at 14 Marlin Court, just a short walk from the beach, and the first thing I did was wander into Salty Fig Cafe on Jonson Street for a flat white and the best smashed avocado I've had in years. The owner, a cheerful woman named Renata Holm, told me the morning crowd thins out after nine, which turned out to be perfect for reading on the verandah.

We spent the next few days doing the usual things: sunrise walks along the headland, a swim at the Wategos end of the beach where the water was clear enough to see fish, and an afternoon at the lighthouse watching for whales. On the third morning Vivienne dragged me to Ridge Strength Gym for a class she'd found online, and I'll confess I was sore for two days afterwards. Still, the instructors were friendly and the views from the outdoor deck were worth every groan.

If you're planning your own trip, I'd recommend booking anything popular ahead of time, especially around the Easter long weekend, which we unluckily hit on April 18th. The town was packed, parking was a nightmare, and we queued forty minutes for pancakes. Next time I'd come mid-week in late April, when the weather is still warm and the crowds have moved on.

Before we left, Vivienne and I got a little sentimental and made a list of all the places we wanted to revisit. I've been posting photos from the trip under the handle @wanderwithjo_travels, so if you want more tips or pictures, feel free to follow along there. You can also reach me directly at jo.hartley.travels@gmail.com, and I answer every message I get.

All in all, Byron Bay surprised me. It's busy and a little pricey, but there's a warmth to the place that's hard to describe. I left with sand in my shoes, a sunburnt nose, and a plan to come back before the year is out. Vivienne has already started looking at flights.

I am thrilled to share that I have started a new role as Senior Product Analyst at Vértice Logística in São Paulo, and I wanted to take a moment to reflect on the journey that got me here.

Paulo, my first manager there, taught me that good data means nothing unless it helps someone make a decision on a Tuesday morning. That lesson stuck with me. Over the last few years I built dashboards for the operations team in Belo Horizonte, rebuilt our churn model, and eventually led a small group of analysts through a difficult migration to a new warehouse.

Leaving a team you care about is never easy. Paulo and I still talk every few weeks, and he is the first person I call when I need an honest opinion. Even so, the opportunity at Vértice felt like the right next step. They are building a logistics platform that touches thousands of small merchants across the Southeast, and the problems they are trying to solve are the kind I find genuinely exciting.

My first day is set for July 14th, and I am already looking forward to meeting the team in person. If you are in the São Paulo area that week and want to grab a coffee in Vila Madalena, send me a message. I would love to hear what you are working on.

Thank you to everyone who supported me over the past years. Here is to what comes next.

Je tiens à laisser cet avis pour la Boulangerie Lenoir, rue des Tanneurs, à Dijon. Je m'appelle Théophile Marchetti et je suis un habitué du quartier depuis presque six ans. Ce n'est pas la première fois que je viens ici, mais c'est la première fois que j'éprouve le besoin d'écrire quelque chose, parce que la qualité du pain a vraiment changé ces derniers mois, et dans le bon sens.

La baguette tradition est croustillante à la sortie du four, avec une mie alvéolée qui tient bien le beurre sans s'effondrer. Le pain de campagne au levain est, selon moi, le meilleur de la ville. Je l'achète chaque samedi depuis le mois de juin dernier, et je n'ai jamais été déçu. La boulangère, Marguerite, m'a même conseillé une variante aux noix quand je lui ai dit que je cherchais quelque chose pour accompagner le fromage de mes beaux-parents.

L'accueil mérite aussi une mention. Théo, le jeune qui tient la caisse le matin, est toujours souriant, même quand la file atteint la porte. Il se souvient des prénoms, ce qui n'est pas si courant aujourd'hui. Un matin de juin, alors que je pressais le pas pour attraper le train, il m'a glissé un croissant « pour la route » sans que je demande rien. Ce genre de geste fait toute la différence.

Je dois reconnaître deux petits points négatifs. Les viennoiseries du dimanche partent très vite, et il vaut mieux arriver avant dix heures si on veut un pain au chocolat. Par ailleurs, le parking est quasi inexistant, ce qui oblige souvent à se garer dans la rue voisine. Ce ne sont que des inconvénients mineurs au regard de la qualité générale.

En résumé, je recommande vivement la Boulangerie Lenoir à tous ceux qui apprécient un pain travaillé avec soin. Pour toute question ou réservation de gâteau pour un événement, vous pouvez écrire à theophile.marchetti@lamail.fr, je serai ravi de partager mes adresses préférées du quartier. Mon chien Bastien, qui m'accompagne presque chaque samedi, a aussi approuvé en recevant un petit biscuit du comptoir.

My insurance company, Migdal, has been notified separately under policy number 778-40251.

I would ask that you check whether any camera footage from the Herzl Street entrance or from the neighbouring shop exists, and that you contact my brother Gadi if you need a statement about the van he saw. text:
Today is my first day as Senior Product Manager at Fennel & Hart in Limerick, and I wanted to share a bit about the journey that got me here. I'm 41 now, and for most of my twenties I told myself I'd switch careers "once things settled down." Things never settled. What finally pushed me was a quiet January evening, sitting at the kitchen table in Kilkenny, when I realised I'd spent eight years building products I didn't believe in.

The last few months were a scramble. I rewrote my CV three times, took a pay cut I'd been dreading, and spent more evenings than I'd like to admit on video calls with recruiters. My partner Ciarán was patient through all of it, and my rescue greyhound Biscuit gave me a reason to get out for a walk whenever my head was spinning. Biscuit has no interest in career advice, but she is an excellent listener.

To anyone sitting on the fence right now: the leap feels enormous from the inside, but it usually looks smaller once you're standing on the other side. If you're thinking about it, reach out. I'm happy to share what I learned about interviews, negotiating and making the case for yourself. Thank you to everyone who cheered me on, and especially to the friends who told me to stop talking about it and just apply.

El teléfono de la clínica es el 983 214 567, por si alguna vez tengo que cambiar la cita.

Después de la clínica me encontré con Lucía en la plaza Mayor. Hacía años que no la veía. Me dijo que todos la llaman Lucy en su trabajo nuevo, y que a ella no le importa, pero que prefiere que yo la siga llamando Luci, como cuando éramos niñas. Nos tomamos un café y se rió mucho cuando le conté lo del curso de cerámica que hice el año pasado y que dejé a medias. Quedamos en que me mandaría su correo, lucia.navarro.8@gmail.com, para organizar una excursión a la sierra la próxima primavera.

Por la tarde me puse a ordenar los papeles del salón. Encontré una carta de mi tío Ernesto fechada en 2009, en la que me contaba cómo era la vida en el pueblo cuando él era joven. Guardé la carta en la caja de madera donde guardo las fotos.

Antes de dormir he repasado la lista de cosas pendientes para la semana. Buenas noches, diario.

I am writing to formally complain about the service I received from your Lekki branch on Saturday, 14 December, and to request a full review of how my account was handled. The teller told me that my account had been flagged for review and that I would need to return on Monday. No reason was given, and no one from the branch called me afterwards to explain. My mother had to borrow money from a neighbour to settle the clinic bill that same day.

I tried the customer line three times over the weekend. On the first call, the agent asked for my account number, which I gave as 2034871156, and then said she could not see any flag. On the second call, I was told the flag had been placed by the fraud desk. On the third call, the line went dead after I had waited forty minutes. I was never offered a reference number for any of these calls, which makes it impossible for me to follow up properly.

I have also been to Vibe Corner Cafe on Ajah Road, where I usually meet clients, and I paid for coffee there that afternoon using your debit card without any problem. This makes the restriction on my account even harder to understand, since your own system evidently accepted my card the same day. I am attaching copies of my transaction history and the receipt from the cafe.

I am asking for three things: the reason for the restriction in writing, the removal of the flag from my account if it was placed in error, and a written apology along with a waiver of the charges I incurred. I also ask that my vehicle, registered under the plate LSD 482 KL, not be mentioned in any future correspondence unless it is strictly necessary, as it was included in the documents submitted at the branch without my consent.

Growing up in Ōtāhuhu, I learned early that a community is built out of small, repeated acts. Every Saturday my grandmother and I walked down to Hillcrest Road to pick up bread from Mana Bakehouse, and the owner, Tane, always asked me how school was going before he handed over the change. That habit of being seen by people who know your name shaped how I think about belonging. When I started volunteering at the Mangere Community Clinic at sixteen, I found myself doing the same thing: greeting families in Samoan and Tongan, remembering their children's names, and helping them fill out forms in English without making them feel rushed.

The clinic is where I first understood that health is not only about medicine. On 14 January last year, a woman named Losana came in with a toddler who had a fever and no way to get to her appointment the next day. Our coordinator, Mere, and I spent the afternoon arranging transport and writing a reminder card. Losana later posted a thank-you on the clinic's page, tagged as @oliviamakes_nz, and it was the first time I saw how a single afternoon could ripple outward. I want to study public health so that I can make those afternoons routine rather than exceptional.

Beyond the clinic, I have spent three summers working at a cafe on Great South Road, where I have learned how much logistics and empathy overlap. Running a busy counter taught me to anticipate needs before people voice them, a skill I will carry into any role where I work with patients, communities and colleagues. I am ready to bring that same attentiveness to the university's programme, and I hope to contribute to a community of students who believe that caring for others is the most practical thing we can do.

C'est avec une immense tristesse que je vous annonce le décès de notre père, Jean-Baptiste Lefèvre, survenu le 14 novembre à l'âge de 78 ans, entouré des siens à son domicile de Quimper. Il laisse dans le deuil son épouse, Marie-Claire, ses enfants Julien et Anne-Sophie, ainsi que ses petits-enfants qui n'ont jamais cessé de le faire sourire.

Jean-Baptiste est né à Brest en 1946, dans une famille de pêcheurs. Très jeune, il apprit à lire la mer comme d'autres lisent un livre. Après des années passées sur les chalutiers de la baie d'Audierne, il reprit en 1978 le petit atelier de réparation de filets de son oncle Yves, qu'il transforma en une entreprise respectée de toute la région. Jean, comme nous l'appelions tous, aimait répéter que la patience était le premier outil d'un bon artisan.

Il était aussi un homme de famille, profondément attaché à ses racines. Chaque dimanche, il recevait ses proches autour d'une grande table et racontait, avec sa voix grave et ses mains toujours tachées de goudron, les tempêtes qu'il avait affrontées. Il savait aussi écouter, et beaucoup d'entre vous se souviendront de ses conseils donnés sans jamais rien imposer.

Ses derniers mois furent difficiles, mais il les traversa avec une dignité qui nous a tous bouleversés. Il tenait à remercier l'équipe de soins de l'hôpital de Quimper pour leur présence et leur douceur. Ceux qui souhaitent lui rendre hommage peuvent prendre contact avec la famille au 06 48 27 19 53 ou par courriel à jean.lefevre.famille@mailbox.fr.

La cérémonie d'adieu aura lieu le mardi 19 novembre à 14 heures en l'église Saint-Corentin de Quimper. Pour les personnes qui le désirent, des dons peuvent être adressés à la Société nationale de sauvetage en mer. Pour l'administration du dossier, nous rappelons le numéro de pièce d'identité du défunt, 09AB27561, afin de faciliter les démarches auprès des services compétents.

Je vous remercie, au nom de toute la famille, pour votre présence, vos messages et votre affection. Jean-Baptiste repose désormais en paix, face à la mer qu'il a tant aimée.

Growing up in Haifa, I used to watch the ships slide into the port from my grandmother's balcony, and I believed that everything worth understanding could be seen from up high. That belief changed the summer I spent volunteering at Rambam Health Care Campus. I was assigned to the paediatric wing, where I learned to fold blankets, carry charts, and listen. Mira, a nine-year-old with a stubborn grin, taught me more about patience than any textbook. On May 14th, she asked me to read her the same chapter of a science book three times, and I did, because I finally understood that attention is itself a form of care.

Since then I have tried to bring that same attention to my studies. At the Technion, where I completed my first year of engineering, I found myself drawn to biomedical design, particularly to devices that help children recover mobility after surgery. My lab partner, Omer, and I spent long evenings sketching a lightweight brace prototype, and when it failed our first test, we treated the failure as data rather than defeat. Our professor later said that the difference between a good engineer and a great one is how quickly they can turn a mistake into a question.

I want to continue asking those questions at a university that values collaboration between clinicians and engineers. I believe my experience in Haifa, from the quiet hospital corridors to the crowded lab benches, has prepared me to contribute as both a thinker and a listener. I hope to be part of a community where curiosity is rewarded and where every problem begins with the people it affects.

Hi all, I've finally started sketching out our trip for next summer, and I wanted to get everyone's thoughts before I book anything. Mum's turning sixty-two in late September, so my plan is to make the whole thing about her. My sister Sabine has already said she can take two weeks off, which is a miracle, so I'm building the itinerary around her availability. Brother Tomas, you're in charge of the car rental, since you're the only one who actually enjoys driving on the wrong side of the road.

Here's what I'm thinking so far. We start in Florence for four nights, mostly because Mum has been talking about the Uffizi since she was a teenager and I'd like to let her finally see it without us rushing her through in a single morning. From there we drive south to a farmhouse outside Montepulciano that I found through a friend of Sabine's husband. It has a pool, a big kitchen and a terrace that looks over the vineyards, which is exactly what we need after a city stretch. I've pencilled in six nights there, but I'll confirm once the owner gets back to me on the exact dates.

The last leg is the coast. I know some of you want Amalfi, but honestly the traffic on that road is brutal in the afternoons, so I'm leaning towards Sorrento instead, with a couple of day trips by ferry. Everyone's dietary stuff is noted, so I'll make sure the restaurants I shortlist can handle the gluten-free and nut allergy requests. Tomas, I know you'll want to nap in the shade after lunch, so I've picked a place with a proper garden.

Budget is the thing I'm least sure about. My rough estimate is around four thousand euros for the whole group, excluding flights, but that number moves a lot depending on whether we go for the farmhouse or split into two hotels. I'd rather we decide this together, so if you can reply by the end of the month with a yes or no on the overall plan, I'll start putting down deposits. Let me know if anything is a hard no for you, and I'll see what can be worked around.

Love you all, and I'm genuinely excited about this. Mum still has no idea, so please keep the group chat quiet around her. I'll send a proper calendar invite once we've locked in the final dates.

Sophie

The first real test was registering at the clinic on Herzl Street, the one run by Dr. Shapiro's team. I was so nervous I forgot half my documents, but the receptionist, a woman named Ruthie, was so patient that I almost cried. She even printed out my appointment card and wrote Tamar's number on the back in case I got lost again. Honestly, Vered, that small kindness made the whole week feel survivable.

Then there's Café Lilach, which has basically become my office. The owner, Nadav, remembers that I take my coffee with oat milk and no sugar, and on Tuesday he slipped me a free slice of lemon cake because I looked exhausted. I've been working on my translation project there every morning, and the Wi-Fi is fast enough that I can finally send files without the usual panic. If you ever visit, you have to go.

I've also started going to a small gym called Iron Olive near the port, mostly because the trainer is strict and I need someone to shout at me about my form. It's been good for my head, even if my legs hate me. I joined on June 4th, which feels like a lifetime ago now, and I'm already noticing the difference.

If you need anything from me, the best way to reach me is still vmarkovitz@gmail.com, though I'm checking my phone less these days. I miss you and your terrible jokes. Tell Yoni I said hi, and that he owes me a rematch at backgammon. Write back soon, okay? I want to hear everything about your new job.

Love,
Vivi

If you're planning a trip in May, I'd recommend building in time for both cities. Bring comfortable shoes, carry some water, and don't be shy about asking locals for their favourite spots, because they will always have an opinion. Clara has already started a list of places we need to revisit, and I suspect the bakery will be at the top of it. Hi, I'm not really sure how to start this, so I'll just write it out. My name is Noa Ben-David and I'm 34 years old. I work as a night nurse at Hadassah Ein Kerem in Jerusalem, which I've loved for almost nine years, but lately I feel like I'm running on empty and I can't figure out why.

The shifts themselves aren't the problem, or at least I don't think they are. I've always been able to handle a double and bounce back. What's different is that I wake up on my days off already tired, and I catch myself dreading the drive in on Sunday night even when the schedule is fine. My supervisor, Yael, has been kind about it, but I can tell she's noticed I've gone quiet in the break room. Ben, my partner, keeps asking if something happened at work. Nothing specific did. That's what worries me.

I've tried the obvious things. I cut back on coffee, I started walking after dinner, and I even downloaded one of those sleep apps, which mostly just tells me I'm restless. I also tried talking to my mother on the phone every evening, thinking it would help, but she mostly wants to know when I'm going to settle down and have kids, and I come off the call feeling worse. My closest friend from nursing school, Maya, moved to Haifa last year and we only text now.

I guess what I'm really asking is whether this sounds like burnout, or like something I should see a doctor about, or maybe both. I don't want to overreact, but I also don't want to wait until I snap at a patient or make a mistake that matters. Can you help me sort out what questions I should be asking myself, and how I might bring this up with Yael without it sounding like I'm quitting? Thank you for reading all of this.

I'm a data engineer based in Portland, Oregon, where I have spent the last eleven years building pipelines for logistics companies and, more recently, a small healthcare analytics startup. My path into the field was not a straight line. I started out studying marine biology, spent two summers counting seabirds on the Oregon coast, and eventually realised that the most interesting part of my work was never the fieldwork itself but the spreadsheets afterward. That curiosity pulled me toward software, and I have never looked back.

At conferences I tend to talk about one lesson above all others: most data problems are really communication problems. The schema is rarely the hard part. The hard part is getting the people who collect the data and the people who use it to agree on what a single record means. Over the years I have developed a habit of writing short glossaries before writing a line of code, and it has saved my teams more time than any clever algorithm.

Outside work I am an amateur baker and a slow but persistent hiker. Eitan Shalom passed away peacefully on March 9 at the age of 71, surrounded by his children in Rehavia, Jerusalem, the neighbourhood where he had lived for nearly forty years. He was a man who measured a day by its small pleasures: a strong coffee at Café Hillel on Emek Refaim, a long walk along the Valley of the Cross, and the newspaper read cover to cover before noon.

Eitan was born in Haifa in 1953 and spent most of his working life as a structural engineer at Mekorot Ashdod Engineering Ltd., where colleagues remember him as patient, exacting and quietly generous with his time. He could explain a load-bearing wall to a twelve-year-old and make it sound like a bedtime story. Those who worked beside him say he never raised his voice, only his eyebrows.

To his family he was simply Abba, Saba and Eitan, and each name carried its own weight. He taught his daughter to ride a bicycle on the quiet paths of Gan Sacher, sang off-key at every Shabbat table, and never once missed a grandchild's recital. Every Thursday he went to the Maccabi clinic on Ben Yehuda for his blood pressure check, and he always brought the nurse a box of sweets from the Mahane Yehuda market.

Eitan's family asks that, in lieu of flowers, donations be made to the Hadassah children's ward in his memory. Friends are welcome to share their own memories of him online; his grandson has created the page @eitan.remembers, where stories and photographs are being gathered.

The shiva will be held at the family home on Rabbi Akiva Street from March 10 to March 16, and visitors are welcome at any hour. Eitan leaves behind his wife of forty-six years, Miriam, two children, and five grandchildren, who will carry his stubborn kindness forward in all that they do.

May his memory be a blessing.

Ellery works as a senior analyst at Northwind Logistics in Calgary, and she has been planning this trip since we first met at the office holiday party. Ellery just laughed, handed me a pair of mitts, and said I'd get used to it by lunch. She was right, mostly.

Our guide, a quiet man named Gordon Ashby who has run tours out of town for nearly two decades, drove us in a heated tundra buggy along the frozen shoreline. We spotted a mother bear and her two cubs resting near the old fort ruins, and Ellery kept whispering that she could hardly believe we were so close. Between sightings we warmed up in a little café on Kelsey Boulevard, where the cinnamon buns were the best I've had anywhere in the country. Ellery swears the baker makes them fresh before dawn every morning, and I believe her.

If you go, pack more layers than you think you need and book early, because the tours fill up fast in January. I'm already texting Ellery about returning next winter, this time for the northern lights. Let me know in the comments if you have a favourite cold-weather destination in Canada, because I'm hungry for new ideas.

Friends, family, thank you for being here today. I stand before you with a heavy heart and a full memory of the person we are gathered to honour. He was a man who believed in showing up. When the rains came and the roof leaked, he was the first to climb the ladder. He never kept a tally of the favours he did, and I suspect he would be embarrassed to hear me list them now. He had a laugh that could fill a room, usually at his own expense. He loved telling the same stories over and over, and somehow they never got old, because he told them with such delight. Some of you have heard about the fishing trip that went badly wrong, and the dog that refused to leave the boat. He would have wanted me to tell it again today, so consider yourselves warned.

He was also stubborn, and I will say that with love. Once he had made up his mind, arguing with him was like trying to turn a braai fire with your hands. He could be wrong, and he would admit it eventually, usually grudgingly and with a grin. That combination of conviction and humility is rarer than it should be, and I have tried, not always successfully, to learn it from him.

As we say goodbye, I hope we can remember him not only in our grief but in the small everyday acts he taught us. Pour the tea for someone who is tired. Stop on the side of the road. text:
My grandmother always said that Hadar was born in the wrong city, and I used to think she meant it as a joke. I was born in Safed in the winter of 2006, in a hospital where the windows looked out over the hills toward the Sea of Galilee. My parents had moved there from Haifa only a year before, chasing a job at a small print shop that eventually closed. Growing up, I learned to measure distance in bus rides: forty minutes to my cousins in Tiberias, two hours to the coast, and a single number I still know by heart, 04-6990213, the landline my father kept for the shop long after everyone else switched to mobiles.

My first real lesson in leadership came at fourteen, when our youth movement was asked to organize the winter food drive. The old community center on Herzl Street had a leaking roof and no heating, and the volunteers were mostly bored teenagers like me. I wrote the schedule on the back of a receipt, called every family on the list myself, and discovered that people will give time if you ask them directly and explain why it matters. By the second week of December we had collected more than three hundred boxes.

I have also learned that leadership sometimes means stepping back. In my tenth grade debate team, I was so eager to be the one who spoke that I cut off a quieter classmate, Noam Levi, during a practice round. He never said anything, but his notes showed me what I had missed. Since then I have tried to listen first and speak second, a habit that has made me a better partner in lab groups and, I think, a better friend.

When I think about what I want to study, I return to that community center and the boxes stacked to the ceiling. I want to understand how cities like Safed balance tourism, old traditions and new families, and how public policy can support small communities without erasing them. Economics and urban planning seem like the right tools for that work, and I hope to bring the same direct, personal approach I learned as a teenager to larger questions.

My grandmother, I suspect, would still say I was born in the wrong place. Perhaps. But I have come to see Safed as the place that taught me how to care for a community, and I would like the chance to take that lesson further.

She was the one who taught me to ride a bicycle on that narrow road, always shouting encouragement from her doorway whenever I wobbled too close to the gutter. Vicky, as the whole street called her, never met a stranger. If you walked past her gate, you were getting a plate of pancit or at least a long conversation about the weather.

Victoria passed away peacefully on the 14th of March, surrounded by the family she loved more than anything. Many of you know how fiercely she guarded her Sunday mornings at the parish of San Roque, where she sang in the choir for over forty years. She never once missed a fiesta, and she never let anyone leave her house hungry. Even in her last weeks, she asked whether the neighbours had eaten, and whether the kids on Mabini had finished their homework.

So today, let us remember her the way she would have wanted: loudly, generously, and with a little too much food on the table. Vicky, thank you for every lesson, every meal, and every time you waved me back from the edge of that road. Rest now. We will keep the gate open for you.

When I was nine, my grandmother Galit taught me to bake challah in her small kitchen in Haifa, and I have been trying to get it right ever since. She never measured anything. She would press the dough with the heel of her hand, close her eyes, and tell me when it was ready. Those Sunday mornings taught me that patience is a kind of attention, and that the things worth doing rarely follow a recipe.

That lesson followed me into my work at the community food bank in Haifa, where I volunteered every Thursday during my last two years of high school. I started by sorting donated tins, but soon I was helping coordinate deliveries to families in the Hadar neighbourhood. I learned to keep a ledger, to call suppliers when a truck was late, and to listen when someone told me what they actually needed rather than what the form asked for. On March 14 last year, we served a record two hundred and twelve households in a single afternoon, and I remember how quiet the volunteers became when the last box was handed over.

I want to study public policy because I have seen how small logistical failures become hunger, and how careful planning can prevent it. If admitted, I hope to continue this work. You can follow our food bank's updates through my account, @galit_bakes_hope, and I have included my passport number, 2847 6193, on the enrolment form so the office can verify my records.

I've been putting off writing this for weeks, mostly because Dr Byrne said I should try to get things down on paper when they feel too heavy to say out loud. So here goes. Sinéad is the name I answer to, though my sister still calls me Neasa when she's annoyed with me, which is most of the time these days. I work as a senior analyst at Lakeshore Data Solutions in Athlone, and since the restructuring in early November I have been sitting in meetings where nobody quite meets my eye.

The mornings are the worst. I've started going to Brew & Bloom on Church Street before work, mainly because the barista, a young lad called Ciarán, remembers my order and doesn't ask how I am. That small kindness has become the best part of my day, which tells me something about where I've ended up. Afterwards I walk along the canal with our old spaniel, Biscuit, who is fourteen and moves like she's apologising for every step. She doesn't need me to be anything other than present, and I find that very restful.

My mam rang on Sunday, as she does, and wanted to know whether I'd be coming home for her birthday on the 22nd. I said I would, which was a lie I told out of habit. I haven't told her about the job, or about the nights I lie awake running through spreadsheets in my head. My brother Eoin thinks I should just be more positive, which is easy for him to say from his desk in Galway.

I posted something on Instagram last week, a photo of the canal at dusk with a line about starting again, and tagged it @sinead.walks. A few people I hadn't spoken to in years commented with hearts and encouragement. It was nice, but it also made me feel like a fraud, performing a recovery I haven't actually got.

Dr Byrne asked me on Tuesday what I need right now, and I didn't have an answer. I think I need permission to not be fine. I need to stop measuring each day against some version of myself from last spring. I'm going to try to book the next session for the 14th, if the clinic has a slot, and bring the list I've started writing in my phone under the heading "things I'm allowed to feel."

After almost six years at Lumière Analytics, I am excited to share that I have joined Vectra Logistics as Senior Data Lead, starting this May in Lyon.

When I joined Lumière in 2019, I was a junior analyst who mostly cleaned spreadsheets and hoped someone would let me build a dashboard. Looking back, the most important thing I learned there was how to explain numbers to people who don't live in them every day. Those lessons came from long Thursday lunches at the little bistro on Rue Saint-Dominique, where my colleague Mathilde Durand would sketch charts on napkins while we argued about whether our churn model deserved to be trusted.

Mathilde taught me that a good analysis is only as good as the question behind it. She also taught me to stop apologising for asking "dumb" questions in meetings, which may be the most useful career advice I have ever received. When I mentioned I was thinking about moving on, she was the first person to tell me to go for it, and the first to remind me to keep in touch.

The new role gives me the chance to lead a team of six and to build the data infrastructure for a company that moves goods across three countries every day. I am particularly looking forward to working on forecasting problems that affect real people: drivers, warehouse staff and customers who just want their parcels on time.

If you are in the Lyon area, or if you have experience in logistics analytics and would like to talk, my inbox is open at rmoreau.data@gmail.com. I am always happy to swap notes with people who are thinking about their own next step.

Thank you to everyone at Lumière for six good years. I will carry what I learned with me, along with a few napkin sketches I may or may not have kept.

I have been asked to write something for the Hartley family's notice in the Yorkshire Post, and I find I cannot do it in the usual way. My name is Ian Crowther, and I was Iris Mallory's neighbour for almost thirty-one years, first on Brackenfield Road in Harrogate and then, after the move, in the cottage at the end of Cold Harbour Lane. Iris died on 14 July at the Harrogate District Hospital, with her daughter Joanne holding one hand and the crossword folded under the other. She was eighty-three.

Iris taught Latin and history at the girls' grammar school for nearly four decades, and I am told she once made a Year Nine boy cry over a misplaced ablative and then spent the rest of the lesson helping him fix it. She did not suffer fools, but she never once refused a favour. When my wife Margaret was ill in 2009, Iris arrived each Tuesday with a casserole, a library book and an opinion about whatever I had been reading. She was right more often than I liked.

Her rules were simple. Post the letters before noon. Never buy a car you have not driven in the rain. Her Vauxhall, registration K 214 HWR, was the most reliable thing she owned and she drove it until the week before she went into hospital, usually to the Saturday market for lemons and gossip. Joanne has asked me to say that the account for the church flowers is still in her name and she would like someone else to take it over. Those with a question about that, or about the memorial bench, can write to joanne.mallory@harrogatemail.co.uk.

Roughly a hundred people came to the crematorium on 19 July, and Jenny Ashworth from the crossword circle read a poem Iris had copied out by hand years ago and kept in her handbag. Several of us stayed on afterwards and told stories until the staff politely began stacking the chairs. I was asked to speak at the funeral and could not get through the first line without stopping, so I am grateful to have a page on which to say it properly.

Iris, you were a terrible driver in the wet and an excellent friend in every other weather. I will miss the lemons, the arguments and the crossword clues you were certain I could not solve. Rest well.

I write this with a heavy heart, as my wife Sheila passed away peacefully at home on 14 August, surrounded by those who loved her. She was born in Kendal in 1947, the eldest of four children, and she never quite lost the Westmorland vowels that made everyone in our kitchen smile. Sheila spent thirty-one years as a district nurse in Lancaster, and I don't think a single patient on her round ever forgot her steady hands or her habit of bringing a flask of tea on the cold winter visits.

She was a keen gardener, a terrible card player and the most generous host you could imagine. Her Sunday lunches were legendary, and the rhubarb crumble she made every summer will be missed by everyone who ever sat at our table. Sheila loved the fells above Kendal, and in her last months she would ask me to drive her up the valley just to look at the hills one more time.

She leaves me, our daughters Sarah and Helen, and six grandchildren who adored her. Those who wish to pay their respects are welcome at the service at St Thomas's Church on Thursday 21 August at 11am, followed by refreshments at the Golden Lion. Donations in Sheila's memory may be made to Marie Curie. Sheila, you were loved more than you knew, and you will be missed every single day.

I finally made it to Kyoto this September, and I want to share a few notes before the details fade. I stayed in a small guesthouse in Gion, on a narrow lane off Hanamikoji Street, run by a woman named Keiko who insisted on serving miso soup at 7 a.m. no matter how many times I said I could grab a convenience store breakfast. She also reminded me, very kindly, to keep my passport number handy for the hotel registry, which is apparently still a paper-and-pen affair in many places. My passport number is ending in 4471, if you're wondering how paranoid I got about carrying it.

The real highlight was a day trip to Nara, where the deer are far more aggressive than any guidebook warned. I'd been told by a colleague at Hartwell Logistics, the freight company I work for back in Chicago, that the deer bow for crackers. That is technically true, but only if you have a cracker in hand and are prepared to be mobbed. Dan, my travel partner, learned this the hard way when a young buck nudged his camera bag right off his shoulder. We laughed about it for the rest of the afternoon over matcha and mochi near Todai-ji.

If you go, book your ryokan early, especially on weekends, and don't underestimate how much walking the temples require. Ten kilometres a day is normal here, and your feet will tell you so by evening. Dan and I both agreed the trip was worth every yen, even the moment I realised I'd left my phone charger at the guesthouse and had to ask Keiko to ship it to me in Osaka.

Yolanda had planned the whole trip on a spreadsheet, colour-coded by day, but the spreadsheet fell apart the moment we reached the promenade and saw the penguins at Boulders Beach waddling across the path as if they owned it.

My cousin Thandeka met us on the second morning. She is a senior programme coordinator at the Bokamoso Youth Trust in Woodstock, and she insisted on driving us through Bo-Kaap before the tour buses arrived. The pastel houses were freshly painted for the season, and an elderly man sat on his step selling koeksisters from a steel tin. Thandeka grew up two streets over from there, and she pointed out the school she attended with the kind of fondness reserved for places that taught you something hard.

For the Winelands day, Yolanda insisted we book with a small operator run by a couple near Stellenbosch. The owner, Pieter van Wyk, walked us through the cellar with a glass of chenin blanc in each hand and talked about the drought years with real emotion. We lunched on a veranda overlooking vines just beginning to bud, the mountains purple in the distance.

On our last evening we walked down to the harbour at V&A Waterfront, where the sea was rough and the sunset turned the water copper. Yolanda kept her phone out, sending photos to her sister and typing little notes. If you ever plan this trip, message her at yolanda.m@capemail.co.za or call +27 21 555 0148 and she will happily send you the spreadsheet. Go in May, bring a warm jacket, and do not skip the koeksisters.

She ordered a full blood panel and an ECG, which I had done the same morning in a small room that smelled of antiseptic. The nurse, Marisol, was kind and explained each step before doing it. Dr. Ortega said the ECG looked normal, which was a relief, and that the bloods would take about five working days to come back.

text:
When the admissions committee asks what has shaped me, I could point to any number of achievements, but the one that matters most happened in a hospital corridor in Heidelberg. Oskar Lindemann was my grandmother's name for me when I was small, and it is still the name my family uses, so I have grown used to hearing it in the mouths of nurses who were trying to find me in the waiting room at Universitätsklinikum Heidelberg. I was there for my grandfather's surgery in the first week of May, sitting with a clipboard and a phone that kept buzzing with messages from home.

What I noticed that week was how much of the work happened in the gaps between official procedures. A ward clerk who knew that Mr. Berger preferred the window seat. A cleaner who explained the rules of the staff football league to a bored teenager. Lindemann, the name on my grandfather's file, was the thread that connected all of it, because every form I signed had to be matched to the correct patient record before anything could move forward.

I came to see that those forms were not bureaucracy for its own sake. The tiny reference codes, including the insurance number ending in 4471 and the account number 2026-7713, were how a hospital of thousands of people kept track of one man's knee. I wanted to understand the systems that make care possible, and that curiosity is why I have applied to study health informatics.

At my school in Mannheim I had already started building small tools for the science club, a timetable app and a spreadsheet that tracked lab supplies. Those projects taught me that the most useful software is often the least glamorous. In the hospital I saw the same lesson at a larger scale, where a slightly confusing screen can cost a nurse several minutes she does not have.

My grandfather is home now, grumbling about the physiotherapy exercises and asking me, in the mock-serious tone he uses for things he loves, whether I have finally decided what to study. I have. I want to work where patients meet the systems behind their care, and to make those systems clearer, faster and kinder. I hope this university will give me the training to do that.

Mate, I still can't believe what happened last Tuesday, so let me tell you properly. I'm writing from my flat in Newtown, Sydney, the one above the bakery on King Street that you always said smelt like a Sunday morning. Anyway, Yasmin rang me around seven in the morning, which is never good news, and said she'd been admitted to St Vincent's Hospital overnight with a really bad asthma flare. I was out the door before I'd even found my keys.

When I got there she was sitting up in bed looking grey and furious at the nurses for making her wear the oxygen mask. Yasmin Hadid is the stubbornest person I know, and I say that with love. She'd tried to ride it out at home for two days because she didn't want to make a fuss, which is classic her. The registrar was lovely, though, a tall guy named Patrick who explained everything without making me feel stupid for asking the same questions twice.

Here's the bit that really got me. While she was being monitored, Yasmin asked me to email her uni supervisor at the University of Sydney, because she had a submission due in May and she was panicking about an extension. I typed it out on my phone in the corridor, sent it from yasmin.hadid@sydneyuni.edu.au, and the supervisor replied within the hour saying no problem at all. Honestly, a small mercy.

She was discharged the next afternoon, and I drove her home to Marrickville, where her mum has been fussing over her ever since. We got pho on the way back, the good place near the station, and she ate two bowls, which the doctors would have approved of. She's sounding much better now, though she's still banned from doing the stairs at her place without someone around.

Anyway, I just wanted to get that off my chest, because I felt pretty helpless sitting in that waiting room. Call me when you're free this weekend and I'll tell you the rest, including the ridiculous thing the orderly said about my hair. Love you, Sarah.

I'm Tane Whakaari, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a civil engineer specialising in stormwater and flood resilience. I grew up in Te Atatū South, Auckland, where my grandfather ran a small hardware store on Te Atatu Road, and I still think of that shop whenever I open a set of drawings. Those early Saturdays taught me to read a problem by walking around it before touching anything, a habit that has shaped every project since.

My first major role was with a regional council team in Hamilton, where I helped redesign culverts along the Waikato River floodplain after a run of heavy rain in December 2013. We had three weeks to model the worst case, and the lesson I took away was that data is only useful if the people living with the outcome understand it. Since then I have made a point of running community sessions before any construction begins, usually in a school hall with bad coffee and a lot of questions.

For the last four years I have been a principal engineer at a Wellington consultancy, Harbourline Infrastructure Ltd, leading a team of nine on coastal defences in the Hutt Valley. Our work now centres on sea-level projections and on designing barriers that can be raised over time rather than replaced. It is slower and less glamorous than building a new bridge, but I find it more honest about what we can and cannot promise.

Outside work I am a keen cyclist and a fairly average runner. I ride most mornings along the Hutt River trail, and in winter I can usually be found at the Petone rowing club, which has taught me more about patience than any textbook. I also write a small blog about infrastructure for non-specialists, and I am most active online as @tane_builds_rivers, where I share photos from site visits and the occasional frustrated rant about drainage codes.

If you are reading this before my session, thank you for coming. I hope to leave you with two things: a clearer sense of how flood risk is actually decided, and an invitation to ask me the questions I should have answered better in my own reports. My office details are in the programme, and I am always glad to hear from you, especially if you think I have got something wrong.

Those evenings taught me to read by candlelight and to notice how much of daily life depends on systems most people never think about. I began asking why the power failed, who decided where the lines ran, and what it would take to change things.

That curiosity led me to volunteer with a community water project, where I helped record which households had access to clean supply and which relied on untreated stream water. The work was tedious. We walked from compound to compound with clipboards, and many people were suspicious of anyone asking questions. Slowly, though, I learned that good data only matters when it reaches the people who can act on it. I started translating our findings into simple charts for community meetings, and I saw residents begin to argue for their own needs with confidence.

I want to study engineering because I believe the problems I have seen up close are solvable with careful design and honest collaboration. I am drawn to programmes that combine technical rigour with fieldwork, because I know that a solar microgrid or a water filtration unit only succeeds when it fits the community that depends on it. So I was driving home from the depot in Utrecht, the usual route along the Amsterdamsestraatweg, and I stopped at the light by the canal near Lombok. My car is a grey Volkswagen Golf, plate XB-471-K, which I know by heart because I've been fighting the parking fines on it for months. Anyway, the light turned green and this cyclist came out of nowhere, no lights, no helmet, just a blur in a dark hoodie. I braked hard and she (it was a she, Marleen, I found out later) went over the handlebars onto the cobbles.

I got out, my heart pounding, and she was sitting there holding her wrist and swearing in Dutch that would make a sailor blush. Turned out she was fine, mostly scraped up. Her name is Marleen Dekker and she works at the same logistics firm as my colleague Joost, which is how the whole thing got sorted out. Joost rang me the next morning, May 14th, to check I was alright, and apparently Marleen had already sent him a message complaining about me. Typical.

What got me is that she didn't press charges, and she even asked if I'd like to grab a coffee to make sure she hadn't cracked anything. I said yes, obviously, because I'm a bit of a fool when it comes to people who've just fallen off their bikes in front of me. We met at a little place on the Oudegracht last Friday and she laughed at me the whole time for worrying.

So that's my week. Tell me I didn't make a complete mess of things, and tell me you're coming to the drinks on the 22nd, because I need someone to witness the awkward way I'm going to explain this to my mother.

I am writing to report that on the evening of a weekday in January, while I was walking home from work, a man approached me on the pavement and demanded my bag. He was of average height, wearing a dark jacket and a grey cap, and spoke German with an accent I could not place. When I refused, he pushed me against a wall and took my handbag before running off in the direction of the station. I was not seriously hurt but I was shaken. I would like to ask that any available camera footage from the area be reviewed, and I am willing to provide further details to the investigating officers.

On the evening in question I had finished work later than usual and was walking home along a narrow street lined with vending machines and small restaurants. The area was quiet but not deserted. Shopkeepers were pulling down their shutters, and a few people were waiting at the bus stop across the road.

As I passed a parked van with its hazard lights blinking, I heard a sharp noise behind me, like a bag being dropped onto concrete. When I turned, I saw a man in a dark jacket moving quickly away from the entrance of a convenience store. He had a cap pulled low and was carrying something under his arm. I did not see his face clearly, and I cannot say whether he was on foot or had come from the direction of the station.

I went into the store myself to ask the cashier whether anything had happened. She seemed shaken and told me that the rear door had been forced open, though nothing appeared to have been taken from the front counter. She had already called for assistance before I arrived, so I did not make a second call. I waited with her until a patrol car came, and I gave my account to the officer on duty there.

I have tried to be careful not to add details that I did not actually observe. I am not certain about the colour of the van, the exact time I left the office, or whether the man spoke at all. Where I was unsure, I have said so, and I would rather the statement reflect honest gaps than guesses presented as facts.

I am willing to attend the station again if further questions arise, and I can provide my contact information to the investigating team. Please let me know if there is anything else I should clarify or any documents you would like me to review.

I am writing this statement in relation to the theft of my bicycle, which I reported at the Hillcrest Road station on the morning of 14 September. My name is Sophie Anderton and I have lived at 27 Carrow Lane, Bristol, BS5 8QT, since I moved back to England from Lyon last spring. I worked for most of the past three years as a translator in France, so this is the first time I have had to give a formal account of anything to the police here, and I apologise if the details below are not in the order you would prefer.

On Friday 11 September I cycled to the offices of Northfield Legal Services on Dock Street, where I met my colleague Marcus Hale to review a set of contracts before a deadline. I locked my bicycle, a dark green Pashley with a black rear rack and a brass bell, to the railings outside the main entrance at about 8.40 in the morning. Marcus was with me and saw me lock it. I was inside until shortly after five in the afternoon, and when I came back down the bicycle was gone. The cable lock had been cut cleanly, and the cut pieces were still attached to the railing.

I have since been asked by a member of the building staff whether I had left anything else in the bicycle basket. I had not. My helmet was hanging from the handlebars, and it was still there when I returned, which I mention only because it seems odd to me that a thief would take the bicycle and leave the helmet. My house keys and phone were in my bag, which I carried inside with me.

I have spoken with Marcus about the afternoon and he has confirmed the timings above. He also remembers a man in a grey hooded top walking slowly along that stretch of pavement twice while we were working, though he did not pay particular attention to him. I have not been able to recall a face. I am happy to provide a copy of the purchase receipt, which I have located in my email, along with the serial number recorded at the time I bought it.

I would like to know whether any cameras cover the entrance to Northfield Legal Services or the adjoining car park, and whether footage can be requested before it is overwritten. My contact number is 07700 900412 and my email address is sophie.anderton@mailbox.co.uk. Please do let me know if you need anything further from me.

Sophie Anderton

I am writing to apply for the Junior Data Analyst position at Northwind Analytics, which I found through your careers page. My name is Lucia Ferreira, and over the past six years I have built a career in operations reporting, first in Lisbon and, since relocating to Toronto in early 2021, in logistics planning for a mid-sized freight company. My training is in statistics. I completed my undergraduate degree at the University of Coimbra and later a postgraduate certificate in applied data science at Seneca Polytechnic, which I finished in June. I am comfortable with SQL, Python and Tableau, and I have started teaching myself dbt on my own time, mostly by rebuilding dashboards I use at work.

In my current role I maintain the weekly performance pack for four regional managers. When I took it over, it took nearly two days to assemble by hand. I automated the data pulls and introduced a validation step that flags mismatched totals before they reach anyone's inbox. Managers now receive the pack every Monday before 8 a.m., and the number of corrections issued after distribution has dropped to nearly zero. I also began sharing short tutorials with colleagues, which led to my being asked to run a monthly internal workshop on spreadsheet and dashboard practice.

I am also drawn to Northwind because of the work your team publishes on demand forecasting for smaller retailers. I have followed your research since the spring, and I particularly admired the methodology note you released in January. I share some of these posts and comments on my professional profile at @lucia.builds.data, where I write about analytics practice for people who come to the field from other disciplines.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my background in both operations and statistics could support your analytics team. I am available for an interview at any time that suits your schedule and can provide work samples on request. Thank you for considering my application.
