I'm Elena Duarte, and I was born in Rosario, a river city in Santa Fe province where the Paraná runs wide and brown past the old port. I grew up above my grandmother's bakery on a noisy corner, and I still measure most things by the smell of bread at six in the morning. At 34, I work as a civil engineer on water infrastructure projects across the Litoral region, which means I spend more time in mud boots than in conference rooms, though I'm happy to trade one for the other today.

My path into engineering was not straight. I studied at the Universidad Nacional de Rosario, then spent two years in Mendoza on a drainage study that taught me more about flash floods than any textbook. Between site visits I kept sane at Cafe Lunares, a tiny place on Calle Córdoba where the owner, Marcelo, remembers everyone's order. Much of my best thinking about sewer capacity happened over his terrible-but-lovable cortado. Last spring I also started going to the Club Atlético Ferro gym after my shifts, which has been the only reliable way I've found to stop worrying about pipe gradients.

What I care about most is making sure that when it rains in Argentina, the water goes somewhere useful and not into people's living rooms. I'll be presenting our team's findings on stormwater retention in peri-urban neighbourhoods, and I would be delighted to talk with anyone who has tried to solve the same problem. You can reach me through the conference app or at elena.duarte@ingenieria-litoral.com.ar. Thank you for having me, and I look forward to hearing what everyone is building.

When I first walked into the chemistry lab at Hartwell Grammar School in Leeds, I had no idea that a single afternoon would change how I think about medicine. Zara Okonkwo-Reid, the lab technician, had set up a titration for our Year 12 group, and I was the one who misread the burette and nearly spilled the whole flask. Instead of scolding me, she walked me through the calculation step by step, and by the end of the lesson I understood not only the chemistry but why accuracy matters to people who depend on it.

That moment stayed with me. Over the following months I volunteered on Saturday mornings at the Leeds General Infirmary, where I helped sort prescriptions and shadow the pharmacy team. I learned that a dosage error is never just a number on a page. It is a patient, a family, and a decision someone has to live with. Watching the pharmacists double-check every label, I began to see clinical work as a discipline of care as much as of science.

I am applying to study Pharmacy because I want to be the kind of practitioner who explains, not just dispenses. I have been asked to write something about my mother, and I keep starting and stopping, because she would have found all of this fuss a little embarrassing. She was the kind of woman who fed everyone who walked through the door, who remembered the names of the neighbours' dogs, and who could fix a broken hem faster than most people could find the thread. She taught me to cook by feel rather than by recipe, and she never once measured anything, which still drives me a little mad whenever I try to recreate her beans.

She loved music, especially the old samba records she played on Sunday mornings while she swept the front steps. She sang along badly and without shame, and she would wave the broom at anyone who tried to correct her. Her laughter carried through the whole house. Those mornings are the ones I think about most, the sound of the radio, the smell of coffee, the scrape of the broom on the tiles.

To those of you who knew her, thank you for your kindness over the years and for the many visits, the phone calls, and the casseroles. She was proud of her friendships and of the family she built with patience and humour. We will miss her terribly. We are grateful that we had her for as long as we did, and we will carry her stubbornness, her generosity, and her wonderfully terrible singing with us for the rest of our lives.

text:
Okay, so you know I've been dreading telling you this, but I finally want to get it off my chest. Last Thursday I got let go from Brightwater Logistics. Yeah, after almost six years. They called it a restructuring, which is corporate for "we don't need you anymore but we're too polite to say it." Marcus from HR sat on the video call with his camera slightly off-center the whole time, like he couldn't bear to look at me. I think he was more upset than I was, honestly.

The weird part is that I saw it coming, and I still wasn't ready. Back in February my manager, Dana Whitfield, started cancelling our one-on-ones and stopped answering messages in the team channel. I kept telling myself it was just busy season. Then in early March they moved all my accounts to someone in Ohio without telling me first. I found out because a client emailed me asking why I'd stopped replying. Embarrassing. I should have pushed harder for answers.

So here I am, a week later, sitting in my kitchen in Columbus, which is not where I expected to be on a Tuesday. I've been trying to keep things light online so my family doesn't panic. I posted a little something on my Instagram, @mikaela.drives.coffee, just a photo of a latte and a line about taking some time to figure out the next move. Got a bunch of sweet comments, a couple of old coworkers reached out, and one recruiter slid into my DMs before I'd even finished my first cup of coffee that morning. Not sure how I feel about that yet.

Here's what I'm trying to do now. I'm updating my résumé tonight, which I keep avoiding because it means admitting this is real. I'm also going to call my cousin Renata on Saturday, since she's worked in operations for years and always knows who's hiring. And I'm giving myself until the end of the month to be sad, angry, relieved, whatever shows up, without judging it.

Anyway, that's the update. Thanks for not making it weird when I went quiet on you. Can you come over this weekend? I'll make the good pour-over and you can help me figure out whether I should apply to the jobs that keep emailing me or just take a few weeks off. I really need someone to tell me I'm not crazy.

text:
I have been going to Brennan's Hardware on Kilmore Road in Drogheda for about six years now, and I keep coming back for one reason: Fiona behind the counter actually knows what she's talking about. I came in last Saturday, the 14th of May, with a leaking tap that I was sure needed a whole new unit. She had me look at the washer first, showed me the old one, and sent me home with a 40 cent part and a tiny bit of advice that saved me a plumber's call-out fee. That kind of honesty is rare.

The shop itself is a bit cramped and the aisles can be hard to navigate when there's a delivery in, but everything is labelled and the staff are happy to walk you to the right shelf. Prices are fair, and they will order in anything they don't stock, usually within three or four working days. I've had a garden hose fitting and a set of replacement hinges arrive exactly when promised.

Fiona also remembered my dad's name when he came in with me last week, which I found genuinely touching. There's something to be said for a shop where the staff know the regulars and treat them like neighbours rather than transactions. Several of the other customers were chatting with her about the local GAA results while they waited, which tells you a lot about the place.

If you're in Drogheda and need something fixed around the house, go to Brennan's. Ask for Fiona, tell her what's going on, and let her point you in the right direction. You can also reach the shop at info@brennanshardware.ie for special orders, though I'd recommend calling in person if you can. I wrote this review on the bus home, having just tested my new washer successfully, so I'm happy to report the tap is no longer dripping.

Five stars from a loyal customer, and I'll be back the next time something breaks, which in an old house in Drogheda is always soon.

Rosalind Okafor-Brandt has spent the better part of fifteen years moving between two worlds, and she still describes herself as a translator first and a researcher second. Born in Enugu, she trained as a nurse at the University of Nigeria before taking a post at Royal Infirmary Ashdale in 2012, where she met her closest collaborator, Heather Lindqvist, over a shared frustration with discharge paperwork. Their partnership led to the paper that first brought Rosalind's name to the wider community of clinical educators.

She now lives in Millbrook with her partner Tomas and their dog Juniper, a rescue greyhound who has opinions about every walking route in the valley. Rosalind arrived in the city on 9 April 2016, carrying two suitcases and a box of notebooks that she still refers to as her real luggage. Her friends say the move changed her teaching more than her research, and that she is at her most animated when explaining how a hospital ward looks different depending on which side of the ocean you stand on.

Rosalind is looking forward to the spring session, when she will present on bilingual patient handover. Those who know her say to expect a talk that begins with a story about a patient in Enugu and ends with a question for the audience. If you see her in the coffee queue, ask her about Juniper; she will happily tell you more than you asked for.

text:
I'm writing this down so I remember what Dr. Ferrer told me at my appointment on 14 February at the centro de salud in Valencia. My name is Olivia Brennan and I came in because of the tightness in my chest that started after my sister Marisol's wedding last month. I was worried it was my heart, the same thing that runs in our family, so I wanted to be sure before I went home.

Dr. Ferrer listened to my chest, took my blood pressure, which was a bit high but not alarming, and ordered an ECG and bloods. She said the ECG looked normal and that the tightness is most likely muscle strain and stress from the last few weeks, especially with all the wedding planning. She asked me to cut back on coffee and to walk for twenty minutes each morning, and she wants to see my blood results when they come back.

I told my husband Tomas everything when I got home, and he laughed at me for going in without him. Marisol called too and asked me to make sure I am not hiding anything. So for the record: no heart problem found today, bloods pending, follow-up booked for 28 February. If the chest pain returns or gets worse I should go to urgencias straight away, no waiting. Olivia, please remember this.

Hi everyone, long time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone here has been through something similar. I'm 34 and I live in Wrocław, in the Krzyki district near the Pilczyce side streets, and for the past few years I've been doing a lot of freelance translation work from home. Lately my younger brother Zbigniew (everyone calls him Zibi, which he hates but it stuck when we were kids) has been borrowing money from me every few weeks. Last time it was 1,500 zloty, and he promised it would be back by 12 September. It is now the 20th of September and I have not seen a single grosz.

The problem is that every time I bring it up, he gets defensive and says I'm making him feel like a criminal. My parents keep telling me to just let it go because "he's family." Zibi is also the one who called me last week from an unknown number asking to meet up, and when I called back on his number, which is 512 884 301, he didn't pick up at all. I'm starting to feel like I'm the bad guy for wanting my money back, and I honestly don't know whether to keep pushing or to cut him off for a while.

Has anyone dealt with a sibling who treats your savings like their own? How did you set boundaries without blowing up the whole family? Any advice on whether I should write him a formal message or just talk to him in person would really help. Thanks in advance, I really appreciate it.

My name is Noam, though everyone at work and most of my friends call me Nomi. I'm 34 and live in Haifa, and I've been working as a junior architect at a small firm near the port for about three years now.

The thing is, my younger brother Nadav turned 30 on May 14th and I completely forgot. I remembered at 11pm that night when I saw a photo of his party on Instagram. I sent him a message the next morning with a lame apology and a gif, and he replied with a single thumbs up. Nadav has never been dramatic, but that thumbs up hit me hard. We used to be really close, and lately it feels like we're just two guys who share a family group chat.

I've been trying to figure out whether I should send him something bigger, like a proper gift or a call, or whether that would make it awkward. Our mother says I should just let it go and show up more often. My girlfriend thinks I should own it directly and ask him to get coffee. Has anyone dealt with a sibling drifting like this? How did you rebuild things without it becoming a big thing? Any advice is welcome, thanks in advance.

I keep coming back to the same feeling this week, the one where I'm standing at the edge of something and not sure whether I want to jump or turn around. Sessions with my therapist have helped me name it. She says it's grief wearing the costume of restlessness, and I think she's right, though it's hard to admit that a move across the country, a life I chose, can still leave me feeling like I've lost something. Some mornings I wake up and the light through the shutters is so bright that I forget, for a few seconds, that anything is wrong. Then it comes back, quietly, like a tide.

What surprised me this week was how much better I felt after I stopped trying to fix everything before lunch. I went down to the harbour alone, sat on a low wall, and watched the fishing boats come in. Nobody needed anything from me. I didn't write a list. I just breathed and let my shoulders drop. My therapist would call it a small act of self-regulation, but in the moment it felt more like permission.

I want to remember that. I want to remember that the heaviness is not a verdict on my choices, and that I can hold both the longing and the gratitude without asking one of them to disappear. Tomorrow I'll try again, with less pressure. Maybe I'll swim before the sun gets too strong. Maybe I'll just sit with my coffee and let the day be what it is.

When my family left Lagos for Toronto the summer I turned sixteen, I packed three suitcases and a cardboard box of books, but I could not bring Biscuit, our old tabby, who had been my companion since I was eight. My mother called me Yemi at home, though everyone at school in Lagos knew me as Yemisi, and in Toronto I quickly learned that people could not pronounce either version without hesitating. I started answering to Yem, which felt like a small surrender and also a kind of reinvention.

My father had worked for six years as a site engineer with Adebayo & Sons Construction, and when he arrived in Canada he took a position as a project coordinator with Maple Ridge Builders in Mississauga. He missed the energy of Lagos, and he told me once that the quiet of our new street made him feel like he was waiting for something to begin. I understood him better than he expected, because I was waiting too, for a place where my accent and my habits would stop marking me as a stranger.

The first year was hard in ways I did not anticipate. My grades slipped in the winter term, and I spent long evenings in the school library reading about migration and identity, trying to find words for what I felt. Eventually I joined the debate club, where my coach, Mrs. Kowalczyk, pushed me to speak about my experiences rather than hide them. Her encouragement became the turning point that made me believe my story had value.

Since then I have worked as a tutor for newly arrived students, helping them with English essays and, just as importantly, reassuring them that confusion is part of belonging. Last June I helped a Syrian girl named Rania prepare for her entrance exam, and watching her gain confidence reminded me why I want to study education policy. You can reach me at yem.adeyemi88@mail.com if you have any questions about my application.

I do not think of my move as a loss anymore. It gave me two languages of home, two sets of memories, and a determination to build bridges between them. I hope to bring that perspective to your university, where I believe I can learn, contribute, and eventually help others find their own way across the border between who they were and who they are becoming.

I am writing this with a heavy heart to say goodbye to my father, Wilfredo "Willy" Dela Cruz, who passed away peacefully on November 9 at the age of 74 in his home in Marikina City. For those who knew him, Willy was a man of quiet habits and generous spirit. He drove his beloved silver Toyota Vios, plate number ABC 1234, to Sunday Mass every week and to the market every Wednesday, and he never once forgot to greet the vendors by name. He worked for thirty-two years as a mechanic at the Paranaque motor shop, where younger men came to him for advice long after he had retired.

As a father, Willy taught me that patience and honesty mattered more than any possession. He loved to sing old OPM ballads while fixing engines, and he kept a notebook of every song he had ever learned. Our family would gather on the balcony on November evenings, listening to him tell stories of his youth in Bulacan, and he always ended them with the same line: "Huwag kang mawalan ng loob." Do not lose heart.

When people ask me why I want to read Geography at university, I usually start with the bus. For most of my teenage years I rode the number 42 from Lenton Road to the sixth form college, and every morning I watched the city change block by block: the terraces give way to the old mill units, then the new flats, then the canal. I began to wonder who decided where things went, and why some streets felt like they had been forgotten by the people who planned the rest.

That curiosity turned into a project in Year 12. I chose Hyde Park Road, the stretch between the library and the Co-op, because I had walked it for years without ever really looking at it. Using council planning documents and a notebook full of shop counts, I mapped which businesses had opened and closed over a decade. The pattern was clearer than I expected: independent cafés came and went within eighteen months, while the chain pharmacy never moved. I presented the findings to my teacher, Mrs Adeyemi, and she encouraged me to send a short version to the local community newsletter.

The response surprised me. A woman called Marjorie Quinlan wrote back to say she had run a bakery on that same road in the 1980s and recognised the exact problem I had described: rents rose faster than footfall. We met for tea at her kitchen table in Burley, and she showed me hand-drawn maps from her own years there. Those conversations taught me that data only tells half the story, and that the people who live with the numbers hold the rest.

I now want to study human geography properly, with a focus on urban economies and the lived effects of planning decisions. I am particularly interested in modules on housing policy and spatial justice, and I hope to contribute to research that takes community knowledge as seriously as statistics.

Outside my studies I run a small photography account, @tessa.walks.leeds, where I post the streets I have documented. Many of the images are from my walks along the canal and the lanes behind Chapeltown. Each one is a reminder that a neighbourhood is never just a postcode. I came to this subject because I wanted to understand the places I call home, and I hope university will give me the tools to ask better questions about them.

Hoy me desperté temprano, todavía con el ruido de la lluvia en la ventana de mi cuarto en Rosario. Ignacio me había escrito anoche diciendo que pasaría por casa el sábado 14 de abril para ver los papeles del abuelo, así que pasé la mañana ordenando la caja de zapatos donde guardamos todo desde que él nos dejó. Encontré su partida de nacimiento de Villa Constitución, con esa letra apretada que tenía, y me quedé un rato mirándola. Mi mamá siempre dice que nació allí un 3 de marzo de 1941, en pleno invierno de otra época, y que el médico llegó en bicicleta.

Ignacio llegó a las cuatro con medialunas y un termo de mate. Hablamos de cosas tontas al principio, del equipo, del laburo, de lo cara que está la nafta, y después nos pusimos serios cuando abrimos el sobre con las fotos. Hay una de él de joven frente al almacén de la calle San Martín, con un sombrero que ahora nos hace reír. Ignacio dijo que quería llevarse una copia para su hija. Yo le dije que sí, pero que la original se queda conmigo.

Al final de la tarde me quedé sola en la cocina, con el mate frío y la caja abierta sobre la mesa. Pensé en que tenemos que volver a Villa Constitución antes de que se venda la casa de la tía Nora. Anoté en la agenda: llamar a la escribanía el martes 23 y preguntar por los plazos. Cerré el cuaderno y, por primera vez en semanas, sentí que podía respirar un poco mejor.

My name is Ivan Petrov, and I am the youngest of my father's three sons. I stand here today because Ilse, my mother, asked me to speak for the family, and because I have never once in my life said no to her. My father, Istvan, left our village in Hungary in 1979 with one suitcase, a Polish dictionary, and a stubborn belief that a man could build a second life with his hands. He arrived in Toronto on 14 December of that year, and he spent the rest of his days proving that belief right.

Ivan Petrov, as I was taught to sign my name on every school form, was always the child who asked too many questions. My father answered them all, usually while fixing something. He taught me to measure twice, to tip generously, and to never trust a man who would not look you in the eye. In the last years, when his memory began to slip, he still remembered the exact date of our first family dinner in the new apartment: 21 December 1980. He would tell that story to anyone who sat still long enough.

So I will end the way he would have wanted. Pour the slivovitz, lift the glass, and remember Istvan Petrov the way he remembered us, with a full table and an open door.

I still remember the morning my father drove me to Lincoln Preparatory Academy for the first day of my senior year. I was seventeen, nervous, and carrying a binder full of college deadlines I had color-coded for a reason I could not fully explain even to myself. What I did not expect was how much that school would come to shape the person I am becoming. My biology teacher, Ms. Halvorsen, noticed that I stayed after class every Tuesday to ask questions I was too proud to raise in front of my peers. Instead of brushing me off, she handed me a key to the lab and told me to come in whenever I wanted to run my own experiments.

That invitation changed everything. Over the following months I spent evenings in that lab measuring how quickly bean seedlings responded to different light cycles, and I learned that failure is simply data waiting to be read. When my first hypothesis collapsed on March 9, I spent the night redrawing my procedure instead of feeling sorry for myself. My results were not dramatic, but they were honest, and that honesty is what I want to bring to a university research community.

David, my younger brother, likes to tease me that I approach everything like a lab report. He is probably right. Yet the habit of asking precise questions has given me a steadiness I value more than any grade. I hope to continue that work at a university where curiosity is treated as a responsibility rather than a weakness.

text:
I want to start by thanking everyone for coming tonight, especially those of you who crossed oceans and rearranged your whole calendars to be here. Some of you have known the couple since university, some since a shared flat, and some since a chance meeting at a bus stop that turned into a lifelong friendship. I am honoured to stand here for one of the people I love most in this world.

When I first left home to build a life abroad, I did not expect how lonely the early months would be. Everything that had felt ordinary suddenly felt strange: the bread, the way people queued, the jokes that landed flat because I did not yet know the references. I spent many evenings on the phone with my family, pretending I was fine. What helped most was not grand gestures but small kindnesses from strangers who slowly became friends.

That is why I want to say something about the two of them and how they make room for others. Anyone who has ever moved countries knows that home is less a place than a set of people who make you feel expected. For a long time, the couple we celebrate tonight has been that for me. They invited me to dinners where I was the only one who did not understand the family's inside jokes, and they patiently explained each one until I laughed along.

So much of love, I have learned, is translation. It is the work of explaining yourself to someone who comes from a different background, and the patience to listen when they do the same. Watching these two do that work every day has taught me more about commitment than any book or sermon could.

To the bride and groom: may your home always have space for newcomers, for late guests, and for the old friends who arrive with stories you have heard a hundred times. May you keep learning each other's languages, both the spoken and unspoken ones. And may you never stop being each other's place to come home to.

Please raise your glasses with me. To the couple, and to love that knows no borders.

text:
We gathered today not to say goodbye to a title or a role, but to honour a person who gave so much of herself to the people around her. Anyone who knew her will tell you the same thing: she showed up. She showed up at the kitchen table when a friend needed a listening ear, at the back of the classroom when a child was struggling, and at the end of a long day with a hot meal for whoever happened to be there.

She had a way of making people feel that their small worries mattered. A question about a leaking roof, a letter that needed careful wording, a decision that kept someone awake at night, she gave each of them her full attention, as if nothing else in the world was pressing. She rarely raised her voice, but when she spoke, people leaned in to hear her.

Her patience was legendary. She could sit through an afternoon of rain without complaint, and she could wait for a slow-moving line without a sigh. More than once, those of us who were quick to hurry learned from her that some things cannot be rushed, and that kindness often needs time to take root.

She also had a wicked sense of humour. She loved a good story told badly, and she laughed loudly at her own jokes before anyone else had caught on. Those small moments of joy are what many of us will carry with us the longest, the shared laughter over a board game, the teasing about her terrible singing voice, the way she always saved the last piece of something for someone else.

If there is one thing we can take from her life, it is this: love is measured less in grand gestures than in the ordinary, repeated acts of care. She practised that love every day, and in doing so she taught all of us how to be a little more generous, a little more present, and a little more human.

Rest now. We will keep the kettle on and the door open, just as she would have wanted.

I still remember the morning we rolled into Naxos harbour, the ferry horn echoing off the whitewashed houses while I tried to keep Ptolemy, our scruffy terrier, from leaping onto a fishmonger's crate. My name is Yiannis Halvorsen, though most people in Greece call me Yanni within a day, and I had promised my sister Ilse that I would finally take the holiday she'd been nagging me about since we both finished at Ashworth Medical College. Nobody warned me that a July crossing from Piraeus would feel like sailing into an oven. Still, the Aegean looked impossibly blue, and I felt twenty years younger the moment my sandals hit the stone quay.

We spent the first three days wandering the lanes of Chora, where bougainvillea spills over every balcony and old women sit on doorsteps shelling beans and watching the tourists go by. On the twelfth of July, Ilse and I took the bus up to the Temple of Demeter, and Ptolemy, who had behaved beautifully on the ferry, decided the ancient columns were his personal racetrack. I chased him around the marble for a good ten minutes while a patient guard pretended not to notice. I still laugh thinking about it. That was also the day I got a call from Dr. Asmara Quintero at Ashworth, confirming my follow-up appointment for the twenty-sixth. I had nearly forgotten about it, and I cursed myself for letting my phone's roaming charges stop me from checking my email more often.

The real magic came with the village of Apeiranthos, perched high in the mountains, where I met a silversmith named Stelios who told me, with a wink, that his grandmother was born in the same mountain town where I was born, Ravensworth Hollow in Kent. He laughed at how small the world was. Ilse snapped a photo of us over a tiny cup of Greek coffee, and I promised to send it to him via yianni.halvorsen@mailbox-greece.net once we got back to England. He gave me a silver pendant for Ptolemy's collar, which the dog immediately tried to bury under a cushion.

We ended the trip in Plaka, watching the sun sink behind the Cycladic hills while sipping cold retsina. Ilse said it had been the best holiday of her life, and I had to agree. The island had a way of slowing down my heartbeat and reminding me that rest is not a luxury. As we boarded the ferry back to Piraeus on the twenty-second, Ptolemy stuck his head out of the window like a proud captain, and I made a silent promise to return. Greece, I have decided, is not a place you visit once; it is a place that keeps calling you back.

I am writing this statement at the request of the attending officer following the incident on Saturday 12 April at approximately 9.40pm outside my flat on Ashgrove Road, Leeds. My name is Nadia Okafor, I am 34 years old, and I work as a pharmacist at the Hollins Street branch. On the evening in question I had walked back from my sister Ruth's house with my neighbour, Callum Pryce, who lives two doors down from me and who was carrying my bag because I had hurt my wrist.

As we reached the gate, a silver hatchback with a dented rear door pulled up across the pavement. The driver, a man in a dark grey hooded top, got out and asked Callum whether he "knew where Marcus was." Callum told him he had no idea who Marcus was. The man then took hold of Callum's arm and pushed him against the railings. I shouted and my neighbour's dog, Biscuit, began barking from behind their front window, which I believe is what caused the man to get back into his car and drive off towards the Headingley end of the road.

I did not see the registration plate clearly, though I believe the last three characters were KLM. Callum has a graze on his left elbow and says he is willing to give his own account. I would be grateful if someone could follow up on the CCTV from the newsagent on the corner, which may show the vehicle. I can be contacted on 07700 900412 or at nadia.okafor@mailbox.co.uk.

Hiroshima is a city that rewards slow wandering, and on our last morning I finally took the tram out to Hijiyama Park, where a small crowd had gathered under the cherry trees. I'm Tomoko's guest here, and she had warned me that the blossoms in late March come and go within a week, so we rushed out before breakfast. Tomoko works as a senior nurse at Hiroshima Municipal Hospital, and she knew the paths better than any guidebook. Her son Takeshi, who attends Jonan Elementary School, ran ahead of us the whole time, shouting at every pigeon he could find.

We ate onigiri on a bench by the pond, and Tomoko told me how her shifts had been stretched since winter. She laughed about the nurses' station kettle, which has outlived three directors. Later, when I asked whether she planned to take leave for the spring holidays, she simply said she would go wherever the trains were quietest. I wrote her email address, tomoko.hayashi@hmh-kango.jp, on a napkin so I could send her the photos.

If you visit, go in the morning, bring more food than you think you need, and do not expect the crowds to be polite. The park is calm once the tour buses leave, and the river walk beside it is the best place to finish the day, especially when the lanterns start to flicker along the water.

My name is Dieter Hallmann, and I was born in Leipzig on 14 February 2006. For most of my life I have been the kid who fixed the family's broken radio before anyone else noticed it was broken. That habit led me, at sixteen, to volunteer at a repair café in the Südvorstadt district, where I learned that a machine taken apart carefully is almost always a machine that can be put back together. Dieter is the name my grandmother gave me, and she still insists I bring my soldering iron to every visit.

When the Hallmann family moved into our flat at Karl-Heine-Strasse 47, 04229 Leipzig, I decided to build a small weather station on the balcony. The sensors cost less than a week of my part-time wages at the bakery, so I designed the enclosure myself and printed it at the school makerspace. The first readings were wrong by almost four degrees, and that error taught me more about calibration than any textbook. Dieter, my younger brother, still reminds me that the station once recorded snow in July.

I am applying to your engineering programme because I want to work on problems where precision matters to people's daily lives. My passport number, D4K7R2901, is listed on my registration form, and my email is dieter.hallmann@mailbox.de should you need anything further. I hope to bring the same patience to your laboratories that I brought to a broken radio and an uncooperative balcony sensor.

When I started volunteering at the Kauri Bay community garden in Whangarei, I did not expect it to change how I think about my own future. My first real friend there was Wiremu Parata, a retired surveyor who had given up his Saturdays to teach teenagers how to compost and read soil. Wiremu had a habit of asking questions I couldn't answer, and over the months I found myself chasing those answers in library books and late-night reading. By June of my second year, I had helped plant the winter brassicas and had started keeping a notebook of rainfall and frost dates, which Wiremu said was the first useful data the garden had collected in a decade.

The garden is also where I learned that community work is rarely glamorous. Some mornings it was just me and Wiremu hauling mulch from the depot on Maunu Road, arguing about whether the kale needed more lime. Other days we would stop for flat whites at Harbourside Roasters before heading back to sort seedlings. Those small rituals taught me patience, and they showed me that a place can be held together by ordinary people who keep showing up.

When I think about what I want to study at university, I think about that notebook. I want to understand the systems behind everyday things, like why one paddock drains and the next one floods, and to use that understanding to help communities make better decisions about the land they depend on. Wiremu once told me that a good surveyor leaves a trail anyone can follow. I hope my own work can do the same.

My name is Thomas, and I am Ada's older brother. Ada was 74 when she died on January 9th, in the house on Maple Street where we grew up. For most of her life she was the person everyone called when something needed fixing, whether it was a leaky faucet, a sick neighbor, or a kid who needed a ride home from practice. She never asked for thanks, and she rarely got it in the way she deserved.

When our mother got sick, Ada moved back to Ohio to take care of her, and she didn't complain once. She learned how to change the IV line, how to read the pharmacy labels, and how to sit with a frightened woman at three in the morning and make her laugh. Ada's daughter Megan, who was just nineteen then, watched her mother do all of it and told me later that she learned more about courage from that year than from anything else.

Ada loved crossword puzzles, bad detective shows, and the Cincinnati Reds, even in the seasons when there was nothing to cheer about. If you ever visited her kitchen, you left with a plate of something warm. I will miss her voice on the phone every Sunday, and I know many of you will too. Thank you all for being here to say goodbye to my sister.

STATEMENT OF WITNESS

I, Vanessa Ruatapu, make this statement about the incident I witnessed on Saturday 14 May at approximately 9:40 pm outside 42 Tennyson Street, Island Bay, Wellington. I am 34 years old and I currently work as a radiographer at Wellington Hospital, where I have been employed for six years. I live with my partner two doors down from the address mentioned.

On the evening in question I had walked my dog along the footpath towards Shelly Bay Road. As I reached the corner, I noticed a silver Toyota Corolla, registration plate KLT 482, parked with its hazard lights on. A young man in a dark grey Canterbury hoodie was standing beside the driver's door, speaking loudly into his phone. I did not recognise him at that point, though I have since been told by a neighbour that his name is Tane Whakaari.

As I passed, the man turned and asked whether I had seen anyone run past. I said no. He then said, "Just tell Tane's mum I'm fine, I'll sort it out tomorrow." I thought this was an odd thing to say to a stranger, so I looked back and saw him get into the passenger seat of the car while another man, shorter and wearing a navy cap, got into the driver's seat. The car then pulled away quickly towards the Island Bay shops.

I went home and told my partner, Ross, what I had seen. He suggested I contact the police. I did not have a phone number for the local station so I checked the website and found the non-emergency line. I was advised to come in and give a formal statement, which is why I am here today, Friday 20 May.

I can add that I have no connection to either man and no dispute with anyone on the street. I am willing to provide any further information, including my phone number, 021 555 0148, and my email address, vanessa.ruatapu@xtra.co.nz, if the officer needs to follow up. I understand this statement may be used in court and I confirm that everything written here is true to the best of my knowledge.

Signed: Vanessa Ruatapu

text:
I'm thrilled to share that after nine wonderful years, I've stepped away from my role at Harbourline Logistics in Wellington and taken up a new position as Operations Lead with Kōwhai Freight in Christchurch. It's a big move, both professionally and personally, and I wanted to take a moment to reflect on it.

When I joined Harbourline, I was fresh out of university and not entirely sure what I wanted. Frank, my old flatmate, used to say I'd never sit still long enough to find out. He was half right. I did sit still for a while, but I learned more in those nine years than I ever expected: how to keep a warehouse running through a storm, how to talk a driver down from a bad day, and how to build a team that actually trusts each other. The people there, from the dock crew to the finance team, made every hard week worth it.

The decision to leave wasn't easy. Wellington has been home for most of my adult life. I have my favourite coffee spot on Cuba Street, a Saturday routine at Mojo Coffee in Newtown, and a gym at Fitzroy Street Strength that has kept me sane through more stressful quarters than I care to count. Leaving those rituals behind felt strange. But when Kōwhai came calling with a role that combined ownership of a regional network with the chance to grow a new team from scratch, I couldn't say no.

Christchurch is already teaching me new things. The rebuild has created a city full of energy, and the business community here is generous with its time. I've been meeting people for coffee at Cafe Gamma and Hargreaves Street, and I'm slowly learning the local shortcuts that make the commute work.

To anyone reading this who is weighing a similar move: take the leap if the work excites you and the people feel right. You'll miss what you leave behind, but you'll also find out how much you're capable of. I'm grateful to everyone at Harbourline who helped me get here.

If you're in Christchurch and fancy a catch-up, send me a message. I'd love to hear what you're working on.

text:
I've been going to Maple & Rye on Dundas Street West for about three years now, and I finally sat down to write something about it after last Saturday. My name is Lauren and I live a few blocks over in Little Portugal, so this is pretty much my local. The place is small, maybe twelve tables if you count the two-top by the window, and the staff know most of the regulars by name. That is probably the biggest thing I'd tell anyone thinking about trying it.

Last Saturday, February 14, I came in around 11 with my sister Lily, who was visiting from Halifax. We ordered the smoked trout toast and the brown butter pancakes, and both arrived hot and well portioned. The trout was properly cured, not that rubbery stuff you get at chains, and the pancakes weren't drowning in syrup. Our server, a guy named Tomas, recommended the cardamom latte when I said I wanted something less sweet, and he was right. The coffee is roasted by a small outfit in Hamilton and you can taste it.

The one real complaint is the wait. We got there before the rush and still waited nearly forty minutes for a table, even though there were empty seats at the bar. I understand they don't take reservations for parties under six, but a little more communication would have gone a long way. Somebody came around with a clipboard and a sincere apology, which helped, but I'd like to see them use a buzzer system.

Prices are fair for the neighbourhood. Two entrees, two drinks and a shared side came to roughly ninety dollars before tip, which feels right for a weekend brunch in this part of the city. The menu changes seasonally, so the pancakes I loved might be gone by the time you read this, but the owners post every update on their Instagram, which is @maplerye_brunch if you want to keep up. They also post honest photos of the daily specials, not the airbrushed kind.

Bottom line: four stars. It's cozy, the food is consistently good, and the team clearly cares. Fix the waiting system and it would be five. I'll be back next month, probably on a weekday, because I already know Tomas will remember my order.

Her garden was the envy of the street, and her tomatoes were the only ones my father would eat without complaint.

She is survived by her children, Ruth, Ben, and me, along with five grandchildren and her faithful companion, a gray tabby named Pickles, who has been sitting by the front window every afternoon since the funeral. Antoine Lefebvre passed away peacefully at home on the 14th of January, at the age of 78, surrounded by the people who loved him most. For forty years he ran the small bookbinding workshop off Rue des Tanneurs in Lyon, where generations of local readers brought him their worn volumes and left with something almost new. He had a dry wit, an unshakeable opinion on every French cheese, and a habit of humming Piaf while he worked. Those of us who knew him will remember his patience with apprentices and his gift for making everyone feel they had been expected.

He is survived by his wife, Marguerite, and their son, Julien, who will miss his father's steady hand at the bench and his Sunday lunches more than he can say. Antoine's old friend and business partner, Bernard Dubois, spent every Thursday evening with him over chess and a bottle of Côtes du Rhône, and has asked that we keep the second chair at the table empty for a while. Their yellow Labrador, Biscuit, has been pacing the hallway since the morning and will need a little extra love in the weeks ahead.

Antoine, we will keep the workshop light on for you. Thank you for every book you saved and every friend you gathered along the way. Rest well, old friend. Your absence fills the room, but your craftsmanship will sit on shelves across the neighbourhood for many years to come.

Louise Moreau

Hey, I still can't stop thinking about what happened at the bakery last week. You know the one near the tram stop, the place with the cramped little tables? I went in just to grab a coffee before work, and the woman behind the counter, who I've seen every morning for ages, looked up and actually remembered my order. It sounds small, but after the rough winter I've had, it genuinely made my whole day. I sat by the window with my pretzel and watched people hurry past in their heavy coats, and for once I didn't feel like I was rushing through my own life.

That got me thinking about how much we underestimate those little routines. Some mornings I'd dread getting out of bed, but the walk through the park and that familiar bell over the door gave me something to look forward to. I'm not saying everything's fixed, because it isn't, but there's a steadiness in those ordinary moments that I'd forgotten about. Honestly, I think I needed the reminder more than I realised.

So that's my update. Wendy would tell you I've been overthinking things again, and she's probably right. Anyway, next time you're in town, let's go there together. I'll buy you the pretzel and we can talk properly over a long, lazy breakfast. I really miss our conversations, and I'd love to catch up on everything you've been up to.

I am Aditya Raman, and for the past eleven years I have worked as a data engineer at Vantage Lattice Solutions in Pune. Most mornings I take the metro from my flat in Kothrud to our office in Hinjewadi, though on rainy days I give in and book a cab. People often assume that a career in software means a life lived entirely behind a screen, and while there is some truth to that, I have always tried to keep one foot in the physical world. Pune has been generous that way. The hills, the old lanes near Deccan, and the steady hum of its tech corridors have all shaped how I think about my work and my community.

My journey into data began almost by accident. As an undergraduate in Nagpur I was fascinated by how small patterns in messy information could reveal something meaningful about people. That curiosity led me to a internship at a logistics firm, where I spent a summer building pipelines that tracked delivery routes across Maharashtra. I remember the first time a dashboard I had built helped a dispatcher avoid a costly delay. It was a modest win, but it convinced me that technical work could have a very human impact.

Outside the office, I am fortunate to have a close circle of friends who keep me grounded. My closest colleague and friend, Sanjana Iyer, has been my partner in more late-night debugging sessions than I can count. We share a love of long walks around Kothrud Lake and an unreasonable enthusiasm for filter coffee. Together we have mentored a small group of junior engineers, and watching them grow has been one of the most rewarding parts of my career.

Home life is quieter but no less important. My golden retriever, Mango, greets me at the door every evening with more enthusiasm than my day usually deserves. He has become something of a neighbourhood celebrity on our lane in Kothrud, and he has taught me more about patience than any management course ever did. Whenever a project feels overwhelming, I remind myself to slow down, take him out, and let the evening air reset my perspective.

If you would like to discuss data quality, team mentoring, or the realities of building analytics in fast-growing Indian cities, I am always happy to talk. When I was nine, my family moved into a small rental on Maple Grove Avenue in the Eastside neighborhood of Columbus, Ohio, and that address became the first place I learned to map the world on my own terms. My name is Avery Lindqvist, and for most of my childhood I was the kid who rode the same three bus routes every morning, counting stops and memorizing the way the city fit together. My mother drove a 2009 Honda Civic with the plate reading KRT 4471, and on the long Saturday errands across town I would sit in the passenger seat with a paper map open across my knees, calling out turns before the GPS could.

That habit turned into something larger when I joined the neighborhood transit survey my middle school ran in November. Our team canvassed the apartments along Maple Grove and the blocks near Hudson Street, and we found that nearly a third of families there had no reliable way to reach the grocery store without a two-hour round trip. I wrote the summary report, and when the city council read it in late November, Avery Lindqvist was listed as its author, a sentence I still carry with me.

Today I want to study urban geography because I believe the most important maps are the ones drawn by people who actually live in the spaces they describe. Every number on a planning document represents a street I have walked, a bus I have missed, and a neighbor who taught me that a route is only as good as the person who can ride it. I hope to bring that same attention to every project I take on.

text:
I landed at Ben Gurion on a Tuesday evening in March and by the time I had collected my hire car I was already running late for the drive north. The rental agreement had my name on it, Jonah, and a booking reference that was really just a string of letters and numbers I kept re-reading on my phone, but the car itself was the part I had to remember: a small white Hyundai with the plate 74-512-39 stuck on a little paper sticker in the glovebox so I could tell the attendant which one was mine. The roads out of the airport were quieter than I expected, and the lights of Tel Aviv spread out to my left like someone had spilled a box of sequins across the coast.

The next morning I met my friend Jordan at a bakery in Jaffa, the old port town where the streets bend back on themselves and every doorway seems to have a cat asleep in it. Jordan had been living in Haifa for two years and insisted I try the sabich there, so we took the coastal road up in his battered Peugeot, windows down, the sea glinting on our right the whole way. We talked about everything and nothing, and by the time we reached the Carmel ridge the afternoon had gone soft and gold. If you ever find yourself in the north in March, go slowly. The wildflowers come out in patches along the hillsides and the light makes everything look like a painting that hasn't quite dried.

By the end of the week I had a small notebook full of scribbled addresses, phone numbers I would probably never use, and a long list of places I had promised myself I would return to. Jordan drove me back to the airport on the Sunday, and I remember thinking how strange it is that a country can feel both enormous and intimate at once. I will be back, and next time I will leave the car keys somewhere I can actually find them.

When I was eleven, my grandmother taught me to bake bread in the old oven in our apartment in Haifa, the one that ran hot on the left side and never quite on the right. She would tell me to watch the crust instead of the clock, and I think that lesson stuck with me more than any math problem I have solved since. Zohar was the name my parents gave me, after a book my father loved, and I have spent most of my life trying to live up to the quiet, careful person it describes.

My days now are split between the school bus, a part-time shift at the library on Herzl Street, and the robotics club that meets in the basement of the community centre. Robotics is where I learned that failure is not the opposite of progress but usually its first draft. Last year our team built a line-following robot that worked perfectly on the practice mat and then drove straight off the table during the regional competition. I remember standing there, feeling my face burn, and thinking that everyone would remember the fall more than the design. We rebuilt the sensor array that night, and the following October we placed third in the national round.

The library has taught me something different. Most afternoons I help elderly patrons learn to use the catalogue terminals and access digital newspapers. One man, a retired engineer who comes in every Tuesday, once asked me why anyone would bother reading a physical book when everything was online. I did not have a good answer then. I have one now: a book asks you to slow down in a way a screen rarely does, and that slowness is where I do my best thinking.

I am applying to your programme in environmental engineering because I want to work on water. Growing up in a city where every drop is measured, I became interested in how communities plan for scarcity and how technology can make that planning fairer. I have started a small project with two classmates to map rainwater collection on the rooftops of our neighbourhood, and we have reached out through our account @zohar.hydro_haifa to share our findings with local residents. The response has been modest but encouraging, and it has shown me that engineering is at its best when it listens.

I know that my path is not a straight line, and I do not expect one. What I bring is a habit of returning to problems after they have humbled me, and a willingness to ask the people affected what they actually need. I hope to bring that habit to your university, to learn alongside people whose experiences differ from mine, and to contribute to a future in which the water we depend on is shared more wisely.

Okay so, this is me just talking into my phone while I walk back from the market, so bear with me if it's all over the place. So I got here last week and honestly the heat is something else, like you step outside and it just hits you. But the food, oh my god, I've been eating these tamales from a lady on the corner every morning and I think I might be a little addicted now. Don't tell anyone, it's embarrassing.

Anyway, the thing I wanted to actually tell you about is the bus situation. I thought I'd figured it out, I had like a little map and everything, and then the bus just didn't come, or it came and was already packed so full people were hanging off the door. Which, fine, that's just how it works here I guess. I've kind of stopped being annoyed about it and started just walking more, which is honestly nicer when it's not the middle of the day.

So the people here have been really nice to me, which I did not expect at all. Like the guy who runs the little shop downstairs from where I'm staying, he always asks how I'm doing and then tries to teach me a new word every time I buy water. My Spanish is still terrible, like I can order food and say thank you and that's about it, but everybody is so patient with me. I'm trying to practice more, I've got an app going and I talk to myself a lot, which I'm sure the neighbours think is weird.

I also went to this little plaza yesterday evening where there were kids playing soccer and old men playing chess and some musicians just sort of wandering around. I just sat on a bench for like two hours and watched everything. It was the most relaxed I've felt in months, which is kind of wild to say given that I'm literally in a new country where I don't really know anyone yet.

Okay, I think I'm almost back, I can see the building. Ugh, the stairs are going to kill me. Anyway, I'll send you more soon, maybe a proper message when I'm sitting down and not sweating through my shirt. Miss you, tell everyone I said hi. Bye bye.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Tom, Charlotte's older brother, and I've been given the job of telling you a few things about my sister that she would rather I didn't. Charlie has been my partner in crime since the day she was born, which is a polite way of saying she has been finding ways to get me into trouble for thirty-one years.

I still remember the first time Charlie decided she was going to be a lawyer. She was nine, she had a school tie borrowed from our dad, and she spent the whole of Sunday lunch cross-examining Nan about why she couldn't have a second slice of pavlova. Nan lost that argument. Nan loses most arguments to Charlie, and she has never once minded.

When Charlie met Daniel, I'll be honest, I was suspicious. Anyone who wants to spend their weekends hiking up Mount Wellington in the rain and calling it fun is either brave or slightly unwell. Dan turned out to be both, and somewhere along the way he became the brother I didn't have to be jealous of. He knows how to make Charlie laugh until she snorts, and he knows when to just hand her a cup of tea and sit beside her.

The two of them bought their first place together on Cormorant Avenue in Newtown, a little terrace with a wonky back fence and a fig tree that has never once produced fruit. They have spent every weekend since trying to fix one or the other. Charlie insists the fig tree is just shy. Dan says it's been hiding from her renovation plans. I think it's the most Charlie thing in the world that she would argue with a tree.

So please raise your glasses. Charlie, Dan, you have always been good for each other, and we are so lucky to be standing here celebrating you. Mum is already crying, so I'm going to sit down before I join her. Cheers to the happy couple.

text:
I wanted to write this review because Yasmin Okafor, who runs the front counter at Harbourline Cycle & Repair, went well above what I expected last Saturday. I came in around 10 a.m. with a bent rear wheel after hitting a pothole on Bathurst near the lakeshore. The shop is at 418 Queen's Quay Lane in Hamilton, tucked behind the old bakery, so it's easy to walk past if you don't know it's there.

Yasmin took one look at the wheel, asked a few questions about how I'd been riding it, and told me straight away that the rim was salvageable but the spokes on one side were badly loosened. She didn't push me toward a new wheelset, which I half expected. Instead she quoted a price for a true-and-tension job and said she'd have it ready by two o'clock if I could wait. I did, and I spent the time browsing the used parts bin, which is well organized and fairly priced.

When I came back, Yasmin walked me through what had been done and showed me the spoke tension on each side with a tension meter. She explained that the wheel would need another check after about 100 kilometres because new spokes settle. That kind of honesty is rare. Her colleague Teodor, who handles most of the mechanical work, was also friendly and didn't rush me, even though the shop was busy with the December tune-up rush.

A few small notes: the shop is cash-friendly but takes cards, parking on the lane is limited so arrive early on weekends, and the waiting area is small. Bring a book or plan to browse. I've also seen the shop listed on a community bike co-op's website, so if you're a member you may get a discount on labour.

If you've got a wheel that's out of true, or any drivetrain trouble, I'd recommend Harbourline without hesitation. Ask for Yasmin, tell her Dale sent you, and be prepared to leave with a bike that rides better than when you walked in.

Hey Emily, you asked me to tell you properly what happened with the flat, so here it is. I'd been living at 14 Elmwood Terrace in Leeds for nearly six years, and the landlord, a man called Graham Pritchard, decided in January he wanted to sell. He gave us notice and I spent weeks trawling Rightmove at night. In the end I found a place near Headingley, and the agent asked me for everything: proof of ID, my passport number, the usual. I had to scan my passport twice because the first one came out blurry, which was a nightmare at eleven o'clock on a Tuesday.

The signing was booked for 14 February, Valentine's Day, which Mum thought was hilarious. I rang the agent, Sophie Lyle, on the Monday to confirm, and she said to email any last documents to sophie.lyle@haywardandbrooke.co.uk before ten. I nearly missed it because my phone kept dropping signal in the lift at work. Still, I got it sent, and on the day I walked in with a coffee and a folder and signed everything in about twenty minutes.

So I've got the keys now, and the new address is 27 Ashworth Gardens, LS6 3PQ, which I've already had to write on about nine forms. Honestly it's a bit of a relief. The kitchen is tiny but the window looks over a park, and there's a bakery across the road that smells incredible at seven in the morning. Come round when you're back from Glasgow and I'll make you a proper cup of tea in my actual mugs, not the ones from the old place that I had to fight with the removal men over.

Wandering the alleys of Jaffa with my friend Pini, who everyone at Hadar Logistics calls "Pinchi", I finally understood why people fall in love with this city. We ended the day with falafel on December 14th, and I still can't stop thinking about it.

My name is Shira Levi, and I was lucky enough to be Sagi's older sister for thirty-four years. Most of you knew him as the man who ran the early Saturday group at Kafe Hadar on Dizengoff, who could talk a stranger into a second espresso and a long conversation about football. Some of you knew him from Maccabi Tel Aviv's fan chats, where he went by SagiTheSpur on Instagram, and where he once argued with me for three days straight about whether a bagel counts as bread. He was loud, he was generous, and he never once forgot a birthday.

Sagi worked for nearly a decade at Tahal Software in Herzliya, first as a junior tester and later leading the team that rebuilt their scheduling platform. He used to say the job taught him patience, but I think the truth is he simply loved solving problems that other people had given up on. He would come home from the office, eat standing up in the kitchen, and then spend another two hours helping a neighbour's kid with physics. That was Sagi. He never kept a good thing to himself.

On the morning of December 14th, he went for his usual run along the Yarkon, and he waved at the old man who sells newspapers by the bridge, the same way he did every day. I want that to be the last thing we remember about him: a wave, a smile, and someone who always made room for everyone else. We will miss you more than words can hold, Sagi. Yehi zichro baruch.

I'll admit I nearly didn't book the guesthouse in Dingle after the email came through with the wrong postcode, but Victoria Keane, who runs the place with her brother, was patient with me on the phone and sorted it out in minutes. My name is Vanessa Doyle, and I'm writing this from the back room at 14 Strand Road, Dingle, Co. Kerry, which has the best view of the harbour I've had on any trip so far. If you want to ring ahead, the number is 066 915 2287, though Victoria mostly answers messages on Instagram under @vickeane_dingle, where she posts photos of the morning fishing boats coming in.

I'm originally from Ennis, so the drive down the Wild Atlantic Way felt like coming home in a strange, rewritten way. Victoria recommended I leave early on the 14th of September, before the coaches arrived, and she was right: I had the cliffs at Slea Head almost to myself, with only a few sheep and a very confident robin for company. Lunch was a bowl of chowder at a pub on the pier, and the woman serving it asked where I'd come from before I'd even sat down, which is the kind of welcome you only get in small towns.

If you go in September, pack a proper waterproof, because the weather changes three times before lunch, and bring a notebook for the little things Victoria tells you over breakfast. Dingle is quiet by then, the hikes are clear, and the pints taste better when the evenings start to cool. I already have the next trip planned for the end of the month.

Okay, so you asked how I ended up in that mess with the landlord in Valencia, and I think I finally have the energy to tell it. My name is Pablo Ferrer, I'm thirty-four, and back in April I was supposed to be moving out of the flat on Calle de Sueca by the 12th. Instead, I spent the whole week chasing a deposit that Mr. Navarro swore he'd already sent. I kept emailing him from pablo.ferrer88@gmail.com, copying in the agency, and getting nothing but silence and a single "we'll see".

What really got me was the morning of April 9th, when I sat in the little café near Ruzafa with my laptop and a cortado, rereading every message like a detective. Pablo, my brother-in-law, kept telling me to just let it go, but I'm stubborn, you know that. I'd already booked the removal van for the 14th, so there was no room to be patient. I actually cried a bit into my coffee, which was embarrassing, and the waiter pretended not to notice.

In the end the money turned up on the 13th, a day early, thanks to a single phone call from the agency's office manager, Lucía, who was far more helpful than anyone else in the whole saga. I still think about how close it came to going badly. Anyway, I'm buying the drinks next time, and you're not allowed to laugh at the cortado incident.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Paloma, and I've had the honour of being Marisol's older sister for thirty-one years now, which means I have also been her unpaid editor, her driver, and occasionally her alarm clock. Tonight I get to be the one who talks, and I have been practising this speech in the car for a week, mostly in the traffic around Colonia Roma, so if I sound a little rushed, blame the Insurgentes at rush hour.

Marisol has always been the person who notices things. When we were kids in Coyoacán, she was the one who saw the stray dog waiting outside the bakery every morning and quietly started leaving bread for it, long before anyone else thought to. That is Marisol. She sees the small thing that needs doing and she does it, without a speech and without wanting any credit. So when she told me that Gabriel had spent three months quietly learning the names of every street vendor on his block, I was not surprised at all. I was just relieved she had finally found someone who pays that kind of attention too.

Gabriel, I want to say something to you directly. You came into our family at a moment when my mother was still getting used to the idea that her youngest daughter would be living in another neighbourhood. You never tried to take anyone's place. Instead you asked my mother for her tamale recipe, got it wrong twice, and asked again. Your brother Mateo told me you once drove four hours to help a friend move a sofa, and then complained the whole way back that the sofa was ugly. That, I think, is a good sign.

To Marisol and Gabriel, may your life together be full of ordinary Tuesdays that turn out to be better than you planned. And if either of you ever needs me, you know my number is 55 4821 9073, though I would ask that you call during daylight hours. Please raise your glasses. Salud to the two of you.

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for Victoria Lindqvist, who worked under my supervision as a senior nurse coordinator at Mercy Lakeside Hospital from March 2019 until she accepted a position elsewhere in late January of this year. My name is Gregory Whitfield, and I served as the Director of Nursing for the medical-surgical division for nearly nine years. In that time I came to know Victoria as one of the most capable and steady clinicians on our floor.

Victoria joined us after completing her Bachelor of Science in Nursing at the University of Minnesota Duluth, and she quickly distinguished herself. During her first year she volunteered to lead our discharge planning initiative, which had been struggling with long delays and missed follow-up appointments. Within six months, Victoria had redesigned the workflow, trained eleven staff members on the new process, and reduced average discharge delays by more than a third. She approached the work with patience and a clear sense of accountability that I rarely see in people with less experience.

What I valued most about Victoria, however, was her character under pressure. During the winter surge in January of last year, when our census ran well above capacity and several colleagues were out sick, she never once lost her composure. She stayed late to cover gaps, mentored newer nurses through difficult admissions, and made sure that patients and families felt heard even when conditions were chaotic. Several families wrote to our administration specifically to praise her compassion, and I have kept those letters in my personal file.

Victoria is also a dependable collaborator. She worked closely with physicians, pharmacists, social workers, and our respiratory therapy team, and she was known for communicating clearly and directly. When disagreements arose, she addressed them professionally and focused on what was best for the patient. Her reputation across the hospital reflected this, and she was frequently asked to represent our unit on interdisciplinary committees.

I recommend Victoria without reservation for any clinical leadership role in which she would be responsible for a team and for patient outcomes. Should you require further information, you may reach me at gwhitfield@mercylakesidehealth.org, or contact our human resources office, referencing her employee file. Thank you for considering her application.

Sincerely,

Gregory Whitfield
Director of Nursing, Medical-Surgical Division
Mercy Lakeside Hospital
National ID on file: 482913067
